Question: My iPhone 12 Pro battery health has dropped to 91% in 8 months. It’s dropping by 1-2% every month. Should I be concerned?
Answer: It's entirely dependent on how many times you fully charge it. An iPhone battery is good for about 500 full charges. So if you run down to 0% each day, you can charge about 500 times before you need a new battery. If you put it on your power adapter at 50% charge each night, it should last 1,000 half charges. An LCO battery — by industry standard — is considered “used up” when it can only charge to 80% of the original charge level, which as said is after about 500 full charges. Doing that math, you can expect the battery “health" to drop by 1% every 25 full charges. Drop that bad boy on your power adapter near dead every night and you can certainly expect to lose a point or two each month. Some Li-ion formula, such as NMC, NCA, and LPF batteries have a longer cycle life, and are still reasonably viable when they’re down to 70% of their charge capacity. These are not used in portable electronics because they have a lower specific energy, and the big push among smartphone makers is device runtime, not battery longevity. You might note, if you followed the link, that Apple’s warranty is 500 cycles for iPhones for 1,000 cycles for everything else they make. They could be using alternate battery chemistries in iPads, MacBooks, and Apple Watches, or they could be short-cycling LCO batteries so they never charge beyond 80%. Most portable power tools use LMO batteries, which optimize specific power, not energy, and have a much shorter battery cycle life, probably around 300 cycles. Read More

Question: Obama liked to use Twitter, but had to stop when he became President (for security reasons, we were told). Why is Trump still able to tweet?
Answer: In the case of Obama, it’s an easy answer: Obama loved his Blackberry and wanted to keep using it, or at least, some kind of secure mobile phone. Now, in 2008, the NSA still hadn’t worked out a proper secure cellular phone system (the NSA is responsible for government security standards). But Obama insisted on having a secure mobile phone, and Presidents generally get what they want. So the NSA outfitted a BlackBerry 8830 World Edition with a whole mess of security enhancements.[1]No iPhone, either. [2] They actually made ten of these, they could only make encrypted calls, and there were ten of them. They could only call each other. No Angry Birds, no Twitter. At the time, only a select few advisors got these phones, being limited. The NSA absolutely did not want the “hardened Blackberry” to become a standard, because, while secure, it wasn’t secure enough. You can, in fact, test for just how secure a device can be. I’ve spend many, many hours in test labs having my hardware designed examined and occasionally sent back to the drawing board over this sort of thing. In his second term, Obama replaced that Blackberry with an Android phone running the NSA’s own version of Android, called Security Enhanced Android (SE Android), based on the NSA’s SE Linux. The first of these was a modified Samsung Galaxy S4, made easier on the NSA because Samsung based their “KNOX” security technology on SE Android.[3] While the phones can access the internet over standard cellular radio, it’s always connecting via VPN to a government server. There’s no direct access to the Internet. No Angry Birds. No Twitter. No camera. There are some apps, but only available from a government server. Since other government workers can get these, they’re not as limited as the secure Blackberry was. And it’s technically possible for a VoIP call, routed to a government server, could be relayed outside of the protection of the VPN. But that’s controlled by the security folks, not the phone’s user. There may have been some kind of secure iPhone in the White House as well, but I don’t know the details. The NSA did publish a set of guidelines for regular folks in government using smartphones,[4] [5] but those are not sufficient for anyone working in classified information. I Naturally, all of the security features available to President Obama were available to Trump when he took office. He kept tweeting simply because he ignored the security protocols that are in place to protect sensitive data, and while every security agency in the USA can ask the President to do the right thing, they can’t force him (or her). Trump claims he was given a secure cellphone, and that makes perfect sense. But he also apparently had iPhones [6] … otherwise, no mobile tweets. It’s pretty obvious. He used one phone which had been a bit secured, for tweeting and reading a select set of news web sites. It apparently had been set up to disallow access beyond a set of internet destinations. He made calls on the other iPhone, dubbed his “burner” phone, which was far easier than on the secure phone to anyone not also on the secure system… and because he didn’t necessarily want to leave a record of who he was calling. Just like he stopped keeping records of who visited the White House. According to the security experts, Trump was never alone on a call. [7]When you have government level resources and a specific target, it’s not that difficult to intercept phone calls with consumer-grade encryption. Trump was of course informed of this, but since he had already made his decision, he’s not the sort of guy who admits he’s wrong… ever. Most of us trust the systems in place because they’re handy, because they’re difficult for the average crook to hack, and because we’re simply not big targets. That said, for work-related things, I’m going through a VPN most of the time, which adds another layer of encryption over VoIP calls, texts, etc. It’s not even necessary to hack the phone itself, though that’s possible. It’s far more effective to crack the neworks in use, and as well, target not just Trump but the people he’s calling. While it’s not known how much Trump personally used email or other messaging — he reportedly didn’t like anything that left a record, thus his lack of interest in his secure phone, which does. However, much of his Administration used private (not-secure) email[8][9] and WhatsApp (a private texting system bought by Meta in 2014 for $19 billion)[10] [11] in order to avoid the Presidential Records Act, which requires all official communications to be archived. WhatsApp provides consumer-level security, and it’s been a popular app for Presidential campaigns, having been used by both Trump and Biden staffers… and recently hacked in that use, too. [12] It’s telling that the Trump Administration blatantly and intentionally did what he accused Hillary Clinton of doing with her email (though the investigations found lax security practices but no actual crimes). Question: I fired an employee when I learned she voted for Trump. Is this illegal?
Answer: Not likely... though she might have a legitimate complaint if you bullied her into revealing her voting history. And you can thank the Republicans for that. Nearly all work positions are “at will” employment, though of course, if you’re actually a boss with employees, I think you’re know the laws of your state before firing anyone, but Montana is the only state in the union that’s doesn’t allow at-will employment. There are some variations in the law based on the specific state, since these are all state-level laws. Regardless. “at will” employment means that an employer can fire a person for anything that’s not strictly a Federally defined protected class. In general, you can’t fire a person for “what they are”: female, LGBTQIA, black, pregnant, disabled, age, nationality, etc, and some case also “things you choose,” like marital status, union membership, or religion, for example. Some states will have additional protected classes over an above those defined at the Federal level, but they can’t eliminate a Federal class. An employer can fire an employee for just about anything else: their work ethic, their politics (assuming of course they make that known, particularly if they’re outspoken about it in the workplace), their physical appearance, their “attitude,” their educational level, their criminal history, and of course, their lack of US citizenship or work authorization, etc. Or for now reason at all! And the employer does not have to tell the employee why they were fired. One exception has been many classes of Federal Government employees. But the Republicans plans for 2025 include changing the status of hundreds of thousands of government employees to at-will, which would allow them to be fired over their political affiliation, or “just because.” Note that at-will employment isn’t a law, but rather, a series of legal decisions that arose from the courts after the Civil War. After slavery had been banned, powerful employers such as the Railroads looked for still-legal means of enforcing their will over their workers. Railroads had previously used slaves, former slaves, and bonded immigrants for labor, and got away with often brutal treatment of such workers. The argument was that, as workers could quit anytime they liked without reason, employers ought to have the same ability to fire them. Courts agreed, without any regard to the vastly different power dynamic between worker and employer. Read More

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Can I add my brain power and become more intelligent than I was born with?
Answer: Given the usual context of the word, no, you can’t become more intelligent. The standard definition, anyway, is that intelligence is basically what you arrive with. Your innate mental acuity. But fret not, because there are other, far more useful measures of mental acuity. You might think of intelligence as a potential, but not necessarily a potential everyone takes advantage of. And just like building muscles, just like playing music, spending an effort to accumulate knowledge, learning to apply that knowledge, affects your smarts or, less awkwardly put, your wits — your functional mental acuity. As intelligence is innate, your wits are the combination of your intelligence, your knowledge, and your ability to put the two together. Let me illustrate in another area: physicality. I just put this image up in a chat with my three sisters a few minutes ago. This is our Uncle Collin, our Dad’s older brother. My niece Jorah probably looked the gymnastic equivalent of this at her peak in gymnastics, but my sisters, me, my kids do not look like Uncle Collin. Though my daughter Kira’s in really good shape, as a runner. That’s the potential. I’ll wager that most of us in the family had similar potential. But we didn’t develop it to this extent, and certainly not in the same way. I’ve been very strong my whole life, and these days I get good exercise from several workout regimens, but I never did serious bodybuilding, and for me it was Judo and Aikido, not boxing. Today, it’s Yoga, walking, cycling, and a VR workout. And home maintenance and building… I worked on clearing some overgrown plants yesterday from 10am to nearly 5pm. So I guess I did develop at least a bit of that potential. That’s kind of the story around intelligence versus wits versus wisdom. In short, you’re smart when you have a developed innate intelligence honed sharp by regular use and a constant exposure to new ideas. I spend hours a day reading… that doesn’t make me more intelligent, but it makes me smarter. I hone my wits, my ability to apply combined intelligence and knowledge, In a very real way, wits are applied intelligence. You could be the next Einstein, but if you don’t learn things, if you gain no useful knowledge, you have nothing to do with that vast intelligence. Wisdom is basically the result of being apply your wits over time. If you’re doing anything interesting in your life, you will fail at some point. You can learn from that failure. You can lean from your success. The accumulated real world experiences, both the acknowledged and understood failures and the acknowledged and appreciated success, makes you wise. It’s essentially the integral of your life’s graph of witty and, well, not so witty, even dumb decisions. Yeah, I’ve had those. If you haven’t, you’ve never tried to figure out a hard thing. You build wisdom in the feedback loop between those ideas, decisions, actions and how your best wits result in real world success or failure. If you’re never able to admit your failures, you’re unlikely to ever become wise, no matter how smart you might be. At least that’s my take on it, with my background in Cognitive Psychology and a long career in engineering. I didn’t research this one, I wanted to offer my personal observation. As well, you can train your brain up on anything, which is actually building those wits — getting smarter— but might seem indistinguishable from intelligence. That’s okay, because no one really knows their innate intelligence in any useful way. It’s only the application of that intelligence over one’s knowledge — what I’m calling wits — that ever makes a difference. I taught myself to play guitar. That sort of thing is difficult because, in order to play any musical instrument, you have to get your brain and body in sync in a way that kind of bypasses the active mind. My wisdom applied here: I had studied cognitive psychology and understood what a slog it can be to learn a new thing like this. I knew about this thing, muscle memory is basically the best name: your brain automates part of a repetitive thing you do with your body. An example: when you walk, you’re thinking perhaps about walking. You’re not actively processing “lift foot. move foot. drop foot. watch balance. lift other foot… “ No, your brain has automated that stuff. When I play a guitar chord I know, I don’t think “finger 1 goes here, finger 2 goes here”, etc. I think “D chord,” “G chord,” etc. and my brain just kind of does it. That’s part of the phenomena we call muscle memory. Just like walking. Lately I’ve been doing Sudoku puzzles at night while I watch a bit of TV, because even the best TV is only so engaging, and I’ve found, if I have one stream of drama and one of math in my brain, they really don’t conflict with one another. I’ve found that I’m doing simply addition in my head almost without even thinking… so kind of the math version of muscle memory. Because while it’s called muscle memory, it’s all about the brain automating things you need to have automated. That’s earned mental acuity — “smarts” — but of course, no one watching me play the guitar has any idea if the result was hard work or innate talent… or both! When I was a kid, I got into Thomas Edison for awhile. I read all the, well, watered down books about Edison that didn’t get into what an asshole he could be. But as well as hundreds of inventions, he did kind of create the modern method of engineering with a corporation. Anyway, I was struck by one of his quotes: “Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration.” — Harper’s, 1932. His take was that the pure intelligence was important, but the hard work — making yourself smart about the problem at hand — was the real thing that gets you dubbed a genius. I agree with this assertion. So never ever ever think your innate intelligence is the limit to what you’d like to achieve in life. And don’t be too attached to one goal, if you’re just starting out or starting anew. When I was in college, I was triple majoring in electronic engineering, computer science/math, and cognitive psychology, with the kind of AI done in the 80s — nothing like today’s crazy shit — in one CS class and multiple Psych classes. I guess I kind of wanted to build a terminator! When I left school, my first job at General Electric promised Space Shuttle work. I was right there! Maybe robots later, but the frickin’ space program! My Dad made sure to wake me up if there was ever an Apollo launch, rerentry, Moon landing, space walk, etc. He took the family on a Florida vacation to watch Apollo 8 lift off. One of the main things in my young life that pushed me into engineering, other than my Dad, was the space program. The other? Chitty Chitty Bang Bang… but hey, I was a kid! That turned out to be bogus… they brought you in promising Space Shuttle, but they had me working on tools that would be used by the folks working on nuclear missiles. I left. My next job had me in microcomputers at Commodore. It had simply never occurred to me that such a job — engineering my next home computer, my next toy — was an option. Once it was, there was no other work for me. If that had lasted, I’d still be doing it, regardless of what they payed.

Question: Who is credited with inventing atheism and what was their motivation? Are there any individuals who have renounced their belief in God without identifying as agnostic?
Answer: No one “invented” atheism. Atheism is the natural state of humanity. Each and every one of us was born atheist. We had to be indoctrinated into some religion. Which is, of course why, if you believe in a religion, it’s damn near always the one your parents and your community’s tiny slice of planet Earth believed. If it’s not, that’s because you chose to become indoctrinated some other religion. Gods had to be invented. Early on, they were simply things in nature that primitive man didn’t understand. Later on, as humans went from hunter-gatherers to develop communities and agriculture, the best storytellers, over generations, exaggerated real stories of great deeds among their people into legend and then myth, which is, of course, just “someone else’s religion.” In very primitive societies, gods and magic were beneficial. They were some of the first aspects of human culture, a thing other than pure survival that could knit together communities. The useful part was simple: gods and magic gave very simple answers to complexities in the natural world that humanity, in their childhood, was completely unable to understand, questions our ancestors couldn’t begin to comprehend or even ask. Regular folks were free to only worry about useful questions. Over time, though, these benign myths became toxic. As communities expanded and met each other, they fought conflicts, sometimes over resources, but also over their mythologies. In time, control of those mythologies became an obvious means to power. Sure, the village Shaman had a pretty good life, but might have also been a student of the local folk medicine. So he mixed pure myth with the best results a primitive society could deliver. But over time, religions grew to be powerful, and exert that power over their societies. That really came to head when humanity got better at science. Once we could learn the real reason these complicated things happened, religion became a roadblock to progress. As it, in its worst form, exists today. Humanity has left its childhood. Religion is no longer an advantage to use as a civilization. As a comfort to people in dealing with personal issues, it’s fine and still useful. But as a tool against progress, as a tool of oppression, it’s toxic. It needs to die.

Service workers, like waiters and bartenders, are legally paid peanuts — often well below minimum wage, depending on the state — with the idea they’ll make it up in tips. If I were in this situation, I’d go after that: I’d want that exclusion eliminated instead. Or certainly, first. This is also why the USA, uniquely in the world, has gone so tip-crazy. It’s only a matter of time before the server at McDonalds or the clerk at your local convenience store wants a tip, presumably because the wealthy corporate structure has found some loophole that allows them to be paid $2,23 per hour, versus $13.25 for non-tipped employees. That’s the actual numbers in Delaware, one of the bluest states. It’s surprisingly less bonkers in Florida, where the “tipped employee” minimum wage is $8.98 per hour versus $12.00 per hour for non-tipped. Not taxing tips would, at least, be a nice band-aid for those working in such jobs. Here’s the problem: if this kind of bill were passed, it’s almost certain that high wage financial, legal, and sales people would seek to reclassify their commissions as “tips,” thus making them free of taxes. Bonuses granted to employees? Now they’re tips! Did you not see this part coming? This was suggested by Donald Trump recently, as the question points out, and a bill was introduced by Trump sycophant and prominent Cuban/Canadian Senator Rafael Edward “Ted” Cruz. If the Party of the Uber Rich ever backs anything that seems designed to help regular people, don’t assume there’s an ulterior motive. There is. Go find it. And technically, tips are only tips if they’re voluntary. But if you’ve eaten in many restaurants, you’ll find that for parties over a certain size, they’re an “included tip.” That’s still legally voluntary — you are not obligated to pay that, or it wouldn’t be a tip. But few people dispute that addition. More recently, there’s a “service fee” in some restaurants that’s probably not a real tip, probably not optional, but clearly the voice of the restaurant saying “hey, we know we’re not paying our servers properly, so now you get to.” There’s a restaurant right near by, Crabby Bills in Indian Rocks Beach, FL, that does this: 10% “service fee.” If it’s not optional, it’s not legally a tip, but it amounts to the same thing: workers are being cheated. So no obligation to tip on top of that, of course, but hey, I solved the problem: I don’t eat there anymore. If they had actually posted that the company was paying their workers fairly in the normal way one does that, I’d probably eat there more often. But hey, their issue. Those in tipped jobs only represent about 2.5% of the whole US workforce. It would not be a problem to simply eliminate the special lower minimum wage for such workers. But if you thought the ever-present drive from people asking for tips for essentially walking something from the back of the store to the counter is annoying, imagine if “tips aren’t taxed” gets in there without any limits. Tips will explode and be everywhere, and while they may be legally optional, there are many ways folks will come up to make them functionally mandatory. And here’s the other thing: most service industry workers aren’t actually paying all that much income tax on their tips anyway! A single person has to make over $13,850 in income before they pay their first penny in Federal Income Tax. The average salary for a waiter or waitress — who tend to be female, single, and young — is $24,770 nationally (Zippia), though a mean of $36,530 factoring in tips (BLS). So basically no income tax at all (but still FICA and state sales tax, etc) for the first third to half of the year. They would be far more positively impacted by eliminating the tip factor in their minimum wage. Vice President Harris has also backed this basic idea. It’s been a thing discussed for at least a decade or more. But the devil is, as always, in the details. A thing that helps lower income workers and does not lend itself to the abuse of rich folks? Perhaps a good idea, but maybe less so, for the individual and our society, if it’s pushing more big companies to put more people in tip-earning jobs. The good people working long hours to do the service jobs many of rely on should be fairly compensated without the necessity of holding out a cup to every person they serve. Question: How come many of the sci fi concepts have become real? Does imagination always precede reality and what could be possible?
Answer: Looking down on empty streets All she can see Are the dreams all made solid Are the dreams made real All of the buildings All of the cars Were once just a dream In somebody's head -Peter Gabriel, Mercy Street Of course! For any human-made thing to exist, someone has to think of it first. That’s true of technology, true of art, true of music. And while we don’t actually create the things investigated by science, it takes imagination to figure out how to investigate those hidden secrets of nature. When I design a computer system, I start building a model of what I want in my mind. I factor in various constraints for the project, put them down a bunch of “fixed points” in the design, then begin to figure out what I need for the rest, and what’s the best way to implement those fixed points when there are options. Before anything’s real, there’s a CAD drawing of the system (schematic) and then of the implementation (PCB/parts) that’s been transferred from the model in my mind. Sure, it’s not a direct transfer, but more of a feedback loop: as I draw the system, I get to think about some of the details that might not be in the model, and iterate on how those ought to go, too. It’s no foregone conclusion that any given science fiction concept — even with good science fiction, perhaps extrapolated in creative ways from today’s known science — will actually become possible some day. Sometimes science fiction concepts are found to have real-world analogs. Sometimes they’re still just imagination… for example, we don’t have any good way just yet to even begin to build a real Star Trek style faster-than-light starship. And we may never. We don’t have sentient machines, and a good body of science fiction points out that might just be a good thing. But science fiction, as with all art, can at least inspire those creating things that might strive for similar capabilities in reality. While we don’t have those sentient robots yet that Isaac Asimov wrote about, we’ve been making various robots since 1954. We’ve built robots that revolutionized multiple industries, we’ve made robots you can use in your house, and we’ve sent robots to every planet in the Solar System! On the other hand, we routinely build “communicators” that do way more than Trek’s communicators. Well, other than that whole “reaches a spaceship in orbit” thing. We reached the “practically everything’s a computer” point in our technology faster than most science fiction would have had it. But our flying cars kind of suck so far!

Question: If there was no atmosphere on Earth, then we should be able to see stars during daytime, right? At least around sunrise and sunset. So why aren't there stars seen in photos of the moon landing?
Answer: Well, assuming “we” all had space suits, sure. And that we were pointing our cameras (or eyes) up at the stars and setting an exposure for those stars. It’s absolutely no different that shooting photos on Earth at night, with an atmosphere. So I shot this from planet Earth, with an atmosphere. You can see plenty of stars. This was shot with a fisheye lens, 180 degree field of view, at 60s and f/1.8, ISO 800. This was shot at Cherry Springs State Park in Pennsylvania, a certified “Dark Sky” area. So no local light pollution. Here’s another shot of stars at night, from planet Earth with atmosphere intact. This was shot with an ultra-wide-angle lens, not a fisheye, at f/2.8, 20s, ISO6400. Also gathering a ton of light. You need to grab all that light on a camera to be able to see stars, or even the trees in a nearly pitch dark area. This wasn’t completely dark, but shot on an island in New Hampshire, with just a few small lights in the general area.. you see those on the tree to the left. Now here’s a photo I shot at Bethany Beach, close to my house in Delaware. See any stars? Of course not… not even the one you maybe think you see. That’s not the Sun in the photo… that’s the moon! I shot this — handheld! — at 6 seconds, f/4.0, ISO 1600… that’s overexposing the moon like crazy, but it lets you see that, yes, just like the sun, light from moon (which is of course just reflected light from the sun) scatters in the atmosphere. You just can’t see it when the camera’s exposure is set to capture the moon properly, rather than overexposing it. Here’s the moon shot at f/8, 1/2500s, and ISO800. As you’ve seen with my other photos, I’m including exposure data because, if you don’t understand how photography works, you can’t understand the answer to your question. Any exposure can be reduced to a single value, the exposure value or EV, which is essentially a measure of the light you’re capturing, and on a power-of-2 exponential scale. So my first shot is -7.33EV 100 , second shot is … what-do-you-know, also -7.33EV 100 . The third shot is -2.67EV 100 , that’s a -4.67EV difference. That means that the star shots are capturing 25x as much light as the moon-on-the-beach shot. The last shot, the moon by itself, is 14.33EV 100 . That’s a -21.67EV difference from the starfield shots. I’m capturing 3,336,721.9x as much light to capture the stars as the moon by itself. The camera I’m using has a 12EV dynamic range, which means the brightest stars in the background are about 11EV too dim to make even the slightest different in the light captured by this exposure. That range is about the same as most films in the moon landing era. That’s why you don’t see a single star in that last shot. They’re there, and if I pointed a bit away from the moon and let the camera expose for 20s or more, I’d see plenty of stars. And in fact, more and more, the longer I left the exposure going, but eventually, depending on the lens focal length, I’d start seeing star trails. The rotational motion of the Earth becomes visible in long star exposures. Professionals use a clock drive to move the telescope/camera exactly opposite the Earth, to cancel this out. I have one of those on my telescope, but not what I’m shooting handheld moon shots with an 800mm lens. You eye has an incredible overall dynamic range of about 24–30EV depending on how you measure it. However we get there by “cheating”.. the eye has two completely different kinds of sensors: rods and cones. There are about 6 million cone cells, which detect bright light and color — different kind of cones detect different color ranges, and your brain integrates the output to deliver the perception of color. The rod cells number about 120 million. They fully saturate and “switch off” in bright light, but kick in when you’re in low light. The trick in low light is that there aren’t enough photons for a good image… this is why you see noise in a photograph shot in very low light. And why you see similar noise if you’re looking around in a very dark room. Your rod cells can detect a single photon, but in low light, there are never enough photons to excite every rod cell. So you get them randomly firing, each contributing to an overall image of the dark scene. Regular cameras don’t have redundant sensors, but have a much wider range of exposure than your eyes. It would have been dangerous for the eye to wait 20s or a minute to collect light before letting you see what’s in front of you. That’s no problem for a camera, as long as it’s no a good support. But it can’t deal with more than that 12–14EV of light to dark range. The Hasselblad C500 cameras, specially modified for Apollo use, were fully manual cameras, as most were in those days. The astronauts were not expert photographers, either. So the engineers at NASA set things up to be easy to use, hard to screw up. Each film magazine had simple instructions for its use. The film used, a special thin emulsion film made custom by Kodak to allow 100 shots per magazine, was ASA 160, which is the same as ISO 160 in today’s film sensitivity numbers. Same thing. The magazine tells the astronauts to shoot at 1/250s at f/5.6 in the shade, f/8 in partial sunlight, and f/11 in full sunlight. That yields EV numbers of 12.22EV 100 , 13.33EV 100 . and 14.33EV 100 . So in bright sunlight, on the moon, using a film camera made in the 1960s, the astronauts were shooting exactly the same exposure I shot from Earth to properly expose the moon. Imagine that… the physics of physics hasn’t changed all this time! One of the first popular point-and-shoot cameras in the Apollo era was the Kodak Instamatic. This camera shot at a fixed 1/100 second, fixed f/8 aperture, onto film that was usually around ISO64 for regular daylight shooting. That gets you 13.33EV 100 , exactly the middle exposure used on the Moon. Kodak counted on film latitude to stretch the range of the resulting prints, rather than make a better camera. If you had a slightly better camera, you could adjust the exposure. I had one something like this as a kid, a hand-me-down from one of my grandfathers. No meter, but it did have exposure and aperture control and variable focus. How did I set the exposure without a meter? Well, the first thing I learned was the “Sunny 16” rule. This tells you to set your shutter speed to the reciprocal of ISO/ASA, then use this chart… f/16 for full sun. So if I had ISO64 film, I’d round off to a 1/60s exposure. That combination at f/16 gets to an exposure value of 14.67EV 100 in super bright light, 13.67EV 100 in partially bright light, and 12.67EV 100 . So yes, friends and neighbors, the scientists at NASA basically told the astronauts to shoot with the Sunny 16 rule on the surface of the Moon! But hey, it worked. And you’d need a few million times more light to be able to capture a star, though that would have everything you see in the photo ridiculously overexposed… just like my shot of the Moon that looks like the Sun. Question: What is the process after filing a provisional patent? Do you need to file a non-provisional patent or can you wait for the original application to be approved before taking further action with your idea?
Answer: Well, for those who haven’t, I’ll cover the provisional filing process: Now, that’s going to cost you quite a bit more if you can’t prepare the provisional patent yourself. You might need to hire a draftsperson, you might need a patent attorney. It’s not required, but your patent application should be as complete as you can make it, as if you were filing for a non-provisional patent. You don’t need the section on prior art disclosure. So okay, you filed your provisional patent. Here’s the thing: the provisional patent is not examined. The only rejection can come from your failure to correctly fill out the cover sheet. Once the USPTO has accepted that, you’re good. You have bought the right to say “Patent Pending” on your invention for a year, and to secure the filing date of your provisional patent to be transferred to your non-provisional patent, assuming you file that within the next year. And assuming that they provisional is good enough that it’s fundamentally the same invention filed in your non-provisional application. It should be obvious, of course, that if you’re ready to file your non-provisional patent right now, there’s little point in filing the provisional patent. The idea is buy a little time… and yeah, a year can sometimes be a surprisingly short amount of time. You don’t have to file a non-provisional patent. Sometimes a provisional patent is filed to discourage copying of your short-term, small money invention. Sometimes you file to potentially protect the invention while you shop it around, or while you raise money to help fund the much greater expense of the non-provisional application. If that’s not successful, maybe you don’t bother. Read More

USB 3 can use Type-C, and USB 4 requires Type-C, but there is a distinction between “USB data protocols” and “Type-C connectors.” With USB4, all things are sadly optional. Question: Why do they make chargers with USB C to USB C cable now instead of plain USB to USB-C like before?
Answer: It’s several basic things. First thing: Type-C is the current USB connector. Type-A (what you’re calling “plain” though no, it’s Type-A) is the legacy connector. Increasingly, devices will use Type-C and move away from Type-A. When you’re selling a new thing, you probably want it to support what’s happening today, sure, but also what’s happening over the lifetime of the device. Second thing: the Type-C connector, like the Micro-B connector, was engineered for the demands of the reality that we’re plugging things in and out all the time with USB, for charging. When USB was invented, it was designed to replace mouse, keyboard, printer, and modem connections on a desktop computer. So there wasn’t a huge thought given to longevity of connectors. The Type-A jack should last you 1,500 plug-unplug cycles if you don’t abuse it. The Type-C jack should last you 20,000 plugs/unplug cycles. Third thing: Type-C can support the new Power Delivery protocol. The power over USB was originally just to run small devices like keyboards and mice. That was up to 2.5W, which is actually way, way more than you’d need for a mouse or keyboard. When it became clear that USB was being used as a regular DC power supply for phones, they added the Battery Charging protocol. That could provide at least 7.5W over a special charging cable. The Power Delivery standard and Type-C with the high current cables can deliver +20V at 5A, or 100W, based on the original version of PD, and +48V at 5A, or 240W, with the latest improvements. Power supplies had to get smart for this, so your device has to “handshake” with the power brick and trade capacities, so you don’t accidently get 20V or 48V into a device that’s only good for 5V or 9V. That lets the blue smoke out… not good. Not every Type-C port is going to offer you 100W or 240W, but today’s “chargers” (they don’t actually do the charging, they just provide the power) can deliver the kind of power needed for tablets, laptops, monitors, etc. Not just phones, keyboards, and mice.

Answer: Type-C is just a connector. Connector designs at best establish a standard that ensures every manufacturer’s connector will support the uses of the connector. USB has, since its inception, included error checking. All USB data is sent in packets, and every packet contains a CRC code, which is used by the receiver to ensure the data is correct. That said, USB was conceived as a desktop bus, a better answer to what ACCESS.bus or ADB (Apple Desktop bus) provided. Neither of those did error correction, because for the most part, a short cable on your desktop is not unreliable. If you have a question, ask the question. Stating a ridiculously incorrect premise in your question makes you seem to be nothing but a troll. It’s obvious you did not attempt to learn anything about USB before asking this question.

Question: Why are laptop speakers so bad and crappy, like there's literally zero bass? I mean, why don't manufacturers put better speakers in their laptops, or at least add a mini subwoofer?
Answer: It’s physics, plain and simple. In order to deliver good bass, you need a speaker that can move lots of air. You need power, and lots of it. You need a large speaker and lots of room for the diaphragm to move. You need big magnets. I used to have backyard music parties… on a few occasions, with overhead lights and a smoke machine. I had a mixer going into a 300W amplifier with good PA speakers. This was fine for guitars, keyboards, mics, etc. But not for the bass players. Why? A good bass amp probably starts at around twice that power (this one’s 500W) and goes up from there. You need to move large volumes of air at low frequencies, which means a very larger speaker and/or a very large travel for a smaller speaker. I had to run the bass amps to a different circuit than the 20A outlet — one I wired specifically to power backyard parties — otherwise, we’d blow the breaker. This is well known… low frequencies are high energy. When you’re mixing sound, you put high pass filters on anything that doesn’t need those low frequencies, to keep the overall energy of the mix not just lower, but useful. On LP records - “vinyl” to you kids out there — they compress the crap out of the lower end, because without that, you’d need super wide grooves on the disc, you’d probably only get about 8–10 minutes on a side, and it wouldn’t work anyway, because that much energy on your tone arm would have it skating across the disc all the time. Here’s a speaker/driver for a compact subwoofer. You might actually use two of these if you were building an actual subwoofer. The speaker is 3″ diameter, and this works because it’s got a crazy travel range — it’s called a long throw speaker — and it’s still not as good as a plain old 12″ or 15″+ subwoofer. In order to have that long throw, the speaker needs lots of room to move, and a large, heavy magnet. This one’s not going to fit into your laptop, either. This is not a surprise. Laptops are a compromise, trading off all sorts of things in order to deliver an integrated, portable system. My work laptop has a 17″ 4K display, but it’s a PITA to have to use that for work… I like at least two large monitors (I’m looking at 28″ widescreen and 34″ ultrawide here on my desk). The trackpad on the laptop is a lesser input device than my mouse, tablet, or the “3D mouse” they gave more for viewing 3D CAD files. The storage, at 1TB, is enough for work, but heck, the MiniPC at my vacation house has 8TB of SSD, and that’s not even a real desktop PC. So yeah, audio is compromised on a laptop. If you want better sound, get external speakers. If you want much better sound, send the audio out digitally… I can send computer sound to the 300W audio system here in my office… which includes a 12″ powered subwoofer. That said, there’s bad audio and there’s bad audio. My laptop makes sounds, sure, but it’s a Dell workstation model… pricey, with a pro-grade nVidia A3000 GPU, but they pretty much phoned in the audio. But there are laptops with good audio for a laptop. Apple’s usually done a good job, though you’ll find less compromise on their less compromised laptops. Get a larger Macbook Pro rather than a MacBook Air. Some Dell and HP consumer models, particularly anything sold for gaming, usually has pretty good audio as a built-in.

Question: What is the phone with the highest megapixel camera size and how does its image quality compare to other phones with lower megapixels?
Answer: There are several smartphones that including Samsung’s ISOCELL HP1 image sensor. This sensor provides 200 million pixels at 0.64um pixel pitch, for a 1/1.22″ chip size. The color filter is what Samsung calls the Tetra²pixel RGB Bayer Pattern. The Samsung Galaxy Ultra S24 is currently both the highest-rated smartphone with this sensor, and one you can absolutely buy in the USA. This is how Samsung explains the sensor. The color filter is based on areas of 4x4 pixels, so there are only 12.5 million color sites. Where you see them claiming 50MP and 200MP images, they’re cheating! The color filters don’t move around. Rather, to get a 50MP image, they “rematrix” the captured image by moving around pixels. Same thing when they deliver a 200MP result. That’s moving bits of the image around to places they don’t belong. So the results seem to have increased resolution, since there is more information, but in fact, they don’t have any increase in useful resolution. They scramble the image. This is pretty common on smartphones, but it gets substantially worse as they split the same color pixel into multiple luminance pixels. The good thing about this kind of sensor is that each photodiode can have its own exposure control. So the sensor can shoot single-image HDR photos, delivering an increase in dynamic range as a trade for more noise. In bright sunlight, noise levels are low enough to make this pretty much always a win. And it works in video, not just for stills. As far as quality goes, of course, it depends on who you ask. Consumer Reports has been rating Samsung’s recent phones neck and neck with Apple’s iPhone on camera quality. In fact, the Galaxy S24 Ultra — the one with the HP1 chip — scored 87 (higher is better). So did the Apple iPhone 15 Pro Max. The iPhone’s main sensor is a 48 megapixel “quad Bayer” sensor, which means 2x2 pixels under each color filter, 12 million color sites. The Samsung Galaxy S24+ came in at 85, despite having “only” a 50MP tetracell (same as quad Bayer) sensor, like the Apple. Apple’s iPhone 15 Pro also came in at 85. I’m suggesting the difference in ratings has nothing to do with “200MP” and is based on the more versatile setup in the Galaxy S24 Ultra, the four cameras, plus the fact that the 200MP sensor, like Apple’s 48MP sensor, is larger than those in the next tier of phone cameras. Another datapoint is DxOMark, which does an exhaustive testing and ranking of many smartphones, including some you can’t get in the USA. The Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra scrolled off the page… it’s at #22 with a score of 144. What didn’t they like? They found the S24 Ultra to be noisy in low light. Low light performance has much to do with the magic AI software used on phones that stack multiple shots. Their test put the iPhone 15 Pro Max at #6 overall. The big win on the iPhone… they loved the video performance. The iPhone currently holds the record top score of 158 on video in their testing. The top rated phone in the DxOMark testing is the Huawei Pure 70 Ultra. Huawei has lately been at the top of most international phone camera rankings, and this current time is no exception. This smartphone has the highest marks for still photos — the highest tested in all but one category — and for “zoom” so far rated, which is why it’s #1 at the moment. One win here is that the main sensor is a 1″ chip at 50 megapixels with quad Bayer CFA, larger than the 1/1.3″ or so main sensors in the other phones. The Honor Magic6 Pro is currently the #2 tested and ranked smartphone for camera at DxOMark. It’s telling that Honor split off from Huawei a few years back… so apparently, they share whatever software magic Huawei has been using these years. I was asked to review the Honor Magic4 Pro back in 2022, and found it to be the best smartphone camera I had ever tested… I wanted to use it as my “daily driver” but, back then, being a European model without VoIP support, it was useless as a phone… no voice support, since during the review, our 3G system was shut down (LTE phones without VoLTE support dropped back to 3G for voice). It’s sitting on the charger on my desk right now. This new Magic7 couples a 50 megapixel main camera (with f/1.4–2.0 variable aperture lens), a 50 megapixel ultra-wide, and 108 megapixel telephoto camera, quad-bayer/tetracell on the first two and I think Samsung nonacell — 9 pixels per color filter site — on the telephoto camera’s sensor. If only this worked in the USA! I’ll also point out that the Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra was introduced in January, so it’s a 2024 model. The iPhone 15 Pro Max is from September of 2023, and will likely be replaced in 2023. So it looks like Samsung overall is behind Apple as much as Apple is behind Huawei and Honor. Samsung also offered the HP1 sensor in the Galaxy S23 Ultra in 2023. Prior to that, the Moto Edge 30 Ultra was using the HP1 in 2022. DxOMark didn’t review the Edge 30 Ultra. This year’s Moto Edge 50 Ultra uses 1/1.3″ 50MP main sensor…. apparently offering better results. But again, smartphone image quality is highly dependent on software, and today’s Motorola — a Lenovo company — does well on quality low- and mid-range phones, but great camera software isn’t their thing. In short, all of these weird phone sensors today are some kind of effort to improve image quality without turning the smartphone into an actual camera. In fact, Samsung did that some years back and it wasn’t successful… most users want their smartphone to be a good pocket computer and also a good camera, but they won’t compromise the size of the phone just to get some kind of traditional camera functions. So the smartphone industry had to basically reinvent the camera, using the fact that smartphone is a pocket personal computer, and thus, leaning heavily on software processing. This is also how these became the best “point and shoot” cameras ever — any fool can get very good technical results with a smartphone. Dedicated cameras can do better, but only if you spend the time to learn photography for a couple of years.

Question: What is the purpose of the black band around smartphone camera lenses? Does it have any impact on image quality?
Answer: I guess you’re asking about these black bands, eh? Kind of like the “black band” around the glass on this professional camera lens, eh? Or this one. In fact, if you look into this lens, you’ll notice that there’s matte black all the way down. The reason for this is simple: there needs to be some kind of structure to hold the optics in a lens — the actual lens part. That’s usually called the lens barrel. In serious camera lenses, the glass elements don’t necessarily touch each other, but slot into a precisely machined lens barrels. In smartphones, quite a bit of the stackup of lens elements just snaps together, no need for a full lens barrel. But they still need some kind of structure to keep the lens stack in alignment with the openings in the phone case. So this is just the structure of the lens beyond the optics. It’s matte black to avoid reflections as much as possible, that’s all. If these were made of shiny chrome or something, they would adversely effect the image, by introducing random reflected light into the captured image. Clearly, the lens elements are not all the same diameter, which makes sense, given that a smartphone will have different kinds of cameras. However, for aesthetic purposes, the overall width of the lens cutout — the ring around the black plastic part — is the same diameter for each camera. Just to make it look more consistent. There are limits to that, of course. Some more recent smartphones have enough difference between multiple cameras that there’s no practical way to match them to look similar. Ideally, the needs of the tech outweigh the aesthetics of the physical designer… though some companies do opt for form over function. While there’s not usually a reason to match lens to lens for professional photographic systems, you often find that for cinematography, they are matched. This six lens set of cinema lenses: 12mm, 16mm, 25mm, 35mm, 50mm, and 85mm, has a pretty wide range of lens size differences, but the lens bodies make them all basically the same width. Why? It’s the gears. You can see gearing on each lens body. This is to engage focus and iris control mechanisms used on cinema camera rigs. Here’s an example of this kind of rig. Making every lens in the series the same basic size, at least for the gearing, means that lenses can be swapped without the need to change around the location of controls on your camera rig (you can see the rails here that allow the follow-focus device to be repositioned). The lens shown here has three gears, the third for zoom control, as this is a zoom lens.

Question: Why do my camera photos look even worse than phone photos in terms of quality? For example, if I zoom in on my camera photo it looks blurry and then on my phone it has more details.
Answer: You didn’t mention the kind of camera you’re using. Something like this low-end Sony point-and-shoot model? Yeah, you can easily get a sharper image on a smartphone. This camera has a 20.1 megapixel sensor, as it tells you on the camera. It’s also starting out with an f/3.2 aperture on a 1/2.3″ sensor . That’s a very tiny sensor, much smaller than the sensor in any 2022–2024 premium smartphone. Thanks to diffraction — the bending of light passing though an aperture — you’re probably getting maybe an effective “optical” 10–12 megapixels at full aperture. Zoom all the way out and you’re at f/6.4. You’ll have less than 2 megapixels of optical resolution. In short, the image will be much blurrier than you’d like. With the smartphone, you’re probably getting 12–16 megapixels of actual resolution these days (some claim to have much more, but that’s not exactly correct), but you’ll have a larger sensor and probably be shooting at f/2.0-f/1.5 on the main camera. So no diffraction… you get a sharp image. The phone’s software is also shooting multiple images and merging them for less noise and better dynamic range, and then applying all kinds of sharpening and color modification — often too much — to deliver an image most novices, at least, will find pleasing. If your phone has a portrait or telephoto camera, you might about match the magnification of this camera at full zoom, but of course, your phone is doing with multiple cameras, each with a prime lens, and at least for premium models, increasingly not-terrible sensors and lenses. I did a review of the Honor Magic4 Pro awhile back, which offered a telephoto camera consisting of a 1/2.0″ sensor — largely than the Sony’s — and a 3x, f/2.0 lens. So immediately better than what you can get out of the Sony, probably even at a software-driven 5x magnification. And that’s a two-year-old smartphone! Maybe it’s more like this, a lower-end bridge camera? With this, you have exactly the same problem: a tiny 1/2.3″ sensor and relatively narrow aperture. This Panasonic probably does a bit better than the Sony on diffraction, with a slightly faster aperture range, but that’s probably negated by a lens that’s trying to deliver a 60:1 magnification range. Despite being made of plastic, your smartphone’s lens is going to be sharper. Today’s smartphone lenses are nearly all injection molded of optical plastic, but they’re pretty good at that these days, and they can fit a 6 or 7 element lens with the cheap ability to mold aspherical lens elements. Professional zoom lenses designed today can rival fixed-focus prime lenses, but a lens pushed to these limits, and made pretty cheaply as well, is not going to offer good sharpness. Now, of course, if you’re zoomed all the way in to 215mm on this camera, you’re at a full-frame equivalent of 1200mm… that’s nuts. You will get much better photos than your smartphone at that magnification level. Now, if you’re using a higher-end compact digital camera like this Sony RX100, you ought to be getting much better images than you do with your phone. Certainly sharper at just about any zoom level, because this camera has a 1″ sensor that’s not going to deliver diffraction at any magnification with full aperture, though you can stop down the aperture. This also shoots an honest 20 megapixels. Here’s another option that’ll outshoot your phone, the Sony RX10. This is a high-end bridge camera, and it’s got a 1″ sensor as well, in fact, probably the same one, depending on the RX100 model. And if you have one of these Digital Single Lens Reflex camera... … or one of these mirrorless interchangeable lens cameras, you ought to be getting better, sharper images than you do with your phone. So without knowing your specific case, if it’s any of these last groups, high-end compact digitals, DSLRs, or MILCs, you’re doing something wrong if your phone is delivering better images. So, since you didn’t really explain your situation, I tried to cover a range of cases. Hope that’s useful.

Question: What is the reason for high-end PCs being necessary for gaming, even though the graphics may not always be top-quality?
Answer: High-end PCs always have top discrete graphics processors. That’s part of the definition of “high-end PC”, though of course, gamers opt for “gaming PC” which is a subset of that. I have a high-end PC, but it’s got a nVidia professional graphics card, which is not what you want for gaming: too slow and kind of overkill for gaming needs. The difference between a high-end PC for gaming rather than, say, scientific, CAD, AI, or media work is the specifics of the CPU and GPU. Obviously, the system will require a high-end gaming GPU. As well, it’ll need a CPU that’s typically at the top of the range in single-core CPU speed, but depending on the era, only so many CPU cores will be of value for the typical game. I recall a time when a four-core processor was recommended for high-end gaming, and today it’s unlikely you get a benefit from more than eight cores. Games love cache memory, and some of the best gaming processors today, such as the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, have a huge on-board cache, 8MB L2 cache plus 96MB of L3 cache in this case. There are higher end X3D CPUs, but you’re spending Not sure what you mean by “quality”… the graphics output these days is digital, not analog, so they’re all basically the same. The look and “quality” depends on the monitor, not the PC or GPU. Now, if you’re talking about laptops, that’s all about the screen. Some gamers (and other users) buy laptops but use external monitors or even televisions, so they don’t care all that much about the screen. Thus, a fast laptop with lower quality screen is a bargain if you’re not expecting to do much with the screen. The quality of rendered graphics, of course, depends on the GPU you’re using, as long as you’ve got enough CPU to keep the GPU busy. Thus, my claim about high-end gaming PCs always having high-end GPUs that absolutely will render your game well. Yes, it is true that if you’re using a laptop, you’ll likely have a mobile GPU that’s a bit of a step down from a desktop GPU. Question: Does Bluetooth still have a noticeable sound lag when gaming?
Answer: If you’re using older Bluetooth, or even some modern implementations, particularly with higher quality audio CODECs, yeah, there’s a noticeable latency. After all, you don’t usually care all that much at the gym, on the bike, on the kayak, if there’s a delay between sound on your device and sound on your ears. You may simply not notice. I had a startup company back in 2002 working originally on a gaming robot project, then pivoting to R/C car controllers. We used Bluetooth 1.x back then, for control, because that was already a small bandwidth standard, had potential for small video use. Anyway, the whole gigantic software stack in BT and other issues gave us a typical 70–90ms latency. Audio over Bluetooth back then was worse. If you know anything about latency, that’s pure madness. As a musician, I know I can probably hear about a 1ms latency on a beat. In audio, if you hear a delay of 5–50ms or so, your average person’s non-musical brain processes that as reverb... part of that initial audio event. If it’s much beyond that, your brain processes it as echo, a separate event. On the gaming robot project, we were driving pretty slow and the latency wasn’t much of an issue. On the first R/C monster trucks we had, testing out at my tree farm back then, at 15mph that kind of latency made it nearly impossible to drive. The typical latency on an analog R/C car/truck back then was 20ms or under. Higher end R/C racers ran at 70mph+… a real 70mph, not scale. After switching to a simpler radio chip and our own software stack, we had latency down to about 5ms. Our controllers became very popular among RCers for a shot time (brand name Nomadio). The bosses decided to leave that business, despite the success. I was not happy, but that’s life. Today’s Bluetooth Low Energy with the LC3 audio CODEC does much better, as low as maybe 7.5ms. You probably see 0.5ms-2ms with a wired controller, keyboard, etc. So it’s not terrible.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Why does the USA only have two popular parties, Democrat and Republican, and after 2024 the Republicans will no longer exist?
Answer: Welcome to the mathematics of voting! In the USA, most State and all Federal Elections are run based on the idea of winner-take-all or first-past-the-post voting. It’s very simple: the candidate with the most votes wins the election. They win everything. This is actually worse than that for the Presidential election. Because, of course, we have two elections. In the General election, almost every State runs a winner-take-all election to pick electors, which in turn hold another winner-take-all election to pick the President. Both elections are subject to anti-democratic problems like gerrymandering. The electoral college weighting of some votes more than others violates the ideal of one person, one vote. I’ll get to that, but first, a little background. Presidential Voting in the Constitution So part of the problem, and part of what I’ll get to, is the simple fact that the Founders didn’t want political parties in the USA. As with so many other things, they didn’t put in any rules against parties, as they were idealists and expected that everyone would just do the right thing. So for, well, nearly two years, there were no parties in the USA. One of the main reasons George Washington ran for a second term was over the whole political party thing. So how did we pick the President, in the original Constitution? Each state was responsible for appointing a number of electors equal to the sum of Senators and Representatives assigned the state. They could do this any way they chose — there was no mandate for a popular election. In states that did hold popular elections, the candidate with the most votes won all of the electors. When the electoral college met, each member would pick two candidates, at least one not from their own state. If any candidate won outright with a majority of votes, that person becomes President and the runner-up, with the next-most votes, becomes Vice President. Imagine Hillary Clinton as Trump’s Vice President to have some idea why this was incompatible with political parties. The 12th Amendment put a band-aid on this by having the electors hold a separate vote for President and Vice President. But it didn’t really address the idea of parties having a legal basis, which is actually pretty necessary in a political system dominated by collectives rather than individuals. You may have noticed that, in 2000 we elected George W. Bush, and in 2016 we elected Donald J. Trump, to the Presidency with fewer popular votes then their opponents. The electoral college ensures that voters in small states actually have a more highly counted vote than voters in large states. That’s due to the fact that electors are allocated based on Senate and House members assigned to each state, thus a minimum of three no matter how small the state population. As a result, it’s hardly, likely, but mathematically possible, to elect a President with less than 30% of the popular vote! Voting and Party Power In any given election, there can be only one winner, right? Actually, not right. In some systems of government — particularly those that work parties into their system — there are various means of balancing power in government across the most popular parties. The Parliamentary System used in most Western Democracies awards power to parties closely based on the popular vote. So if you have a small party that’s only able to attract 5% of the vote, your party probably gets about 5% of the power. If no one party wins all, then that party has to form a coalition government with one other party to deliver a sum of 50% or more of the power. This isn’t a perfect system, but it enables small parties and helps prevent any large party from becoming too extreme and thus unable to form a coalition with other parties. But in the USA, the winner takes all. So what if your favorite candidate is in a smaller party? Simple: that candidate has no real chance of winning the election. Your vote on that party is largely wasted. But it’s even worse than that. Who was your second choice? By voting for the candidate who can’t win, rather than your second choice, you help the party you least agree with… the so-called spoiler vote. That’s why Republicans donate money to prop up small parties, like the Greens, who tend to appeal to Democrats, and Democrats, in turn, may donate money to parties like the Libertarians more likely to appeal to those on the right. This process, when analyzed mathematically, tells you there are only two points of long-term political stability in the USA: no parties or two strong parties. If there’s one strong party and two weak parties, the one strong party pretty much wins all the time. Over time, one of those weak parties will get stronger — they’ll both likely being going after the others constituents, as it’ll be natural in most cases to unite against the strong party. Eventually, one of those parties will be large enough to compete against the other strong party. The other will become increasingly obscure and, usually, increasingly extreme, since a small party with no chance of victory can only attract idealists at the extremes of some political axis. Two Strong Parties And so, today, we have only two strong parties, because that’s what the mathematics and psychology of voting tells us is the inevitable outcome of first-past-the-post voting. In the modern era, it’s certainly true that the Democrats and the Republicans work hard to make it clear they are the only choice. If you’re watching the Presidential Debate this week, you’ll notice it’s only Joe Biden and Donald Trump who have been invited… no third parties. There have been debates that admitted third parties, back when the League of Women Voters ran the debates. The major parties didn’t like this, so they formed the Presidential Commission on Debates. And this year, neither candidate particular wanted those guys running things either, so they’re doing debates organized independently. The inevitability of a Republican or Democrat as President, the reality of virtually none of the third parties actually trying to become powerful, to run local candidates in en masse, etc. means that there’s not even a contender for “powerful party”. Thus, it’s unlikely, as the question posits, that any major schism in the Republican Party leads to the end of that party. In fact, it’s been a long while since anything changed. The second party formed in the USA was called the Anti-Federalists — formed as a counter to Alexander Hamilton’s Federalist Party — but also the Jeffersonians (because it was lead by Thomas Jefferson), but more formally as the “Democratic-Republicans.” At this point, the “Anti-Federalists” had pretty much done their job: The Federalists held no more real power. The Democratic-Republicans had won six straight elections. So there was a four-way split, with Andrews Jackson, John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, and William Crawford all running as factionalized Democratic Republicans, and seeing Adams selected as President in a contingency election in Congress, despite fewer electoral or popular votes than Jackson. This lead to a permanent split: The actual modern Republican Party formed in 1854, over an even bigger schism that single-party-rule and Andrew Jackson: slavery. The Republicans brought in Whigs and many from smaller parties like the Free Soilers and the Know Nothings, as well as some disaffected Northern Democrats. So yeah, it’s been 170 years since either of the main two strong parties in the USA changed their name. They’ve changed their politics, swapped ideologies, swapped members, etc. but the names have remained. While there’s no guarantee that any major party lasts here forever, it’s highly unlikely you see the Republican Party simply collapse. It’s more likely, as we saw with the Tea Party, that internal factions wrestle over control and politics, once Trump is history. Better Vote, Better Society The ideal vote in a democratic country sees each party win a percentage of political power matching their vote, but that’s both difficult, and the result. It’s the system that gets us there that’s a problem. American economist and mathematician Kenneth Arrow set out to devise a perfect voting system that could avoid the pitfalls of known systems, and in general, the problem of social choice. His conclusion, now known as Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem, is that no voting system can produce a good result, or avoid all known voting system pitfalls, all the time. However, at least some of Arrow’s work was looking at ranked choice voting, which is in many ways superior to first-past-the-post. This is also known as instant-runoff-voting. If you follow politics, you may have noticed that some states, like Georgia, have a runoff law for some elections, such as the US Senate. The law is simple: if there is not a single candidate claiming 50%+1 of the votes cast, the top two candidates will face a runoff election. That’s an expensive thing to do, and recently, it’s been too common. What if we case a vote that includes all we need to hold a runoff from that original vote? That’s ranked choice voting. You pick from all the candidates in your order or preference. If you don’t like a candidate at all, you don’t have to pick them. When the votes are tallied, the process is simple. If there’s a candidate with 50%+1 votes, that candidate is the winner. If not, the lowest tallied candidate is removed and those voters’ second choice is used. Repeat until one candidate is the winner. That candidate may not have top support from all voters, but they will have support from all voters. No chance of a person with 30% of the vote being elected. This also has the effect of empowering smaller parties. It’s absolutely not as good as power sharing in a parliamentary system, but it does mean that there’s much less of a concern over a spoiler effect. The one problem is when one candidate has a plurality but not a majority, and all other candidates tie for second place. Under RCV, all of the second place candidates are eliminated. Highly unlikely in any nontrivial election. There are some other issues with it versus the unobtainable ideal, but it’s a much better system than in use in the USA… except that a few cities and states do run RCV for local elections. RCV would help smaller parties in the USA by changing the mathematics of our election system. It’s not a permanent cure to all voting problems. It doesn’t prevent gerrymandering. It ensures elected officials are not elected by a minority of voters, but it doesn’t guarantee all parties a proportionate share of the vote intended by the people.
