Question: Can you explain the inner workings of an LED TV? Are there any variations in design between different brands such as Samsung and LG?
Answer: Easy! The very first LCD display was invented at RCA Labs in Princeton, NJ in 1964. But there’s been a ton of progress since! First thing you need to understand is what a polarizer is. If you’re a fisherman, you probably have a pair of polarized sunglasses, which eliminate glare on the water and let you see what’s underneath. A normal beam of light has beams of light vibrating in all directions along the line of transmission. A polarizer aligns light along a single axis. Light being reflected off the water’s surface is aligned by the reflection process, and your fisherman’s glasses has a polarizer that’s oriented the other way. So the glare is blocked, but the other random light is admitted along the lines of the glasses’ polarizers. As illustrated here, two polarizers can be aligned to still pass light. But if you rotate one, you can control the amount of light that’s passed, down to blocking nearly all of it. The next important thing is the liquid crystal. This is a state of matter that’s fluid, like a liquid, but with organized structure, like a crystalline solid. Liquid crystals have interesting properties. Some react to temperature — one of the first uses of liquid crystals was as a cheap, stick-on thermometer. Some react to pressure. And the ones we care about here react to voltage. If you form a liquid crystal material just so, it can bend the polarization of light, and the amount of bending is based on an electrical voltage bias put on the material. And that’s basically all we need to make an LCD display… yes, I did way LCD, but I’ll get all the way there soon. So here is your basic LCD display. There are various ways to make this, and some drawings will show many different layers, but this one’s basic. There are two polarizers, oriented 90 degrees from one another, which normally would admit no light. There’s a color filter, necessary to deliver a color display. There’s a sheet of liquid crystal material, and a hard glass panel with transparent thin film transistors that can provide a tiny voltage bias to each bit of the liquid crystal material. That bias is variable… it’ll be managed by an LCD controller chip, not shown. So depending on the bias voltage applied to the liquid crystal at any given point on the display, the material will pass light straight through, or it’ll twist it. In this example, with no twist, you get a dark pixel. With a full twist, you get a light pixel. And in-between — because it’s an analog effect — you get different brightness levels. Or rather, light transmission levels. Light will pass through this, bottom to top (you’re viewing at the top), but we don’t currently have light. So let’s add some. The simplest way to add light is to use light you already have. Simple LCD displays, often just in monochrome, are reflective displays. Rather than a light, the display simply has a bright, diffuse background that will reflect enough light to let you see the display, not enough to act as a mirror and confuse the image with reflections from your environment. You can buy one of these for about $15 and drive it from a microcontroller if you need a small display for a project. So the first high quality LCD displays, whether for laptops or monitors or televisions, employed cold cathode fluorescent lighting at the edge of the displays. Built just right, a pair at the edges, eventually maybe another pair at the top and bottom, could provide a backlight for the display. Now you have a real LCD monitor or TV that’s providing its own light and capable of much better contrast than a reflective display. This would be an example of a transmissive display — the light passes through. It didn’t take long before the lighting changed from edge-lit to back-lit. In short, a whole array of CCFL lamps could backlight a display, once they could be made thin enough, offering more uniform lighting. In the early 1990s, Professors Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura invented the first manufacturable blue LED (though other efforts had succeeded in the lab). This was followed up by Prof. Dr. Jürgen Schneider inventing a white LED in 1995, using a blue LED with a yellow phosphor coating, and Shuji Nakamura a year later inventing a bright blue LED… two LED elements, no filtering. It wasn’t long before LCD displays could use LEDs rather than CCFLs as backlighting. And so, marketing people being what they are, these were released into the market as LED displays. They were still very much LCDs as well — in fact, the early LED televisions also used edge lighting, basically the worst of the lighting schemes that had been worked out. So as the technology advanced, LED televisions got full backlights, just as they’d had with CCFLs of course… that part was already known. But because it was dozens of individual LEDs making the backlight, someone came up with the idea of making their brightness variable in concert with the LCD display. This allowed a better picture, working a “dynamic” display to enhance the fairly low contrast ratio of LCDs (1:1000 to 1:3000) versus the phosphors used in CRTs and Plasma displays (1:20,000). Over time, these shrunk to the “full matrix” backlight, with hundreds of LEDs, finally leading to the “mini-LED” display I have in my livingroom, with thousands of individual LEDs, each being dynamically controlled to light up just a small part of the display. So in fact, as the technology did better, your “LED” TV became more and more a hybrid of LED and LCD technology. They both contribute to the image quality. The next very cool thing — kind of a side-road in the LED story, but worth knowing — is the quantum dot. A quantum dot is a tiny semiconductor particle engineered with what’s effectively an artificial band gap. The band gap in a semiconductor is the energy level between quantum states. For an LED, they use various exotic semiconductors to deliver a band gap that’s at the right energy level for the color of light we’d like to see emitted. But a quantum dot can be engineered with basically any band gap, from all the same materials… nothing terribly exotic. When you fire higher energy light into one of these, lower energy light, based on the band gap, it emitted. This gives us a few cool things. For one, LEDs are basically monochromatic, aside from blue LEDs which might have two light components that just add up to “white” in our brains. But QDs can deliver a whole range of color if you make them in a few different sizes. It’s also tricky, in making different LEDs from different materials, to ensure you have different color LEDs that have similar brightness… for example, when making a “Smart Bulb” that’s white because of an RGB pair of LEDs, but can take on other colors and even vary the color temperature of white light. QDs let you use the same blue LED for all colors of light. So, the very simple way to make a Quantum Dot LED television — which, again, is an LCD+LED hybrid — is to replace your array of white LEDs with an array of blue LEDs and a sheet of Quantum Dot film, thus creating a perfect white backlight that was tuned to whatever spectrum desired by tweaking the quantum dots. The next way to do this is to replace the traditional color filter for each pixel with a quantum dot filter. That seems to be the way newer televisions are made, but you don’t know until you know, eh… it’s in the details. All of these technologies are tweaked in various different ways by the manufacturers. Each has their own particular buzzwords to describe their particular flavor of display. These are the fundamentals. If you don’t have a good idea of what these mean in the real world, you need to go to a shop and look at different displays. If the technology isn’t spelled out, write down the model numbers that seem close to what you want. Look up reviews online, which will also tell you about the technology. But wait… there’s more! So, now that you’ve got thousands of mini-LEDs on the display, what if instead you went to millions? Well, once you have an LED for each sub-pixel — about 25 million for a 4K display — you don’t need the LCD anymore. And that’s basically what some manufacturers did, even before mini-LED was a thing, with Organic LED displays. Of course, since companies were already using “LED” for any kind of LED TV with an LED backlight, they had to change the name. So OLED it was! OLEDs are, naturally, already LEDs, so they emit their own light. No need for color filters, no need for LCDs. When an OLED is off, it’s off… a perfect black. So they have had an advantage in contrast range over LCD televisions, though as mentioned, as LCD+LED really started sharing the display duties, these televisions got better. The best “LED” televisions are Quantum Dot Mini-LED TVs. And that’s continued into OLED. The original OLED televisions had separate red, green, and blue LED subpixels for every on-screen pixel. Today, you might find a Quantum Dot OLED, which has only blue LEDs, with red and green quantum dots over the subpixels used for red and green. And yet, OLEDs aren’t actually that similar to the LEDs used in mini-LED displays. Organic LEDs can be made in much simpler layers than inorganic LEDs, so it was easier at first to deliver the million of individual LEDs needed for a full LED display. However, OLEDs have some limits in terms of brightness and, at least historically, longevity. So the latest thing is micro-LEDs. These are the same kind of inorganic LED used for most LED applications other than displays, including home and industrial lighting these days. It’s just taken advanced in technology to deliver full displays with millions of such lights. And sure, as with LCD-LED, as with OLED, there are also quantum dot micro-LED displays. That simplifies the design in some ways by making every LED blue, then coating the red and green with quantum dots. Micro-LEDs offer brighter displays and at least the promise of longer life over OLEDs. Aside from the display, the internal part of a TV these days is a small computer, based on a system-on-chip not all that different than what you’d find on a smartphone, but generally lower power. There will of course be a System on chip containing a media processor able to efficiently decode the latest video formats, a CPU able to run a “smart TV” platform (Google TV, Android TV, WebOS, AppleTV, Tizen, Roku, etc), a graphics processor and maybe a full GPU, etc. The SoC will have Ethernet and WiFi connections, and may integrate or include on board a television tuner for OTA TV. Question: Is it realistic for tech companies to create a universal charger that works across devices and brands?
Answer: It is! For example, the various USB connectors have evolved to support just this. Originally delivering 2.5W power available for charging purposes — never enough — the USB specification has evolved through the Battery Charging specification — 7.5W, still not enough — to today’s Power Delivery specification, the most recent of which an support fast charging on phones all the way up to up to 240W for charging or powering high current devices like laptop and even small desktop computers. There’s just one catch: the thing everyone calls a “charger” isn’t a charger. It’s just a power supply. The more recent protocols makes it a smart power supply, sure, but it knows absolutely nothing about charging batteries. It offers somewhere between +5Vdc at 500mA and +48Vdc at 5A, depending on the version of the “charger” and the device it’s asked to power. What the powered device does with that power is up to the device, not the “charger.” This is the critical part of how USB is universal. The charger itself is embedded in any device that charges from a USB connector. That’s the second half of how it’s made universal. Your phone, your laptop, your camera, whatever is designed with a power management system and complete knowledge of its own charging needs. One additional aspect of this architecture is that, unlike the days of the dedicated power supply, a device connected to a USB power supply can’t necessarily rely on that power supply to provide enough power for its operation and charging. In the past, connecting a charger to your laptop might leave the battery completely unused except for charging purposes. Today, as it’s been for ages with smartphones, the device has to be designed to be able to use battery and external power at the same time when power loads get high, dropping back to charging when the loads drop.

Question: In FY 2024, were 99% of Democrats requesting to receive earmarks?
Answer: Don’t get me wrong, Democratic Congressfolks request earmarks. Republican Congressfolks request earmarks. No one else in government, Republican or Democratic, can directly request earmarks: it’s a Congressional thing. And pretty much every person in Congress, Republican or Democratic, has requested an earmark in a regular session at some point in time… but this year, not so much in the House. Earmarks of all kinds in the House had been on moratorium by policy since around 2011, but the Democrats did bring them back in 2021, when they held the House majority. The Republicans left them in place when they took over in 2023, at least initially. After earmarks were re-instituted, in 2022 there were still a few who held out. In Texas, for example, 19 Republican Representatives entirely swore off earmarks. All thirteen Democrats and six Republicans did… the top expenses were from the Republicans, but the Democrats had the long tail. [1] You can, of course, decide if you think earmarks are good or bad… I’d claim it’s hardly a foregone conclusion either way. Texas was kind of unique… despite its size, Red States South Carolina, Alabama, and Missouri out-earmarked Texas. That year, Texas was still #7 in total earmarks value for all projects, not just to non-profits. It’s not really a Blue State thing in general, though there’s a tradition among some on the right of opposing these that goes back to the Tea Party era. In the summer of 2023, the House of Representatives passed a policy against earmarks for any non-profit organization. That was done to block any earmarks for LGBT projects, which, sure, were being requested by Democrats, since Republicans hate the gay.[2] This did, however, shut down that kind of earmark for all of the House. The Republicans did this, of course, because they were getting pressure from conservative groups to officially “hate the gay” but, in order to avoid this becoming a big issue in the press, they blocks all earmarks of this class. This also cuts off hundreds of millions of dollars to a number of upcoming Republican projects, but hey, if you hate enough, you make sacrifices. This cuts off various religious organizations, Boys and Girls clubs, Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts, all veterans organizations, senior housing projects, work force retraining organizations, YMCA and YWCA branches, food banks, emergency shelters, domestic abuse centers, sports complexes for kids, etc. No such rule exists in the Senate. So nearly $1 billion of earmark spending was approved in the final 2024 spending bill passed by Congress, funding more than 900 different projects. The largest earmark for non-profits already legislated was from a Republican, Robert B. Aderholt of Alabama, which was $13 million for a STEM training facility. My sister Kathy — an educational psychologist — has worked on STEM projects in Alabama. They have proven extremely effective.

Question: Do Russians feel confined by an EU barrier? Someone in Moscow can today catch a train as far as Brest, Belarus, but can’t then change platforms & go all the way to Amsterdam via Warsaw & Berlin? How does it also work from Kaliningrad via Lithuania?
Answer: Russians feel confined by the Russian barrier. This is not the EU limiting travel. This is Russia, and their satellite countries like Belarus, limiting travel. Back in the 1990s I had a company in Hildesheim, Germany… in the West. It was crazy fast getting around Germany by car, thanks to excellent roads, a relatively small country compared to the USA, and that most beautiful of all traffic signs… … the end-of-speed-limit sign (without the number, it becomes the no-speed-limit-sign, also a beautiful thing). One year we started a project with the University of Dresden, in the former East Germany. So it was perfectly acceptable to drive to Dresden, so we did. Here’s the thing: there were very, very few roads in East Germany going East-West. The whole travel infrastructure, under Soviet domination, had been engineered to simply make it difficult, annoying, and very, very controlled if you wanted to go to the West. It’s like that in Western Russia. Russians may not always be precisely the same kind of prisoners in their own country that they were under the Soviet Union, but then again, Putin has been working since he took power decades ago to re-invent the Soviet Union in modern Russia. Russians are less free today than they were before Putin. Naturally, at the EU border, a Russian citizen travelling legally is going to need a passport and a visa to enter the EU. That’s no different than an EU citizen travelling to Russia, eh? That’s the normal way of thinking about things when it’s just about country-to-country travel. I need a passport these days to drive across the Mexican or Canadian border, eh, hoser? But when the goal of the traveler in your country isn’t ordinary travel, but escape to a request for asylum, you’re in a repressive country that will do what they need to do to make the means of escape difficult. That’s what prisons do.

Question: How many aircraft carriers did Russia have compared to the US before Donald Trump became president?
Answer: Neither Russia not the Soviet Union ever successfully built the kind of nuclear powered supercarrier that we Americans think of when someone says “aircraft carrier.” This is the Gerald R. Ford, the world’s largest aircraft carrier at 337m long and a 100,000t displacement. This is the first of Gerald R. Ford class carrier, the best of the USA’s fleet. There are four more like it under construction, the next one, the John F. Kennedy, is scheduled to be completed in 2025. A total of ten are planned over the next two decades. The Gerald R. Ford is powered by two nuclear reactors, carries up to 90 aircraft (combined fixed wing, helios, and drones). and 4,539 personnel. It has an electromagnetic launch system, multiple types of missiles, and based on my experience working on military-related projects, a whole bunch of stuff we don’t know about! The current electrical power generation from the reactors is about twice of what’s needed in the currently outfitted ship. There’s reserve for future enhancements such as free-electron laser directed-energy weapons, electric armor, future AI-heavy tracking systems, etc. The USA has also built the second-largest class of aircraft carrier in the world, the Nimitz class, at 332.8m long and a 97,000t displacement. We have ten of these, and they’re not all that much smaller, able to carry 60 aircraft and a crew, air wing, and staff of over 5,000. The flight deck of this ship is 4.5 acres in area, and they’re also powered by dual nuclear reactors. China’s first fully home grown aircraft carrier is the Fujian, with a length of 316m and a displacement of 80,000t. This is not fully deployed, but largely completed and undergoing testing this year. This is pretty comparable to the USA’s Kitty Hawk class, which was replaced by the Nimitz class. It’s estimated to support 40 fixed-wing and 12 helicopters, and it’s using electromagnetic launch systems. Despite the size, this is a conventionally powered ship. Maybe not surprisingly, the UK, a historic sea power, has the Queen Elizabeth class, at 284m long. There are currently two such ships, and the UK does not plan to build more. These ships have a total air and ship crew of around 1,600, and can support 40 aircraft. These are also conventionally powered. The Russians built four of these Kiev-class ships, kind of a classic battle cruiser with a landing deck added on, described as “heavy aviation cruisers” back in the 1970s. These are 273m long with a 45,000t displacement. This was the first type of Soviet ship capable of landing and launching fixed-wing aircraft, though really only VTOLs and helicopters. Russia has a pair of Moskva-class helicopter carriers prior to this. Two of these were sold to China as museum pieces, one was scrapped, and one was sold to the Indian Navy in 2004. The upgrade was the Kuznetsov-class aircraft carrying cruiser, which isn’t far from being a true aircraft carrier, capable of launching and landing conventional fixed-wing aircraft. It are 305m long, with a displacement of 55,000t, designated as an aircraft carrying cruiser rather than an aircraft carrier because the Montreaux Convention prevents full blown aircraft carriers in the Turkish Straights. Which would have made it a problem, given that these ships were being built on the Black Sea! This project began in 1990, but the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, with just a single commissioned ship, the Admiral Kuznetsov, which wasn’t fully functional until 1995. So technically, just before and just after Trump took office, Russia had one carrier. One that was past its useful life, in need of an overhaul. This ship was brought in for an overhaul in 2017, suffered serious damage due to dry dock accident in 2018, was scheduled for release in 2023, but now maybe sometimes this year (2024). This remains Russia’s only aircraft carrier, or aircraft carrying cruiser. A second ship was sold uncompleted by Ukraine in 1998 to China, along with the blueprints. China’s stated purpose in buying it was to launch a floating casino, but in fact, they finished the work and delivered the ship, the Lianoning, as China’s first aircraft carrier. China also delivered a second one, entirely made by the Chinese, in 2019. These two fill out China’s fleet of three carriers, along with the aforementioned Fujian. There was a supercarrier project, dubbed Ulyanovsk-class, but that was never completed. Work began in 1998, was stopped in 1991, and ultimately scrapped in 1992. All that beachfront, and so little interest in a world-class Navy! You can understand, though, with so little access to warm water ports, why all these carriers were originally built in Ukraine, back when it was a Soviet territory.

Question: Why is the 16 MP picture the default in a 64 MP camera?
Answer: It’s not. I bet you’re thinking of a smartphone’s camera, not a dedicated camera. It has to do with “pixels” versus color. Silicon image sensors don’t record color on their own. The image sensor is a large array of photodiodes, which are sensitive to some infrared, visible, and even in some cases ultraviolet light. If you take a photo using just the sensor, you get a monochrome image. In order to get color, the sensor is covered with a Color Filter Array (CFA). The most popular CFA uses the Bayer color pattern, which alternates green-red-blue-green filters in a 2x2 pixel array. This was invented by Kodak scientist Bryce Bayer back in 1974. In order to RGB color for each pixel, the neighboring pixels are interpolated for the missing two of the three primary colors. This can yield some color errors along edges, but it’s pretty good. Unless you camera is from Fujifilm, you probably have a Bayer CFA in your digital camera… Fujifilm has their own “X-Trans” pattern in some of their models. Note that, if your 64 megapixel sensor has a Bayer CFA, you’ll have 64 million color filters as well. Once smartphones cameras went much above 12–16 megapixels, they started using a variation of the Bayer filter dubbed Quad-Bayer by Sony and tetracell by Samsung. The basic idea here is that 2x2 arrays of pixels are covered by a single color filter. So you have 16 million color filters on your 64-megapixel sensor. Why do this? It’s kind of a hack to make the sensor more useful, a bit, for general purpose photography and videography. The standard mode for this sensor would be to bucket each 2x2 cell together, thus delivering 12 megapixels from a 48 megapixel sensor and 16 megapixels from a 64 megapixel sensor. That way, there’s a 1:1 match up between color and spatial resolution. However, there are different ways to do this. The software can shoot exactly the same thing in each 2x2 block, average them together, and get a low noise image. Or, it can run different exposures for each pixel in the 2x2 block, extending the dynamic range of the sensor at the price of additional noise. This allows the phone, for example, to shoot HDR video, not just photos. The other they they use this for is cropping. If you crop that 64 megapixel sensors for a “2x” digital zoom, you now have 16 megapixels of spatial resolution, though only 4 megapixels of color. Depending on how that crop is processed, you may get a better result than simply cropping to 4 megapixels on a 16 megapixel sensor. Though the way these are processed on phones currently, it’s often more an illusion of additional resolution than the real thing. Yikes! A smartphone company doing something just for the spec sheet that won’t be understood by the average consumer? I’m clutching my pearls! The other consideration is that the plastic lenses and small sensors used on smartphones, along with pixel sizes at 800nm, 675nm, even 550nm, means that there’s absolutely no optical 64 megapixels going on here, thanks to diffraction. So while you can probably shoot an image that records 64 megapixels on such a phone, that result does not constitute a real 64 megapixel image in the way a professional camera would deliver it. But wait… there’s more! When Samsung decided to excite the world’s population of smartphone photographers who are impressed by technical specs they absolutely do not understand, they released a 108 megapixel sensor, and used a 3x3 array of pixels under each filter element, which they dubbed nonacell. You read that right: 108 megapixels of spatial resolution, 12 megapixels of color information. These do make pretty good 12 megapixel sensors, for a phone. Samsung’s tag line for this is “More pixels. Epic details.” Nope. That’s not what you get with these things. Pretty much the same actual detail. Maybe some better color, as now a single sensor can both vary exposure and average pixels, some some dynamic range expansion, some noise reduction… maybe. I can see the tool here — the sensor — but not how the software chooses its use. And it gets even worse, because of course it does. Samsung’s ISOCELL HP1 sensor sports 200 million 600nm pixels. They’re grouped as 4x4 under a single color filter, yielding a total of 12.5 million colors on a 200 megapixel sensor. Now, looking at the 200MP and 50MP blocks in the drawing, how do you imagine they get the colors to work like that? Do the filters actually move around, as might be suggested here. No, they do not. Rather, they “re-matrix” the colors. So that “50 megapixel” block gets its red and blue pixel separate by moving around 2x2 blocks of the already-shot image. Ever play a tile puzzle as a kid? It’s basically that. So they’re swapping around actual image pixels to places they don’t begin to belong, in order to be able to use the same Bayer “de-matrix” engine to deliver an RGB image. Same idea going from the 12.5 megapixel image — the one that’s actually shot — to the 200 megapixel image. That’s the big reason I’m claiming it doesn’t come near to an actual 200 megapixel or 50 megapixel image. The 12.5 megapixel image is probably rather good for a phone, so that’s why it’s the 12MP, 12.5MP, or 16MP you get as default. There are far more complex image processing techniques that could get your 200 megapixel phone closer to real 200 megapixel or 50 megapixel images. One is like this: you split off red, blue, and green image planes, and interpolate with 2D curve fitting — basically, making a really good educated guess at the missing pixels in each color plane, not just a linear approximation (though even that’s better than the pixel skiggling). But it won’t matter, because the lens on your phone can’t begin to optically resolve a 50 megapixel image, much less a 200 megapixel image. It might well deliver “better than 12.5 megapixels” in the ideal case, but that real image improvement is lost based on the de-matrixing. You see more detail, because there is more detail, but it’s not correct detail because of the fact you’re moving around all those pixels — moving them away from their proper spatial location.

Question: Why are more people leaning towards hybrid vehicles over electric vehicles according to recent Gallup poll findings?
Answer: It’s not just favoring hybrids, but at least a momentary loss of confidence in BEVs. It’s impossible to say for sure, but I suspect at least part of this is explained in one word: Tesla. Question: If a felon can't vote, how can Trump, who is now a felon, vote & possibly become president?
Answer: The ability of a convicted felon to vote is entirely dependent on the state they’re registered to vote in. Since Trump is registered in Florida, it’s quite true: he can’t vote. Except that maybe he can. Florida has a rule that basically, things like suspension of rights due to felony conviction in other states follow the rules of the other states. This makes some sense, because, of course, Florida can’t directly administer the suspension or restoration of a felon’s right when that depends on another state’s laws. So Trump will fall under New York law, which is much more lax than Florida’s. If Trump is incarcerated in any way on election day, he will be ineligible to vote in Florida. And in fact, if he were to vote by mail, that would at that point in time be another crime. However, as of 2021[1]a felon’s rights are automatically restored upon their release, even if released on parole. No need to file a petition as one would in Florida. Of course, no one will know Trump’s sentencing until July 11, but this kind of white collar crime, while eligible for up to 5 years in prison per offense, rarely results in prison time[2] in New York. It’s possible, particularly given Trump’s terrible attitude during the trial, his complete lack of remorse, the large number of felony counts, his continued attacks on the court, etc. But in his favor, it’s his first felony offence, and he’s an old, obese, sickly man. He’s more than likely going to be released on parole, though as standard in all parole cases, he could be incarcerated for any violation of the parole. That would include regular meetings with his parole officer and explicit permission for leaving New York, just like any other schlub. House arrest is also a possibility. One’s ability to run and service as President is not dependent on one’s state of residency, but by the rules established in the Constitution. All the pertinent parts of the Constitution don’t add up to all that much: Now, it’s true that nearly every State applies their own rules about what a candidate has to do to get on the state’s ballot, though this last year’s ruling in Trump v. Anderson calls to question any state restrictions on ballot access for Federal office. The shit hasn’t hit the fan on that one yet, but just wait. In any case, even with broad interpretation, felons, in prison, on parole, or with restored rights having served their times, are free to run for the Presidency. It’s happened twice before, though not from major party candidates. Eugene V. Debs ran for President on the Socialist ticket in 1920 and won 3.4% of the popular vote! Professional lunatic Lyndon LaRouche ran for President eight times, and in 1988, he ran from prison as well. As with all his other runs, he had negligible support. So there is precedence! Where’s the logic in allowing felons to run? Simple: the Founders expected the population and political leaders to act in the interest of the country and to support law and order. There was no concept that a large number of people in the USA would follow a party or an individual to the detriment of the country. It simply never occurred to them that it would be necessary to ban felons, traitors, etc. from holding office, because it never occurred to them that good people would vote them in.

Question: How likely is it that Donald Trump will lose the right to vote if he's convicted of a felony?
Answer: In Florida, it's automatic. You lose your right to vote on a felony conviction. Your rights can ordinarily only be restored by way of a petition, and only after serving your time and paying any fines that might be involved. Trump, of course, is a Florida Man. Here’s the thing, though… this was a conviction in New York, not Florida. I looked this up, after being prompted by a few comments, and I guess it makes sense: Florida defers to the rules of the conviction state. So Trump will see his rights suspended and restored under New York law. That’s actually better for Trump, because in New York, a felon’s voting rights are only suspended while incarcerated. If he’s released on parole, his rights are restored. So unless he’s in prison or under house arrest on Election Day, Trump will get to vote. This makes sense if you think about it. If Trump were convicted in Florida, Florida would be in charge of administering punishment, including suspension of rights. But the conviction in New York means that New York is in charge. So Florida has no direct control the management of those rights lost or when they’re restored. His major loss of rights, freedom to travel, prison or parole, etc. are entirely up to New York, not Florida. The judge in the case will pass sentence on July 11. No word on whether he’s ordering a physical or psychological evaluation of Trump prior to sentencing. That would be pretty likely if he’s being considered for an actual prison sentence. Working against Trump are his abysmal childish behavior during the trial and the large number of felony counts. Working for Trump are his advanced age, poor health, his first time felony conviction in New York State, and the fact it was 34 low level non-violent felonies, which generally do not land those convicted in prison all by themselves, but typically sentenced but released on parole. If released on parole, Trump would have to get permission from a parole officer for any out-of-state travel. But he’s probably used to that, since he’s restricted to the Southern District of Florida as condition of his bail in the Espionage/Stolen documents case and can’t leave without permission from the court.

Answer: After looking at bill, I suggest that you actually look at the bill yourself, rather than just parrot the lies you’ve heard from some provocateur on the far right. This is a bill, not a law, and it’s still in formation. Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Is it possible for someone who has never written before to write something meaningful and get it published?
Answer: Well, it’s probably a good idea to write things before trying to get something published. It’s awfully difficult to publish a book you haven’t written yet :-) And your very first writing assignment? Probably not a novel or even a short story for publication. Much as your first time driving a car should not be in a stock car race or a {purposeful] demolition derby. Much as your first time picking up a guitar should not be the same day you’re recording your new album. Natural talent is an amazing thing if you have it, but everyone needs practice. Think about it… every writer has a first book, a first article, a first whatever. I mean, I’ve had well over 100 magazine articles published back in the 80s and 90s, I’ve written small sections in non-fiction books that were published, but I found far more readers here on Quora, and still have not published my own novel or anything. If I did write a book, I’m not exactly “a person who has never written before”… but I would be a person publishing a first novel. This is Andy Weir, a software engineer who also became a self-published author. He published his own stories and comics on his personal web sit going back to the early 2000s. He tried to publish an early novel, but failed. He got some real attention in a short story, “The Egg,” published on his web site, that was adapted in some other small productions, including YouTube videos, a play, and rapper Logic’s third album. Andy put on his engineering hat for a new novel, “The Martian,” working out the details of several scientific fields to create his realistic and, IMHO, excellent story about an astronaut stranded on Mars. This was published as a serial, in the fashion of many famous 1940s and 1950s science fiction stories, though on his website, rather than in monthly magazines like “Analog.” When complete, he put up the full eBook “self-published” on Amazon for $0.99… this is a pretty easy thing to do on Amazon. It became a Kindle Bestseller — when I first heard about it, bought it, read it, loved it — and then was sold to a conventional publisher. Hey, it’s always easier to find a publisher if you already have a hit! Once published conventionally, it debuted as #12 on the New York Times bestseller list. The book was optioned by 20th Century Fox in 2013, worked into a screenplay, then produced as a major film directed by Ridley Scott and starring Matt Damon. Pretty good, eh? This is why Andy’s occupation is now listed online as “novelist” rather than “programmer!” So what’s the lesson? I think a big part of it is, if you’re a writer, you need to write. You almost certainly won’t be this successful with your first — or in this case, second — novel. But you can write, you have more resources to help you find an audience today than every before in human history, but just as much competition. Every other author is working toward these same goals if they’re interested. There are a number of novelists I know here on Quora who are able to build an audience for their writing in a purely organic way — if folks are interested in what you’re writing, they’re more likely to want more!

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: What is the process for a sitting president who has been impeached but resigns before their trial in the Senate?
Answer: Process? If a President — or any other elected or, in some cases, appointed person in office — is Impeached, the goal of those backing that Impeachment is the removal of that person from service in office for a cause. The trial in the Senate evaluates that cause, and before anyone points it out, yes, this is a political process, not a matter of civil or criminal law. So if the present day politics have most members of a party agreeing “my party, right or wrong”, then perhaps the person is acquitted in the Senate. However, if that person does resign before a Senate trial, then the goal of the Impeachment is met. There’s no additional process necessary. The one advantage of resigning is that, in the event of a conviction in the Senate, an additional vote can bar the impeached individual from holding future office. That’s more difficult to do in the event of a resignation.

Question: Why did NASA astronaut Don Pettit say that we don’t have the technology to go to the moon, that we destroyed it? What was he intimating?
Answer: So here’s Don Pettit: astronaut, chemical engineer PhD, renowned space photographer, and the first man to invent a thing in space and win a patent for it (the Zero Gravity Coffee Cup!). Dr. Pettit has logged more than 370 days in space and over 13 spacewalk hours. Like most astronauts, he’s a truly exceptional human being, and currently at 69 years old, the oldest serving astronaut at NASA. His actual quote: I'd go to the moon in a nanosecond. The problem is, we don't have the technology to do that anymore. We used to, but we destroyed that technology and it is a painful process to build it back again. So, maybe you need an engineer’s explanation… I volunteer (I’m also a photographer, but tragically, not an astronaut). What Don is referring to isn’t our simple lack of an Saturn V rocket, but rather, the loss of the system that delivers the parts to make additional rockets. NASA rockets are built by a hugely complex coordinated effort of hundreds if not thousands of private companies contracted by NASA to build the various components. But that’s really not the core of what he’s saying here, I believe. President Richard Nixon cancelled the last several Apollo missions in September of 1970, thus ending the production of new Saturn V super-heavy lift vehicles and other critical components. NASA still flew Apollo 16 and Apollo 17, both missions in 1972, but NASA had planned to fly though Apollo 20. So, lacking any orders for new Saturn V rockets from NASA and any likely possibility of such orders, all of those contractors who built the parts for Saturn V rockets started dismantling their production lines and repurposing them for something else. The same thing they do for any other contract project. It’s not as if NASA had a full soup to nuts Saturn V production line (they did final assembly) and sent Neil, Buzz, and all the boys down with sledgehammers to “Hulk Smash” the remnants of the Apollo program. I’m not pretending to speak for Dr. Pettit, but I have a pretty good idea that he was expressing his frustration in NASA’s directions, which were my frustrations as well, as a kid who grew up watching manned rockets take off and fly farther every time, only for all that to end before I could get involved. Astronauts fly to space, and so of course, as an astronaut, he was heartbroken by the end of travel to the Moon and beyond. Quite a few scientists, NASA and otherwise, love their probes and robots and don’t see so much value in manned travel, and so today we have Mars, a planet entirely occupied by robots. Had NASA been funded and, of course, permitted by the political winds to keep sending people up, we’d likely have humans there today. What he’s absolutely not suggesting is that you’d want Saturn V today, but rather, if the Apollo program had not been cancelled, if we had kept flying manned missions, the Saturn V would naturally have been replaced by improved rockets, and those replaced by the next generation. If you’ve seen the television show For All Mankind, that’s kind of the idea. The technology would have evolved faster and more cleanly than waiting 35 years to restart, and even at that by fits and sputters: Constellation, Asteroid Redirect Mission, Orion, and finally SLS and Artemis. But the Artemis I mission has flown around the Moon, and while it was unmanned, the SLS super-heavy lift vehicle did propel the Orion spacecraft that’s designed for humans to travel to the Moon and back. Artemis II is planned for sometime in or after September of 2025, with a crew: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen. The old is always “destroyed” to make way for the new. Ford lacks the technology to build a Model-T today. Intel lacks the technology to build an 8088 today. McDonnell-Douglas lacks the technology to build a DC-3 today. Those were single products, sure, but also product lines that were in continuous development and improvement. And still continues today. There was a Kickstarter project called Reflex launched in 2017, with the goal of creating a new fully manual, modular 35mm camera system. They last posted in 2021, discussing problems, then the apparent impossibility, of obtaining a mechanical focal plane shutter mechanism. That technology had been destroyed, and while they could manage other parts of the camera system, that was apparently beyond the capabilities of a small group like this. Pentax is supposedly working on a more modest compact film camera for release this year… maybe they’ll have better luck. But even existing camera companies didn’t simply have that technology lying around… I suspect they’ll adapt modern parts. The old stuff makes way for the new. That’s true of ideas, too, particularly those silly ideas of pre-scientific people that expired about 2,500 years ago, like “Flat Earth,” in the light of improved human knowledge. Question: Is it advisable to invest in a high-quality camera and use inexpensive lenses? Why or why not? If yes, what setup do you recommend?
Answer: You can, though I wouldn’t advise it. Here’s my Fujifilm X-Pro1 with four lenses, each made by 7artisans in China, each fully manual, and at an average cost of under $100.. I bought two of them used. This isn’t my main system, but I bought this for a project. These lenses are based on old Zeiss optical formula, not modern optical CAD — the reason you can pay $2,000-$3,000 for a state-of-the-art high-end prime lens for Canon or Nikon — and so you may not be happy with such glass. I was going for a very film-like look. It worked, in part because we associate film photography with older lens design. In general, though, if you’re just starting out, get a low-end camera and lens. But that’s also why, once you master your camera, you’ll get far better results than with any smartphone. When you do spend money, know why you’re buying a thing. Your first move should be a better lens, because that will be your weak link with nearly any camera, even an older used one like the X-Pro1. At some future point, yeah, you might upgrade the camera body, assuming by then you’ve figured out that you chose right when you picked the system you’re using. Maybe you didn’t! Once you understand photography and your place in it, you’ll be experienced enough to learn about the gear that’s available and perhaps make a better choice — for you — going forward into owning a complete system.

Question: Can screens be created with a "perfect" quality that resembles real life rather than just having high resolution?
Answer: Resolution-wise? Sure. There’s no need for “perfection” since our eyes are fairly limited instruments. But there are levels of complexity here you might not understand just yet. Each of your eyes has about 6 million color “sensors” called cone cells. Yeah, lots of people like to claim there are way more, but that’s misunderstanding how the eye works. Your combined vision is able to use the gigantic computer your eyes are attached to — your brain — to about quadruple the effective resolution. So a display with more or less 24 megapixels per eye is about what you need. An UltraHD-8K screen is about 33 megapixels, pretty close, so let’s start with that. And that’s not even taking into account the imperfections in the lenses of your eyes. Let’s magically turn the 75″ UltraHD-4K television in my Florida Room into an UltraHD-8K television. At some distance from the television, your vision won’t be acute enough to differentiate the 8K display from a 4K display, which suggests, just based on image resolution, you won’t be able to differentiate the view from reality, eh? There actually multiple metrics for viewing a television in terms of a theater display. One is what I just mentioned, the distance needed to get “value” in the higher resolution of a display, versus the next resolution down. If the display isn’t large enough for your viewing distance, there’s no value in additional spatial resolution. The other is the ideal viewing distance from a cinematographic viewpoint: how should you best enjoy a film experience? Not everyone absolutely agrees on this. Sony recommends the minimum viewing distance for a 4K display at 1.5x the height, and for an 8K television at 0.75x the height. My 75″ television is about 37″ high, so the minimal distance for my actual television — the point at which my eyes (with average vision) can’t resolve individual pixels — will be 55.5″ = 4′ 7.5″ = 141cm. That’s closer than I’m actually going to sit. Make that an 8K television and that distance shrinks to 27.75″ = 2′ 3.75″ = 70.5cm. I’m pretty sure I’m not sitting just ~3ft from the television. Not my Florida Room How far should I sit working the math the other way, as a cinema screen? There are both SMPTE and THX recommendations for this. The recommendation is based on the ideal angle of view for a motion picture screen. SMPTE recommends only a minimum recommended viewing angle of 30° viewing angle, which means about 10.2ft = 3.1m. THX specs a recommended viewing angle of 27° and a recommended viewing angle of 36°, 11.8ft to 8.4ft away. I’m actually sitting at a maximum of 8ft = 2.4m. So based on a proper cinematic experience, I’m about as close as you’d want to be, and yet, I’m plenty far away enough to not be able to tell my display from reality — I can’t see the pixels. Most people with 4K televisions have them so far away, they can’t really tell them from Full HD. Except that for 4K, you also got wider color range, aka HDR, so in fact, if your in to high quality video, a 4K display with HDR is valuable because it’s increasing color resolution, even if your not going to see an effective increase in spatial resolution given the limitations of your human eyes. I also have proven to myself, and hopefully my readers, that replacing that 75″ 4K television with a 75″ 8K television is just plain silly. It won’t change my viewing experience. As well, going to a larger display to maybe try and justify 8K will start to make normal cinematic viewing less comfortable, like when you have to sit in the front rows in a theater … well, other than the craning your neck looking up part. The problem here isn’t my display resolution, but the fact that reality isn’t a flat, fixed screen. It doesn’t stop at the corners, it’s all around you, in three dimensions. Your static view is stereoscopic — each eye sees a slightly different representation of the three dimensional world, and yeah, the television industry had their flirtation with 3DTV. That failed, in part because of very limited content: good stereoscopic video requires real stereoscopic cameras, dual cameras with proper interocular distance between them, in order to give you a comfortable 3D representation, rather than something that gives you a headache or makes you motion sick. Most content was “fake 3D” — some computer algorithms applied to standard films to create a stereoscopic mish-mash representation. But the other part was simply that reality isn’t stereoscopic, either. It’s actually three dimensional, which you experience in subtle ways you don’t even think about. So your brain can tell the difference between a “3D” screen and a window, because the view you see through the window doesn’t react as you move your head. It might be close, given that most films are showing action at a distance, but it’s not perfect. The place to look for a better “seems like reality” display is, not surprising, the VR Headset. My Oculus 2 is far from perfect. But when you’re viewing through such a device, because it’s got excellent motion tracking, the virtual world of the display reacts close to the way your brain expects reality to behave. The 3D model of your virtual surroundings is rendered slightly different for each eye, but you’re seeing things the way you expect to see reality. If you look up, there’s an up, if you look down, there’s a down. There are things happening at the periphery of your vision. Now, sure, you’re always going to know you have a headset on your head. But with higher and higher resolution micro-displays and faster GPUs, these things will eventually get good enough that, visually anyway, while you will of course know you’re not experiencing reality, your mind probably will accept what you see as real, if it’s rendered to be real. It’s going to require such a device. This can never happen in a flat display panel, no matter how good. And at least for home cinema, we’re already pretty much at the point of overkill. We’re getting 8K displays, which are kind of a “because we can” thing for the television industry, but there’s really no use for them. 16K displays still make sense for micro-displays in your 3D VR headset. That gets you coverage to the periphery of your vision, and lets you create a 30°–36° virtual cinema screen in full resolution within your virtual environment. Once that’s possible, we’re pretty much done with expanding spatial resolution in micro-displays, too. The reason no one has these 16K VR displays just yet isn’t the display. Such displays are possible today. What’s not possible is a head-mounted, battery powered GPU that’s able to render yet-again-better imagery at that resolution to justify the higher display resolution. Read More

Question: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis signed legislation into law that eliminates squatters' rights and increases penalties against offenders. Do you think this is an effective way to quell the chaos?
Answer: I don’t usually agree with DeSantis and the Republican trifecta and triplex that we’ve got in Florida these days. But in this case, they’re not wrong. Yes, this is currently a Republican talking point, and they absolutely exaggerate problem, as one does. Many on the left kind tend to minimize it, suggest its rare, or ignore it completely. Squatting isn’t new, and became an issue, including a political issue, in much of Europe before it was much discussed — or abused — in the USA. In recent times in Europe, many countries have moved to varying degrees of criminalization. Though, of course, there’s some reasonable space for argument between an organized group of squatters occupying a long abandoned building and working to make it habitable, versus an organized criminal gang looking to move into individual homes that are only vacant for short periods of time. It’s this latter case that the Florida law it targeted. There have been laws, built up over the years pretty much everywhere in the USA, designed to protect legitimate rental contract holders from being unduly evicted from the rental properties they occupy. Such laws help protect the renter against abuse by the property owner. If eviction were not regulated, a landlord could immediately evict a renter in the case of any dispute, regardless of who’s in the right. So these laws are important. And increasingly, they’re being abused by squatters. These days, a group of squatters may come prepared to assume control of a home. These may be organized criminals, looking to sack a house while they live their rent-free as long as possible. They’re not just homeless looking to shelter in a long abandoned building. They plan ahead, even doing research on the property they plan to take over. They’ll bring a forged tenant’s contract, for example. So when the owner summons the sheriff to have them evicted, they can often remain, as now this becomes an issue for the courts. The new Florida law includes a number of criminal penalties for doing this. Most states, including Florida, also have adverse possession laws that enable those squatting or otherwise occupying land that is not theirs but has effectively been abandoned, and this does not alter these laws at all. The basic idea is that, if a person occupies and maintains or improves land that’s functionally abandoned, after some period of time, they may file to claim adverse possession, which would ultimately grant them permanent title to the land. I ran into this when I bought my shore house in Delaware. It turns out that the property lines were drawn rather weird, houses are largely parallel to the street, not relative to property lines or each other. And so I discovered my neighbor’s driveway extended a bit on to my land. If I chose to ignore that, she could have at some point claimed legal possession, simply by the fact that she was occupying it with my knowledge as the owner. I offered to formalize the situation by leasing her the land, but ultimately she decided to remove the driveway that extended over the property line. This no doubt happened because the Homeowners Association, which governs the building of structures, doesn’t consider driveways a structure and so doesn’t look over any plans, if such plans even exist on a new driveway project. I do think they missed one really obvious thing: could the property have been rented at all. One sure fire way to ensure that there’s no confusion with regular homeowners is to require all rental properties to be declared as rental properties (even part time, like an Airbnb, which is a big thing in parts of Florida), and to make it illegal, with stiff fines, for anyone to rent without registering. This would allow the local governments to offer rental home mapping, creating the additional benefit of offering perspective home buyers an idea of whether they’re considering a home with actual neighbors or not. Under this rule, when the sheriff gets a call about squatters, he knows without question that they’re squatters. If they produce a tenant’s agreement, he’ll have good reason to suspect it’s a forgery, and given that’s now a crime, grounds for arrest, not simply eviction. Of course, tenants, when renting, would have a copy of the landlord’s renter certification, so they know up from they’re not being scammed in some way by the landlord. No, it’s not perfect — not Florida HB 621, and not my additional solution. But I understand the issues, and they do make sense. Florida has a large number of part-time residents, either “snowbirds” who winter in Florida (like Donald Trump) or “sunbirds” who summer somewhere cooler… I guess 90F+ days in April are not for everyone :-) This means that an unusual percentage of homes are left vacant for months at a time, potential prey for organized squatters. Laws have to evolve to meet the changing tactics of criminal enterprises. Read More

Question: Why did Intel discontinue the use of Pentium chips in laptops? Was it due to a decrease in performance or other reasons?
Answer: Intel released the first Pentium, also known as the i586, in 1993. This was Intel’s next major push both into technology but also into branding. Competitive x86 processors by then could also work a “5” or a “6” into their names, but they couldn’t copy Intel on a new brand for their product line. The Pentium brand persisted through the Pentium 2, Pentium 3, and Pentium 4 as Intel’s consumer flagship processor. However, the Pentium 4 had become a bit problematic. Dubbed the Netburst Architecture, this iteration pushed to very high clock speeds — clock speed had sadly become an important consumer metric in the marketplace — with super long pipelines, lots of power consumption, but little real improvement in performance. The Netburst Architecture proved very fast at some things, but basically, any time code didn’t run quite as expected, it took massive penalties thanks in a big part to the deep instruction pipeline: 20 stages in Willamette, 31 stages in Prescott. That’s versus 14 stages in the Pentium III and 12 in the AMD Athlon64 at the time. In addition, Intel had expected to keep tweaking up the clock speed — one of the main reasons for such a deep pipeline — but failed to really get there. Intel had initially claimed they’d get the Pentium 4 to 10GHz! They topped out at 3.8GHz. Did I mention the high power needed? In order to support laptops, Intel, specifically Intel Israel, proceeded along parallel lines and evolved the P6 architecture — specifically, the last version of the Pentium III — toward a lower power design, versus their previous process of evolving the high-end processor down for lower power use. This became the Pentium M in 2003. Which became a hit in tiny desktops and embedded processing in addition to the laptop use. As it turned out, this was a good move. Intel eventually introduced a whole new architecture, branded the Intel Core Architecture, as their replacement for the Pentium 4. Could they simply have called it Pentium 5? Of course, it’s only branding. But the Pentium 4 had seriously damaged Intel’s reputation. While they’re not brand new, the last versions of the Pentium are still available in off-the-shelf laptops. Intel has announced that they’re staring to phase out the Pentium and Celeron lines, but they have not yet at the time of this writing. This one, for example, the Lenovo IdeaPad 1 14IGL7. This incorporates the Intel Pentium Silver N5030, a four core processor running at a 1.1GHz base clock, with overclocking to 3.1GHz. The laptop contains 4GiB DRAM and 128GB of eMMC flash. It’s $185 on Amazon. Intel’s line, from top performance, on down, includes: Core i9 Core i7 Core i5 Core i3 Intel Processor Pentium Gold Pentium Silver Celeron Atom Intel is pushing the Pentium and Celeron lines into very low cost laptops, including Chromebooks. Some of these lower end processors also make sense in embedded applications, and that’s the only target for Intel’s Atom processors. They had a bit of a failure of their own when first sold into Intel’s NetBook concept. It’s pretty clear: Intel needs to stay far away from using the word net in any future products! Question: Will having both an M.2 NVMe and SATA improve the speed of a computer?
Answer: Mass storage has an effect on a computer’s speed, but it’s largely just for the operating system partition. Depending on what you’re doing, other things may or may not even care about your storage performance. Many things are CPU or GPU bound, but booting your system, loading up programs, etc. will benefit from the fastest system drive you’d like to get. Adding a second drive of any kind will only impact that if you’re building a RAID, and in that case, you want both drives to be the same. I have this mini-PC on my desk at my vacation house. It’s got a 4TB M.2 PCIe/NVMe drive as the main drive, which pretty much helps define overall performance. It’s also got a 4TB SATA drive, which is just dandy for storing large amounts of data, but has no significant effect on system performance. Sure, copying between the two would be faster if that second drive were also PCIe, but that was not an option on this unit. This one is about as tricked out as a tiny PC can get, but if you want more available options, you probably need a bigger system.

Question: How long can a hard drive disk store information when powered down?
Answer: There’s quite a bit of variation in data longevity on a hard drive, particularly if you’re looking back over the years. A modern drive using the gigantic magnetoresistance (GMR) effect for storage might last 20 years on the shelf. An older, heavily-used drive might start losing data after a month. The concern with that new drive isn’t the magnetic storage as much as the mechanical components. When a drive dies, usually after around five years of continuous use, it’s nearly always a mechanical failure. There’s no guarantee that some problems won’t have developed in the mechanical bits over a 20 year storage period. Depending on storage conditions, things can corrode, lubricants can dry up, etc. The Active Drive HDDs and SSDs are, in fact, used in servers for many, many years. But these last long though active means, not simply sticking the unit on a shelf. HDDs for reliable storage are always put in RAID configurations. The RAID controllers can handle single or sometimes double drive failure without loss of data, and they let an administrator know when to swap out a failing drive. SSDs themselves have on-board garbage collection software that watches cell aging, stale/deleted data, and will move data around to keep the it fresh before failures can occur. This usually runs when the SSD is idle, but it’s basically up to the manufacturer. This can be enhanced manually via the TRIM function in systems that support sending that command over the disc interface. Anyway, actively managed SSDs are reliable for a very long period of time, their lifetime generally measured in terms of data written, not hours of operation. Most modern drives have self-monitoring that warns a computer operating system of the aging and potential failure of portions of the drive. Not all operating systems use this information, but it’s there. This helps prevent an unexpected sudden failure of a drive. Small bit dropouts are hidden by the redundant encoding of data on your drive (ECC), so there are times, HDD or SSD, when you pass a threshold and the whole thing just fails. That’s why backup is critical… it’s easier and more reliable than trying to restore data from a just-failed drive. Alternatives: Flash/Charge Trap Memory What’s your alternative? The world is quickly moving to SSDs as prime storage, so what about those? It’s true that a flash or, these days, a charge trap device can last ten years or more on the shelf without bit rot. Maybe longer. However, those are not the devices you’re using. A flash or charge trap memory cell works by storing electrons on the floating gate of a field-effect transistor. It’s called a floating gate because it’s surrounded by some sort of insulator on all sides, so that once the charge is put in place, it basically stays put. That charge can be read back without being disturbed. Flash is written by Fowler–Nordheim tunneling, a quantum effect in which, under high voltage, electrons can cross an insulating barrier. Once written, the charge is fairly stable, but due to quantum uncertainty, electrons do gradually find their way though the insulating barrier, even when off. So it’s not stored charge forever. That’s for what we call single-level charge (SLC) flash today, which means each flash cell stores a single bit of information. Thing is, that’s kind of wasteful. The charge stored can be, in fact, an analog value. You’re storing lots of electrons on your floating gate, so why not precisely control the charge written to allow each cell to store more than one bit! That’s exactly what’s done. A cell can store 1, 2, 3, or 4 bits of information by using different charge levels. But storing more per cell results in shorter cell life — fewer write-erase cycles — and shorter data longevity. Most consumer flash storage is TLC or QLC. I just priced a 32GB USB SLC drive at $131 (DigiKey), while the first consumer drive I found on Amazon, probably QLC, is three for $18.50. That’s why your SSD doesn’t likely last ten years on the shelf. There are JEDEC classes for SSDs. As the chart shows, they rate a consumer drive with moderate use for one year on the shelf, and an Enterprise drive used 24/7 for three months on the shelf. This is after 1,000 hours of use without active failure. And that’s a big part of it… that brand new drive, written once, might actually get you 5 years, but you don’t really know. After use, it’s almost certainly to have bit rot in 5 years. Of course, you’re bound to have heard or experienced yourself that time you found the old USB stick or SD card from years back and everything on it was 100%. Sure, that’s possible, but it depends on quite a bit. Some of it’s heat — a flash device stored in the cool will retain data significantly longer than one in heat. If you’re thinking of a very old drive, it’s likely it was an SLC design and used very large flash cells with a very large number of electrons. Those can retain data longer than today’s parts, though not always. Alternatives: Tape One of the oldest forms of computer storage is magnetic tape. For a large business, LTO tape these days can deliver 15–30 years of safe archival, but this requires very tightly controlled temperature and environment. And since most LTO drives cost several thousand dollars, they’re not a popular consumer choice. Older formats like DAT cost far less, but you’re probably looking at used or refurbished hardware, though data tapes are still available new. Alternatives: Optical Consumer-based optical discs have long been a handy means of portable storage, but are they any good sitting on a shelf? The Library of Congress did some testing on properly stored CD and DVD discs based on standard organic dye technology and found them good for at least 30 years. Organic dyes do eventually fade, but mostly due to ultraviolet light, a bit due to heat over long periods of time. CDs have potential risk of oxidation of the reflecting layer, other than those with gold sputtering. Any CD made for longer term storage is likely to have a more durable lacquer coating than regular consumer glass masters or cheap CD-Rs. DVDs have polycarbonate on both sides, so they’re more resistant to reflective layer corruption, but that’s also dependent on the adhesive used to bind the two platters. Blu-ray’s standard BD-R, now dubbed HTL BD-Rs, use a non-organic layer of copper and silicon. The disc starts out shiny, the laser melts the two materials together to create the “pit”. These are pretty robust, with an expected life of 50–100+ years. However, some of the manufacturers of optical discs had a great deal of money invested in CD-R and DVD-R production lines, and introduce dye-based BD-Rs. These are dubbed LTH (low-to-high) because the way dye-based discs are written, the dye covers the reflective surface and turns clear when hit with the laser. These are not expected to last any longer than conventional CDs and DVDs. In all cases, how they’re stored matters, too. And finally, there’s a proprietary non-organic disc known as M-Disc. These are HTL like standard BD-R but require more power to write, thus, you need a drive specifically designed to burn M-Disc. Companies have made CD and DVD M-Discs as well. While CD-R and DVD-R is normally LTH, the M-Disc drives, which are needed anyway, handle the difference. Reading is universal. M-Disc developer Millenniata, Inc. claims the discs are good for 1,000 years. I can’t say, but if mine start failing in 500 years and I’m annoyed by that, that’s a high-class problem. The main problem with consumer-grade optical media is the small size. The largest disc is the BD-XL 4-layer BD-R, at 125GB. In these days of terabyte SSDs, you’ll need more than a handful of those for a full backup/archival. Alternatives: Online Finally, for your backup and archival pleasure, there are many kinds of online backup available. There was a time when data connections to the internet were too slow and too expensive for this to be practical, but today it’s practical. What you get when you backup to the “cloud” (aka, someone else’s computer) is enterprise-class storage, which is managed by a professional team. So your data is pretty secure, though nothing’s perfect. Most online companies allow data restoration via either download or by shipping out a hard drive, depending on your needs. Of course, you’re subject to the health of your backup company. Some folks choose a dedicated backup company that does a great deal of enterprise work for big business as well as their consumer options, while others leverage huge companies like Apple or Google, who probably aren’t going anywhere any time soon. There can be downsides. You should have questions about the integrity of the data you upload to an online backup company. Their not losing your data is the primary concern, but you also don’t want others to have access to that data. While an online backup is accessible, it’s still not as accessible as the HDD, tape, or optical disc on your shelf. But that’s also a good thing sometimes. If your house is, for example, stomped by Godzilla, your backup will be safe online, most likely. If your backups are in the same room or house as your computers, they’re backups but not true archival companies. Those will be in another location. The Alternative: Redundancy! As the Grateful Dead said, “Too much of everything is just enough.” Which is true when it comes to storing data long-term. When something fails and you can get it all back, that’s an amazing feeling. I had an SSD fail on me last year, and it was one I used to store a large number of photos. I had an online backup… yeah! When I didn’t see coming was the fact that, over some time, the SSD had been dropping a bit of corruption into some of the files as it was failing — there’s that disc health monitoring that Windows isn’t doing. So while I could get my online backups, some were corrupt. One good thing about online backups: you probably have more than one generation of backup. So I proceeded to look back and, sure enough, found a time before things went all weird. But hey… these were photos! I also had a book full of BD-XL backups of my photos. Not the very, very latest, but most of those missing. So by the time I was done, I had it all back. As well as few more BD-XLs full of recent photos.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Can you explain the difference between an M.2 PCIe NVME drive and an M.2 SATA drive?
Answer: All SSDs work essentially the same way. There’s a flash memory controller that parallels multiple banks of flash memory, permitting very high speed operation. There’s usually a DRAM controller that manages a block of DRAM for caching. There’s an embedded processor that’s used to implement the specific protocols needed to read, erase, and write blocks of flash memory, and there’s some kind of interface. These days, we typically use very high speed serial interfaces. Serial ATA (SATA) is one such serial interface, PCI Express (PCIe) is another. There are a whole bunch of different M.2 card types, which are identified by the notch, or key, in the M.2 edge connector. The M.2 card was invented primarily as a replacement for the mSATA and PCIe Mini-Card used in laptop computers. Most laptops implement their WiFi and, lately, SSDs on such cards. B-keyed card is much like a PCIe Mini-Card, capable of supporting either SATA or dual-link PCIe. An M-keyed card supports either SATA or quad-link PCIe. Not all B or M keyed sockets support both SATA and PCIe, that’s up to the implementers of the system. An M.2 SATA drive is using, as you might expect, the Serial ATA interface. That’s a data link with one channel for read, one channel for write, that can run at up to 6Gb/s at the link level, up to 600MB/s drive throughput. This version of an M.2 drive will be implemented with an SSD Controller that uses SATA. Most companies are no longer manufacturing SATA M.2 cards. SATA has largely been replaced by PCIe and NVMe. An M.2 NVMe PCIe drive is very similar, only using the PCI Express interface. PCI Express can aggregate multiple links, two links on a Key-B card and four links on a M-keyedcard. A single Gen 3 PCIe link supports 8GT/s, while a single Gen4 PCIe link supports 16GT/s, where T=transaction. As with SATA, all serial buses deliver slightly lower actual throughput than the low-level rating suggests, because all control information has to run over that same serial channel. A Gen3x2 interface runs at 3.938 GB/s, while a Gen4x4 interface runs at 15.754 GB/s. Of course, the actual transfer to/from the SSD is limited by the speed of the flash, DRAM, controller, etc. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is simply the protocol that’s used to create storage systems over PCI Express, since PCIe is a general purpose interface, while SATA includes that storage support as part of the basic protocol. Question: Can electric vehicles (EVs) be used for interstate travel considering their short ranges and the lack of fast chargers along major routes?
Answer: Here’s a map of Tesla Superchargers — just one option for recharging your EV — set with 124 mile circles. You may not have quite the same choice of routes you’d have in an ICE car, but it’s not much of an issue. Oh, and this one’s from 2019. And back then, you could drive up, down, and cross the USA in a Tesla. It did require planning, but really, any trip across country is going to benefit from some planning… that’s how I managed it in three days some years back. In a Prius, not a BEV. All Tesla chargers are fast chargers — in fact, faster than original CHaDeMo Level 3 chargers that comprised earlier standards of high speed charging. But there’s limited compatibility with non-Tesla EVs, though that’s changing. Here’s a view from ChargePoint’s interactive online route planner of current Tesla, Level 3, and Level 2 chargers. It’s not as sophisticated at that other map, but I think you can get the basic idea. The real point of this map isn’t to show a bunch of chargers, but to plot your route to ensure there are no surprises along the way. And yes, if you’re stopping for a full charge at every stop, you might be waiting an hour on a Level 3 charger. Though if you’re charging to 80%, maybe half that time… Li-ion batteries are like that. This can, of course, make your travel longer, especially if you’re going cross country. My sister Kathy’s first Chevy Bolt ran into a software bug down in Washington, DC, that had it rejecting fast charging. I was expecting her to stop by my old place in Newark, DE which is not far from a Type 3 charger and, at least in planning, lunch at the TGI Fridays next to it. Limping along at 50–60 miles of charge per hour, though, it took her most of the day.. but she didn’t run out of stations to pinball her way up to Delaware. We had a late dinner! Now, as far as your particular EV, you’ll have to understand your charging options (what connectors do you have, how fast can you charge) as well as how far you’re likely to go. Many EVs work this all out as part of their onboard SatNav systems. Range isn’t a problem unique to EVs. I used to get about 200 miles in my 1961 Ford Thunderbird back in college. My 2003 Toyota Prius could pass the 600 mile mark on a single tank, with careful driving, at least until the tank bladder failed and my dealer replaced the tank with a smaller 2004–2007 era fuel tank. When my sister Kathy bought her first EV, it was a Nissan Leaf, Level1/2 charging only and about 80–90 miles on a charge. Basically a golf cart! Her current Chevy Bolt can make 250–300 miles, at least in the summertime… your ICE car has a shorter range in the cold, too. The average EV range in the US market in 2024 is 300 miles, a fair parity against many ICE vehicles. Lucid, Porsche, Polestar, and Mercedes make 400+ mile EVs today, while the Lucid Air Grand Touring edition is rated at 516 miles. Toyota, the company that basically made “hybrid” a household name and had one of the first full EVs on the market, has stayed out of the BEV business (though they do have a FCEV), but they’ve announced plans for EVs starting in the 2027 model year with a 620 mile range, based on a new solid-state Lithium-ion battery technology. Stay tuned! For Tesla chargers, there are currently guidelines. What vehicles can charge at what Tesla Superchargers? That’s good information to have today, because Tesla does have a large network of the highest performing charging stations out there. However, with the entire Supercharger team recently laid off — pretty surprising given that, with the network open to other vehicles, that could be significant new revenue for Tesla — and, of course, the Tesla charging connector now becoming standard, this network will probably become less important over time. Anyway, as Tesla informs: There are 3 types of Tesla Superchargers: In route-planning apps like ChargePoint’s you can filter out Tesla-only chargers. NACS refers to the retronymed North American Charging Standard (NASC, soon to also be SAE J3400), the standardized version of what was the Tesla proprietary charging connector. You can’t yet buy generic NASC adapters for the earlier CCS or J1772 car connectors, though if you visit a Tesla Supercharger with “Magic Dock” those adapters are provided. Your vehicle manufacturer may eventually offer one, after working with Tesla to ensure it’s tested and recognized by their NACS Superchargers. Yeah, some of that’s just Tesla’s slowness in updating Supercharger software, but it’s understandable they’d want to test as well.
