The real argument is that absolutely nothing Trump has been charged with has anything at all to do with his official acts as President. For example, the President has absolutely no official involvement in elections. Thus, he should not have any immunity based on the fact he was President at the time. That should be irrelevant. As well as the fact that in the Espionage case, his serious crimes were actually committed after he left office, not during his tenure in office. The obvious motivation by Trump’s legal team is that, when you have $100 million to spend on legal defense every year or so, your lawyers are going to try every trick in the book to get you off. It’s not unusual for a legal defense to throw everything they can think of at the proverbial wall and see if anything will stick. So this is one attempt to get off on a technicality, basically trying to get a legal backing for Nixon’s old claim, “It’s not a crime if the President does it.” But there’s a darker side to this. If he’s elected, whether the trials take place post-election or not, once in office he’ll have a puppet Attorney General in place on Day 1 who will stop whatever of the two Federal cases that remain, the Espionage/Stolen Documents case and the January 6 Election Interference case. And he’ll contrive some way to issue a self-pardon. The other half of this is that Trump has plans to break many more laws should he get re-elected, and he’d like it on record that he’s immune from prosecution if possible. And Congress can investigate all they want, but subpoenas will be ignored, Contempt of Congress will be ignored, and they’ll have no teeth to do anything about it as long as Impeachment is politically off-the-table. Question: How do atheists explain this contradiction? Atheists don't believe in God, yet they don't think they will go to hell for their beliefs. This only makes sense if atheists secretly believe in God. If even atheists believe in Him, He is real.
Answer: Maybe you shouldn't have slept through that Introduction to Logic class. If a person does not believe in a particular god, it is logical that they do not believe in the rest of that god’s mythology, including their claims about an afterlife of any kind. I’m betting you don’t believe in Odin the All-Father. If that’s said, you probably don’t expect to wind up in Nifflheim, Valhalla (Odin’s hall), Helheim (Hel’s domain), Folkvang (Freya’s field), Náströnd, etc. Unless you die in battle or you’re terribly evil, you’ll walk to Helheim upon your death, and enter a place that’s underground but otherwise isn’t terribly different than mortal life. By your logic, that only makes sense if you secretly believe in Odin and the other Norse gods. Does that help you understand how terribly flawed your logic is? There is very obviously no need to believe a myth, legend, or any other kind of story in order to reject that story. In fact, that’s a contradiction: rejecting the stories related to a god’s mythology is a perfectly consistent expression of one’s disbelief in that myth. If you don’t understand this, or even if maybe you do, do yourself a favor and take a course in logic. It will help you come off more rational and less silly in public. Question: Why did the news medias stop talking about Covid-19? Why hardly hear about it anymore at all anywhere? When did this happen and is Covid-19 still spreading around in May 2023? How it is the same or different than before and why?
Answer: Both the USA and the World Health Organization ended the emergency status of COVID-19 in May of 2023. The SARS-CoV-2 virus didn’t magically vanish, but it’s endemic now, and unlike when it first hit our shores, most of us have good levels of antibodies against it, either as the result of vaccination or contracting the disease. Hospitalization still occurs, but they’re way down. At the peak of the pandemic, we didn’t have the same treatments available today. And there were so many hospital admissions, the system broke down in some places. Not everyone admitted could get the best available treatment. Today, if you contract a bad case of COVID-19, you can get fast and generally effective treatment. Not surprisingly, deaths are also way down, though they’re still occurring. Both charts from the CDC. That doesn’t mean people don’t die, but not so many. The worst week for COVID-19 is usually January. We lost 2,558 people in the second week of January this year (2024), the worst week of the year so far. That’s bad — almost a whole 9/11 — but the first week of January in 2023, we lost 3,869. In 2022, in was the third week of January, claiming 21,335 lives here in the USA. In 2021, the bad week was the second in January, in which COVID-19 claimed 25,974 of our fellow Americans. As well, variants in recent times, as the SARS-Cov-2 virus continues to mutate, have changed the story a bit. More recent variants such as Omicron have been more transmissible but less deadly. So more people caught the disease, but between a less dangerous variant, large scale immunity, and better medicine, it’s harder to spread, and people recover in much higher percentages. This isn’t necessarily a permanent situation, however. Look at the influenza virus. While humanity and this virus have lived together since the dawn of agriculture, we’ve had influenza pandemics in 1918 (H1N1), 1957 (H2N2), 1968 (H3N2), 1977 (H1N1), and 2009 (H1N1/09). Now, influenza is more prone to dangerous mutations, as it can generically mix with animal versions, yielding a strain the population is not all that able to fight off. Anyway, in the fall of 2023, virologists were tracking the Eris (EG.5) variant, which derived from Omicron. Eris was about 5% of all cases in September and 22% by October. However, a mutation of Eris, dubbed HV.1, started taking over, rising to 22% of cases in October. The main observed difference in Eris and HV.1 is a mutation that helps it evade antibodies just a bit better. That said, was not seen as being either more contagious or more dangerous. COVID-19 hospitalizations were up 9% in early November in the USA, but it’s not clear if this was due to the new strain, or just “it’s getting cold” as we moved toward peak COVID, flu, and RSV season. HV.1 was replaced by JN.1, which is also not expected to be more dangerous than previous variants. But it grew fast. In October 2023, it represented 3.5% of studied COVID-19 cases. By December it represented 21%, by year’s end it was 44%, and a few weeks into 2024 it accounted for 85% of the cases. Of course, now, moving in to Spring and Summer, it’s not much of a thread, but it’s wise to get a booster shot in the fall, just as with the influenza jab. The virus changes all the time, the vaccine changes to match. Read More

Question: Should the practice of burning religious books be banned and made illegal?
Answer: I don’t personally approve the burning of any books. That’s my opinion. Yours may well be different. The fundamental problem I have is that the practice of burning books is a signal that those burning them consider the contents to be dangerous thoughts and ideas. That one person or a group of people think some ideas are dangerous does not make them so. They may simply be trying to suppress those ideas for their own reasons… maybe they represent a competing idea. But even if they are in some way dangerous, I think dangerous thoughts and ideas are not only important but necessary for societal growth. Decisions about society made decades or centuries ago should be regularly challenged against the backdrop of modern times. Such ideas deserve their chance to compete in the marketplace of ideas, to succeed or fail on their own merit. Not be quashed via any violent suppression. Yes, even religious books, despite the fact I think they’re all rather silly. Unlike some people, I openly acknowledge it’s not all about me. That’s not the same as saying that I believe book burning should be illegal. There are countries that don’t respect individual freedom and unusually protect religion — or more likely, only some religion — via things like blasphemy laws. Under those regimes, burning certain religious texts would be a crime of blasphemy. While this is rarely a concern in the USA, a few states have blasphemy laws on the books, usually dating back a century or more. Yeah, Trump sure has one over on me on this one, but at least my house isn’t leveraged for more than it’s worth! Here’s the thing about tax-assessed value: it depends on how it’s being done. In some places, a house is only re-assessed when it’s sold. In others, there’s a periodic re-assessment. Think of these, in some cases, as Monopoly Money. They’re not really assessing my house’s value on an absolute scale, they’re deciding how much of the total amount of money the state and country need to raise in taxes I’m going to contribute. I’m paying the same amount on unit value as everyone else, so the actual unit doesn’t matter. When you go to sell a house, you can of course ask any price you’d like. But if you actually want to sell it, you hire a good real estate agent, you look at comparable recently sold houses, and you arrive at your initial offering price. Since current prices and prior sale prices are well known to potential buyers, you’re not going to fool anyone with a weirdly inflated price. In Trump’s case, though, he’s been accused of undervaluing properties for tax purposes and vastly inflating the value for the purposes of obtaining loans. That’s only possible because of the fact he’s got unique, very high dollar properties. Answer: Am I tired of Donald Trump? Absolutely. He needs a real prison’s isolation from the rest of the world and restraints on his personal freedoms, or the country learns nothing from his convictions. I don’t really know what they should do. This is, of course and fortunately, an unprecedented case. We don’t usually elect people we know to be criminals, but this was one case in which it was avoidable. Trump has been running on the edge of crime his entire life, and yet, that didn’t matter to enough voters to put him in office. Another alternative is a cell in a SuperMax prison. He’d be completely isolated from other prisoners, thus safe, and while the hour a day of exercise is more than he’s accustomed to, it might do him some good. And yet, was what he did severe enough to really belong there? I’d claim that if convicted on any of the various attempts to overthrow the country’s legitimate vote, then yes, it would be. If he’s found not-guilty on all charges or somehow avoids facing justice, it’s even worse. That makes everything he did now a lesson. A practice run. A thing he or any other wanna-be despot will try again if given the chance, just because they’ll know they can get away with it if they fail again. As for Trump, he won’t learn. He can’t learn, it’s not in his makeup. And it won’t matter. Unless he’s re-elected in November, he’s no longer of any significance other than as a lesson to future generations. Question: Do you think it's appropriate for journalists to report that Donald Trump fell asleep in court?
Answer: Trial Day :: April 15, 2024 If Trump appears to fall asleep in court, it’s appropriate for journalists to report that Donald Trump appeared to fall asleep in court. Do they actually know if he’s asleep? Probably not, but I was not present in court. If they observed his eyes fluttering from rapid eye movement, they could pretty well conclude he was actually asleep. So yeah, a mention of this is appropriate, as it’s telling something about the mindset of the man. If they were dwelling on it? Trial Day :: April 16, 2024 Once again, in the second day of jury selection, Trump was once again apparently falling asleep. There’s a fine history of courtroom sketches capturing defendants as they were in court. This morning’s nap was discussed by a reporter, in a “xTweet” anyway, which lends credibility to the contention that Trump was sleeping. Is it relevant to the case? Maybe, maybe not, but when you’re reporting, you present facts as they happen and relate them to your viewers or readers. The time for analysis and commentary ought to come just a bit after there’s a whole story available. Frank was live blogging the trial on the-social-media-organization-formerly-known-as-Twitter, he wasn’t dwelling on it. That’s exactly what I was alluding to above: he’s offering a play-by-play, reporting the way a sportscaster does at a live event. The sportscaster tells you what happens, being your eyes and ears. I used to travel from South Jersey, USA to Hildesheim, Germany: take an overnight plane to Frankfort, take a 3.5 hour ICE train from Frankfort to Hildesheim, walk about 1.5km to pick up my rental car, drive to the office, and start work! Question: Donald Trump says that a CEO has no time for the details of business and that all of the potential illegal acts his company committed were done by his assistant and son Eric. Are most CEOs incompetent figure heads whose work is done by assistants?
Answer: Well, of course Donald Trump would throw his son under the bus. That’s just the kind of guy he is. He has never admitted a single wrongdoing. Never admitted a single mistake (see: SharpieGate). No, most CEOs are not incompetent figureheads. And for all publicly traded companies, there’s a board of directors watching over the corporation and leadership of their chosen CEO. The board of directors is supposed to represent the interests of the shareholders. It’s true that in a few cases, there’s a Board of Directors packed largely with “yes” men (see: Tesla), but at most companies it functions correctly as an independent check on the CEO’s proper representation of the best interests of the shareholders. And in the areas in which a company bumps up against illegal activities, a CEO can be held criminally liable for either steering the company in that direction or being criminally negligent by ignoring that others within the company were doing such things “while he wasn’t looking.” The CEO is, ultimately, where the buck stops at any company. Despite what you saw with the “Trump” character played by Trump on his game show “The Apprentice,” there’s no board of directors at The Trump Organization. It’s a private family business, no shareholders. It’s Donald’s company, period. One of the reason that Trump was such a failure as President was that he had never actually had to cooperate with other people in his business. He told them jump, they asked “how high” on the way up. Yes, it’s true that some real companies are far too large for a single individual to know absolutely everything that’s happening, and I’ll get to why that’s the case in a bit. But yeah, it’s true that nearly all CEOs don’t make every single minor business decision. They work with VPs and others to set business directions and oversee larger strategies. It’s pretty likely Doug McMillian isn’t making every minor decision involving the 2.1 million employees, 10,000 stores, websites, etc. comprising the Wal-Mart Corporation. It’s likely Tim Cook is not micromanaging every small decision made across Apple’s 170,000 employees. However, at my company, our CEO Bob is fully involved in every business decision we make. It’s company of about 160 people. The CEO doesn’t make every technical decision, and he’s not choosing business directions alone, but he’s involved in every one of them and has the final say. In fact, he’s one of the few CEOs I’ve worked under who really does the whole job well. There were reportedly 22,450 people employed under at least one of the 250+ shell companies under the banner of The Trump Organization in 2015, though there are fewer today. No, Donald Trump did not oversee every maid or cook or janitor or gardener in Trump managed hotels and office buildings. And yes, much of the Trump business was simply management — far more than ownership — of the buildings and properties with the Trump name on them. But Trump’s corporate office a small thing with less than 150 employees at its peak. And in fact, that’s almost certainly by design: it’s Dunbar's number! According to British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, there are well-defined limits to the number of personal interactions the average person can retain, and that “magic number” is 150. No CEO is going to have regular daily interactions with more than 150 people, and probably far fewer. So in a company with 150 or fewer people, Trump can know just about everyone and certainly everyone he considers worth talking to… he probably doesn’t find the need to deal with every janitor or mailroom kid. But this company size tells you precisely what everyone dealing with Trump tells you: he’s able to and requires interaction on every little detail of company business. He’s a known as a micro-manager. There is no decision made at that company that doesn’t have Donald J. Trump’s approval. It’s never happened. And certainly not for the last 40-something years, which is how far back the fraud in his case went. However, you could rightly claim that may or may not be easy to prove in court. Trump’s father, Fred, learned his corporate management style learning from the mobsters in Queens, NY. Trump learned from Fred and from his mentorship under famous mob lawyer Roy Cohn for fifteen years. That means lots of verbal orders, not much in writing. That means making “suggestions” that his Caporegimes like Mike Cohen and Allen Weisselberg understood to be specific orders, the old “take care of that guy” you see in mob movies, only about things other than [necessarily] whacking some rival. But in the end, the Trump business fraud case hinged on both “following the money” through various financial entanglements of The Trump Organization, and the testimony of others involved that basically suggested that no one did a thing at Trump’s company without Donald’s permission. That’s why trials often involve years of investigation: there’s a story to tell, but it has to be constructed based on thousands of small threads leading to larger threads leading to, perhaps, conviction. Trump was found liable for the bulk of the fraud, with dramatically smaller liability attached to his kids and other Trump Corporation officials.

Question: Will I lose all of my photos if I update and 'reset the camera' on my Sony A6000?
Answer: Your photos aren’t “on the camera”, they’re on an SD card. You should be copying them regularly to other storage, even if you still have room on the camera, because SD cards don’t last forever, and as well, the camera could be damaged or stolen. If you take the SD card out, nothing you ever do to the camera can affect the photos you have already shot. If they’re stored on a PC hard drive, cloud backup, etc. there’s no fears about what happens on the camera. Professional cameras typically have two memory cards, allowing every photo to go to both. That way, if anything happens to one memory card, the photos are still intact on the other.

Question: Why did Intel switch from their own design of CPU (x86) to ARM for mobile phones, despite the x86 being more powerful than other options?
Answer: Intel did not switch from x86 to ARM. For s very brief period, Intel had a product line of ARM chips called StrongARM and then Xscale. They bought StrongARM from Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in 1997, and sold off their ARM technology in 2006. StrongARM and Xscale were used in some PDAs and PMPs as well as a few mostly off-brand Smartphones. Intel returned to the Smartphone market briefly with some versions of their Atom system-on-chip in 2012. They were generally underperforming the various ARM processors while using more power, not what you want in a phone. They tried to enlist OEMs into using the processors for Android phones, even basically paying them to use the chips, but the project ultimately failed and cost Intel about $10 billion. However, the Atom line itself was not a complete failure. They make some sense in embedded computong devices. My company has used them in some of our mesh routers, largely because they have a fast memory interface and good encryption instruction sets. Later ARM processors have addressed some of that, but for a long time ARM chips were supporting accelerated encryption using dedicated encryption processors, some of which were not well designed, and all of which require much more software work to use than with Intel. Question: If there is no God, how do atheists explain how the moon is perfectly circular?
Answer: Your ignorance is showing, Luis Aguilar. It’s unsightly… please cover it up. The Moon is not “perfectly circular”. A circle is a two-dimensional geometric construct. The Moon exists in three linear dimensions which, like the Earth, is an oblate spheroid. The explanation is trivial: it’s gravity. The only gravitationally stable shape for large objects in space is roughly the sphere. Matter in a collection falls toward the center of gravity. In a sphere, all matter forms equidistant from the center of gravity. Any other shape and you’d have things still falling toward the center, as long as the object is large enough and not acted on by other forces. The actual shape, whether it’s oblate — flattened along an axis — depends on such other forces, such as rotation, tidal friction, and the gravitational effect of other bodies. You might be so uneducated you invoke deities to explain things that humanity in collective has known for thousands of year, like some bronze age gothsherd. Question: How can the new M1 Macbook Pro be charged using a different USB-C charger or outlet? Is there a difference in the charging process compared to using its own charger?
Answer: Here’s what you need to know about the MacBook Pro or absolutely any other device that can recharge using a Type-C port: the charger is in the device, not the power brick. Period. That’s how it works. And that’s why it works. Your device is designed to know about it’s battery. The power brick just provides power, it doesn’t have a clue about “charging” even though everyone does call them “chargers.” The MacBook Pro is using the latest power delivery protocol called, simply, power delivery or PD. The power brick is just a power supply, but it’s a smart one. The computer or other attached device can ask the power supply what it’s got to offer in terms of voltage and current: +5Vdc, +9Vdc, +12Vdc, +20Vdc, and in the very latest version of PD, +48Vdc, and either 3A or 5A current. The device will set the power supply, usually, to the most power it can use. This is important, because some power supply systems have multiple ports, and if one device were to ask for more power than it can deliver, the others might not get their requested power. In the MacBook itself is a sophisticated system of hardware and software that does power management. A part of that is the charging circuitry. A battery is either charging, discharging, or electronically disconnected… you can’t do both at the same time. So based on the USB power brick you’re using, the laptop may need both battery and external power to do what you’re requesting, but it’ll of course use the external power first. So if the device is using less power than the brick is supplying, the charging circuitry will activate and start charging this internal battery. So any Type-C PD charger of sufficient capacity can charge up your MacBook pro. In fact, I have a similar system with a Dell Precision Workstation here. The laptop is connected via a Thunderbolt Type-C cable to a docking station, which has its own power brick and breaks out USB, DisplayPort, Ethernet, etc. for connection to my keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera, microscope, oscilloscope, network, etc. That supply is a bit underrated for the laptop, so it complains a bit, but still works just dandy. However, it’s possible if I was doing hours of really intensive computing, the charging wouldn’t keep up and I’d have to fetch the portable power brick from my backpack to fully sate the Dell’s appetite.

Of course, if you’re honestly just trying to add useful information on top of someone else’s answer, you can always post your own and simply write it as some additions to the otherwise fine answer given by Dave Haynie or whomever. The bottom line is that your comments section is a modifier for your article, and absolutely needs to be under your control.

Question: Why do my iPhone pictures look better than pictures taken from my DSLR camera?
Answer: Q: Why do my iPhone pictures look better than pictures taken from my DSLR camera? The bottom line here is that your phone is a better photographer than you are. Seriously… but read on. The fact you can pick up a smartphone and take pretty good photos but are struggling with the DSLR should tell you that you’re missing some understanding of photography. So, let’s consider the iPhone. As a camera, this is the distant descendant of the Kodak Instamatic. Seriously. The Instamatic was designed as a camera for people who had no idea how to take photos. There was nothing to set, your option was basically: flash bulb or no flash bulb. It had a fixed lens, fixed aperture, fixed shutter speed, and that’s that. It worked as well as it did because Kodak got some crazy exposure latitude out of their processing. Anyway, the idea was simple: point, shoot, and you love your photos. Even though they were usually pretty awful! The iPhone is the modern embodiment of this idea: point, shoot, love your photo. It is made for someone with absolutely not a clue about photography. It’s not even a camera, it’s a pocket-sized personal computer with more power than your desktop computer had 10 years ago, and more AI processing power than your present desktop/laptop might offer today. About six or so years ago, companies like Google and Apple started throwing that weight behind their cameras. They didn’t want to increase expenses, they didn’t want to make fatter phones — they ultimately did both in an effort to one-up last year’s models, and each other — but the key with smartphones has been computational and artificial intelligence hardware and software. Not as much the camera sensor. Last I checked, your iPhone is constantly shooting while you run the Camera app. It’s using an AI agent to set exposure, another to set focus, and and maybe one to decide exactly when to shoot. I know Google does that in low light. It keeps 8 photos in memory in a circular buffer. When you press the shutter icon, the shooting stops… usually. That’s why it seems to be instant… the photos are already taken! In bright light, it’ll pick the best of four sets of two. It’s alternating exposures for HDR. In lower light it’ll try to use all eight, and in very low light, it’ll take another long (and probably blurry) photo to try to learn about the color in the scene, because these little sensors don’t get good color in low light at high ISO to avoid blur and shake. There’s an AI agent to direct these things, to merge color, etc. Then there’s another AI agent to decide how to “finish” the image, kind of like using a Preset in Lightroom but certainly more involved, since the AI has to pick the appropriate look. Apple wants to deliver a photo you’ll like, but they don’t give too much concern about realism. Though maybe a bit more than Samsung, who seem to want all their photos so saturated you’ll think you shot them in Oz or Candyland or something. Anyway, my point is that Apple, in particular, is doing all of the work. Not you. They have a network of AI agents that function together to replace the need for a photographer, or more specifically, a photographer’s brain. With an experienced photographer, it’s not the camera. Any camera will do, in part because you’ll make it work, and shoot different images depending on the limitations and advantages of that particular camera gear. If you’re blaming anything on the camera, you don’t understand photography… or you’re using a smartphone, which isn’t allowing you the control you want. Understand that there’s always better in photography, but in the digital age, pretty much any camera made from 2012 on is sufficient to not be your problem. One quick lesson: one way to get to this kind of understanding is to limit yourself. Folks did this with P&S cameras, and they did with older smartphones. But now with all their fake zoom and multiple cameras, smartphones can make you as lazy as DSLRs sometimes do. So try it simple. You should be out and around, shooting photos every week at the least, every day that you can. So take a week or a month, pick one prime lens, maybe turn off the automation (though manual focus is difficult on most DSLRs) and just shoot with that lens, nothing else. In fact, my Olympus Pen-F is sitting here on the desk with a few hundred photos taken with just one 25mm f/0.95 manual lens last Sunday. The single most important component of a camera is the twelve inches behind it! -Ansel Adams There is nothing worse than a sharp image of a fuzzy concept. -Ansel Adams Read that. Understand it. If you are not getting better shots with your DSLR, it’s because you haven’t learned how to get better shots with your DSLR. Period. It’s not the camera. Sure, you can always get a better lens. Then maybe you’ll have a sharper bad photo than you do today. The single best investment in photography anyone can buy once the put down a smartphone and pick up a dedicated camera is knowledge. A serious camera isn’t made for smartphone users, at least not yet, people who don’t know what they’re doing. It’s made as a tool for those who do, and the digital innovations offered in DSLRs and even more in mirrorless cameras are designed to be used and useful to experienced photographers, not novices without any real camera experience. Don’t get me wrong, you learn some creative aspects of photography with a smartphone. Not everything, but the creative side, sure. But you’re not normally controlling focus, you can’t really control depth of field (yeah, they fake it a bit… it’s not the same), you’re not learning to control light if you’re just snapshooting. You’re finishing (editing) your photos and learn what’s entailed in all of that. And it’s not just you. I have seen dozens of video done in perfect seriousness, in which a supposedly experienced photographer is proving that his iPhone or Samsung or whatever can out-shoot him (and yeah, so far, it’s always a dude). If you understand what you’re doing, it’s pretty easy to watch one of these and see immediately what the guy is doing wrong… often it’s just assuming that AUTO mode with a DSLR makes you an expert and that it can match the trillions of AI cycles tossed at AUTO mode on a smartphone. It can’t, and it isn’t even trying. What AUTO on a real camera does is act very, very consistently, which makes it a tool a photographer can use. I’m always in control, even if I set the dial on “P” … which is pretty rare. So, grasshopper, once you can see this too, you are ready to talk about camera gear. Until then, learning is your road to success. You may also not be exercising your photo chops. Taking great photos with a real camera requires practice and regular attention just like painting, just like playing the guitar, just like wood carving, etc. You don’t expect a guitar to play itself, and you don’t blame the guitar if you sound choppy or keep missing chords. You blame yourself. That’s not chastising, it’s accepting the fact that you have more learning to do, and that should be what drew you to photography. In short, any money you’re spending on photography at this point needs to be on learning. I know, it’s so much more work than buying that shiny new lens that half the people here are suggesting you might need. They’re wrong. Learn to be a photographer. That can be lessons online, that can be local classes, and in both cases it needs to be getting out and shooting. Give yourself a project! I decided to produce a B&W photo every day… I did that for 1,000 days. I learned a whole lot about B&W photography in the digital age. I got better, even after 35+ years of prior experience going back to my darkroom as a kid. This is also the edge professionals have: they’re immersed fulltime in the work… well, aside from the other full-time job they have running the business. The negative is the score, and the print is the performance. -Ansel Adams You don’t take a photograph, you make it. -Ansel Adams Dodging and burning are steps to take care of mistakes God made in establishing tonal relationships. -Ansel Adams So, yes, in the days of the darkroom, dodging and burning — the old way of “editing an image” — to create a great print was very much a performance. Today, you have Lightroom, Photoshop, and other tools with “undo” buttons, etc. So while it’s not precisely a performance anymore, it’s still as much a part of making a great image as the shooting is. Particularly for some kinds of photography. True, you have street photography and photojournalism that may rely more heavily on the lightly or unedited image, but if it’s at all art, the finishing, the print matters too. Of course, while we may not be making prints all the time, we’re still releasing a photographs on some kind of medium, even if it’s just a JPEG on Quora. Understanding the result you want is a big part of being able to get satisfaction from shooting. One of the great things about editing, however you do it, is that it lends itself to a whole creative experimentation that’s simply not available if you’re just point-and-shooting. Here’s one example. When I was shooting this at City Hall in Philadelphia, I knew immediately that there was too much contrast in the scene to capture this in one shot. So I composited this by hand. Maybe your camera’s or phone’s HDR function would have captured it, maybe it wouldn’t have. I knew with basic exposure bracketing that I’d nail it, so there was no worry, and I had full control over the final image. So here’s what I started with. Even if the iPhone could capture the dynamic range, is it really going to keep a full tonal range, etc? I’m kind of wondering if there’s so much AI in some of these phones, is it really my image anymore when I see it? And how much longer until it’s not? Here’s another somewhat challenging shot as finished, one of my favorites from my B&W project. This was only a single shot, and taken awfully quickly. This is a default version of the raw image. Now, if a smartphone AI image processor got hold of this, it would look better. In fact, there would likely not be much in the way of shadow areas at all… but that’s actually an important part of the finished image. One more. I shot this in Philadelphia. I liked the interesting look of this old building, and knew it would be a nice B&W image. Of course, I shot in raw from street level, and when you do that with a wide lens, your building tilts backwards. I knew this, of course, and I actually could have applied keystone correction in-camera. But I didn’t bother, I knew Photoshop would offer me more control and not bake any edits into the image. Yeah, technically, I could have done both. Whether your smartphone could do any of this for you is kind of moot… it’s not as much my work if the smartphone gets to make creative decisions. Yes, these are things you can and should learn to do yourself. Learn to use a camera, learn creative photography, learn the “digital darkroom” and you will outshoot your smartphone. Ultimately, only you can decided “best” between images. And that’s another thing: look at other folks photography. That’s part of learning. I mention the great Ansel Adams here because, as a kid, I was obsessed with the outdoors and especially the National Parks. I was also shooting, processing, and printing my own B&W film, and it was seeing Adams’ prints in person that made me really fall in love with B&W and darkroom work. Just knowing that was possible, even if I had no idea how he did it! Read More

Question: What is a person who doesn't believe in God called? Is there any name for them apart from atheist and non-believer?
Answer: A person who doesn’t believe in any god? Well, these all apply, but don’t fully apply to everyone who doesn’t believe in a god. Atheist is the correct name, however, because that’s the only one of these specific to the topic of not believing in a god. The very meaning of atheism is “a” (without) “theism” (belief in a god). If it’s just your god that you’re worried about, there are other words. But you didn’t mention your specific god. Since you said “God” — not a name, a title — I’ll assume you meant Yahweh, the Judeo-Christian god, with or without a son and/or some weird ghost which are also that same god and yet get named separately. It’s quite common that older religions didn’t have a specific name. They had specific gods, and those in the associated religions did what that religion claimed, in terms of prayer, sacrifice, etc. to specific gods. But the religion itself didn’t necessarily have a name until there was some invader killing the society’s strongest and then forcing their religious ideas upon the survivors.

Question: If you are obese, at what age do you believe you will die? Seeing as there aren't many 70+ year olds walking around morbidly obese.
Answer: This guy’s morbidly obese — it’s technically called Class III obesity — though he tries to dress in ways that cover it up (edit: he’s not really Class III — some people can’t take a joke — but he’s been obese and likely Class II for some time, though in fairness, he might have lost weight since leaving office). He’s also really famous — I’m thinking you know about him — and he’ll be 78 in two months. I’m not sure I’ve seen him walking very often, but standing, sitting, and particularly, golf carting, absolutely! You can find any number of lifespan calculators if you’re concerned about longevity, but there are any number of contributing factors. It seems that the guy shown above, given what’s know about his current health, could live to 82–85 years old. But the devil is always in the details, and while this man’s father lived to 93 — pretty good — he suffered from Alzheimer’s Dementia for a decade and eventually succumbed to the disease. Why don’t you normally see obese people in their 70s? It depends on many things. How many morbidly obese people younger than 70 do you normally come across in your average day? It’s easy to imagine having a lifestyle that filters them out. I’m out with my dog 2–4 miles a day… it’s pretty unlikely I’m going to meet too many obese folks when I’m out walking. It takes a particular lifestyle, and sometimes an unfortunate medical condition, to get like that. I also don’t see them too often when cycling or kayaking, but I do see them occasionally at the beach. And now and then in the grocery store, but I don’t got to those all that often. I also don’t eat out all that often, and when I do, it’s not low quality food. I’m not claiming that all obese people eat at McDonald’s or Golden Corral, but one of the contributing factors toward obesity is eating too much poor quality food… Hamburders! And the typical Golden Corral customer is a regular, over 65, and in the USA, they live in the south. The last time I ate out was at the VFW in Madeira Beach, FL… wasn’t crowded, and I didn’t notice anyone terribly overweight. And as well, do you see folks in their 70s on a regular basis? They’re another group that doesn’t necessarily intersect yours on a regular basis. Most at that age are retired, and many retirees leave their former business-friendly locales for something nicer and/or with lower cost of living. In short, you can’t build a useful statistical model about 70+ obese people, or anyone else, just noticing who you meet in your everyday life. Yes, obesity is a leading long-term cause of health issues. It’s a contributing factor to many things that kill you: dementia, heart disease, diabetes, cancer, osteoarthritis, high blood pressure, gallbladder disease, fatty liver disease, and breathing problems like asthma and sleep apnea. But obesity alone doesn’t just kill you when you turn 70. In fact, according to the CDC, 41.5% of Americans aged 60 and older have at least Class I obesity. That’s not all that different than the 39.8% of Americans 20–39 who are obese. So maybe you didn’t know it, but statistically, about four out of every ten people you pass on average in the USA are obese. Maybe some of them are over 70, and maybe you didn’t notice either thing. Are you a trained medical professional? Or maybe this is just so common, only extreme obesity stands out. That statistic alone does tell you that there are lots of fat old people still walking around. And while I mentioned Class III obesity, your question was targeted at any sort of obesity. It’s common being overweight in a prosperous country that revels in junk food and sedentary activities. In fact, I could stand to lose 10lbs… maybe I’ll take the dog out four miles this evening! Self-reflection is always a good thing, eh? CRITICAL UPDATE We went 3.92 miles yesterday, 2.74 today. The weather was perfect.

Question: How did Putin get along so well with Trump, but not Obama or Bush before him?
Answer: George W. Bush met with Putin several times, and it was fairly normal for a US President meeting with the Russian President. You might recall what Bush said after his first meeting with Putin: He's a man deeply committed to his country and the best interests of his country, and I appreciate very much the frank dialogue and that's the beginning of a very constructive relationship. Bush started his Presidency during Putin’s year of his “charm campaign.” Back then, rather than invading his neighbors without provocation, he was actually working to normalize relations with Western Democracies. Putin was the first world leader to call President Bush on September 11, 2001, after the catastrophic terrorist attacks in New York, Pennsylvania, and Washington, D.C. He didn’t forget that. Here’s the difference: George W. Bush could like the man and still do what’s right for the United States of America. He, like pretty much every President before Trump, understood that you don’t make decisions of global importance based on how much one leader flatters you. George Bush’s test came close to the end of his term, when Russia invaded Georgia. Was Bush tough on Russia? It could have been handled better, but hindsight is 20/20, and the “war” only lasted five days. The US instituted economic sanctions against Russia, send warships to the Black Sea, and airlifted Georgian troops from Afghanistan and Iraq back home to fight in Georgia. Though things were over so fast, the US ships and some humanitarian aid didn’t get to Georgia until ten days after the cease-fire. Bush ruled out direct US military intervention. Obama and Putin met and had a fine working relationship, though they didn’t have quite the same one early on, given that Putin wasn’t the Russian President. In his first term of office, Obama’s “reset” on policy with Russia was seen as a big success. This resulted in the new START treaty, cooperation with Russia in Afghanistan, Russia uncharacteristically backing US lead UN resolutions, agreements on civil nuclear cooperation (consider that the USA was already buying most of our uranium for nuclear reactors from Russia in those days), Russia’s entry into the WTO, etc. A big part of that project was that Obama also had a good relationship with Russian President (2008–2012) Dmitry Medvedev. Medvedev, like Obama, has a largely post-Cold War mindset, unlike Putin, and their working relationship was key to the progress they made in Obama’s first term. Before Putin was back as President in 2012 and the troubles started. The main conflict involving Russia came in 2014, in Obama’s second term, when Russia invaded Crimea. This occurred right after Ukraine’s Revolution of Dignity that ousted Russian Puppet Viktor Yanukovych after a huge protest against removal of democratic rights, decline in press freedom, and big Russian-style increases in corruption and cronyism. Yanukovych was removed from power, Ukraine’s constitution restored, and Russia took Crimea in about three weeks. The US and the EU immediately enacted sanctions against Russia. Given that the Russian invasion was swift and aided by Russian sympathizers, as with Georgia, there wasn’t much available to Obama or Angela Merkel aside from such sanctions, particularly in such short a time. One of the retaliations against Russia was their removal from the Group of Eight (G8) political forum. That was worse than it might sound, because years before, Putin had spent considerable time trying to court the favor of the West. That’s in fact part of how Russia was invited into the G7, leading to its rebranding as the G8. Since 2014, it’s been the G7 again. Obama and Merkel both both met briefly with Putin several months later at a D-Day commemoration, though Obama’s primary goal was trying to convince Putin to establish relations with the new Ukraine government, and of course, to cease any further aggressions. Trump’s relationship with Putin was very different. Whether he was simply in awe of Putin, afraid of Putin, or owned by Putin, it’s clear from Trump’s body language in many images with Putin that he’s kowtowing to Putin. His eyes are cast down. He hunches over, despite Putin, at only 5′ 7″/170cm, is a rather short man. This shot is from their conference at Helsinki, at which Trump announced that he believed Putin, verses the FBI and about a dozen other US intelligence agencies on the well documented Russian interference in the US election (which, of course, US intelligence had tracked back to the actual building, as well as having tracked this behavior in other elections around the Western World). "President Putin says it's not Russia. I don't see any reason why it would be." -Donald J. Trump Trump embarrassed the country that day in a way never done before by a US President. The other big difference between Trump meeting with Putin and every other US President: Trump met completely in private and even forbade any transcript being produced. When Obama, Bush, Clinton, etc. met with Putin in the past, he was with a team. Every word was recorded. Putin didn’t launch an new invasions under Trump, but that’s because he didn’t need to. If he had decided to simply march into Kiev under Trump, Trump would have been fine with it. Trump, the foul mouthed narcissist who thinks he’s some kind of genius and never has much of a good thing to say about anyone else, has never spoken a harsh or critical word about Putin. That was apparently well before he ever met with the guy as President. That was clear during the 2016 campaign, when Putin was running his pro-Trump psyops campaign on Facebook, etc. We don’t know exactly what Putin has on Trump, but Trump is like a lonely puppy when he’s around Trump, lapping up any bits of praise or acceptance Putin has to offer. Question: Why do citizen-led ballot initiatives face a steep path to getting on the ballot in Florida?
Answer: It’s not that hard to launch a ballot initiative in Florida. In fact, in any given year, Florida receives tens of thousands of ballot initiative petitions. Unlike some states, there is a defined process for this. The problem, as you might expect, is that there has to be some kind of threshold for these, or you’d have 100 pages of initiatives to sort through in every election. So it’s necessary, to get a ballot initiative to the point it’s actually going to get a popular vote, it’s necessary to get at least 8% of the total vote from the previous Presidential election in validated, signed petitions. That’s currently 877,263 petitions. That’s the easy part, and if there’s some very interested organization backing a ballot measure — all the serious ones have sponsors — with money to get the word out, it’s absolutely possible. Some of the petitions officially logged are over the required number of petitions, but have not necessarily been validated. Yeah, Florida has to validate every petition… I mean, it makes sense. Mickey Mouse may actually be a state resident, but he only gets to sign one petition for any given measure. In order to pass, the measure needs 60% support in an election. Read More

Question: Is it legal to vote at the polls on Election Day if you have an absentee ballot that has not been returned yet?
Answer: It’s different in every state.. because of course it is. Each state has specific laws about voting, because states are in charge of running national and state-level elections. There are plenty of possibilities. In some states, you can vote in person as long as you have not sent in your mail-in ballot. In some states, you can fill out the mail-in ballot and had it in at your polling location. In some states, you can turn in your un-filled-out mail-in ballot and vote in person. In many states, you don’t actually have to mail-in a mail-in ballot, but can return it to state managed drop boxes. Here’s a basic guide… and these things can change any time. It’s worth checking with your state’s election board for the specific rules in any year. I’d bet every state has something online covering simple questions such as this.

Question: Are birds fake?
Answer: Yes, of course… haven’t you seen all the warnings! Birds Aren’t Real! They are government surveillance drones. I mean, would a billboard lie? Clearly, you’re not in on the joke. Birds are real. Birds Aren’t Real isn’t real. Or rather, Birds Aren’t Real is a parody/satire conspiracy theory created by a kid at the time, Peter McIndoe, in 2016… by accident. I’ll let Peter tell the story: It was an actual accident, I swear. I was in Memphis, Tenn., visiting a friend. It was shortly after Trump got elected, and there was a rally happening in Memphis. It was a women's march, and there were also people in red hats shouting things at them. And it was just kind of this chaos. And I'm not really sure why I did this. I think I was just maybe overwhelmed, or maybe it felt like there was so much madness happening, but I decided to pick up a sign and write my own thing on it. So I wrote on the sign the three most random words I could think of to pair together. And as you can guess, they were, birds aren't real. And then I started walking around, chanting, birds aren't real. And people were asking me, what does that mean? And unbeknownst to me, I was being filmed the entire time. The next week, I started being sent pictures of birds aren't real spray-painted on walls in Memphis and high-school classrooms writing it on the chalkboard, chanting it in the cafeteria…. And I was sitting, looking at all this, and just thinking, I would always regret it if I didn't try to lean into that energy that was already there. And he ran with it! McIndoe kept it going, in full conspiracy mode, until 2021. Then, in an interview with the New York Times, he explained the whole thing for what it was: a parody of a conspiracy theory. This was after some years of major media reporting on it as if it was a real conspiracy theory… not sure if it got to the point where Fox News or other fountains of nonsense-claiming-to-be-news reported it as just plain real, but I wouldn’t bet against it. I thought it was brilliant. It wasn’t just the parody, though. But in becoming the “Birds Aren’t Real Field Representative” for nearly five years, McIndoe, always in character, started to understand just how ineffective the usual means of confronting conspiracy theorists are, by becoming that guy and being regularly confronted by angry, irate people. This took serious dedication, and I applaud the guy for knowing what he had and what he could do with it! As you might expect, humorless white nationalist billionaire Elon Musk flew entirely under the whole thing and though it was a real conspiracy theory. Don’t be like Elon. Well, okay, the money is nice, but don’t be that stupid. Please… humanity is counting on it. I took this shot just yesterday… robot? Not a chance. Dinosaur? Maybe a just a bit! Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Do you agree with Chris Christie that a No Labels run would be a "fool's errand"?
Answer: As much as it pains me to agree with my former governor, Chris Christie, he’s been the unlikely voice of reason in Republican politics this year. We here in the USA have a two-party system. It’s not that you can’t have more than two parties, but the only point of long-term stability is either zero parties or two strong parties. Only a strong party can ever win a Presidential election. Today’s strong parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party, just as it’s been since 1860. The last person to win the Presidency not affiliated with either the Republicans or the Democrats was Millard Fillmore, who won the Presidency in 1850, the last of the Whig Party. The Whigs were, in their day, one of two strong parties. A large number of voters in the USA are tribal voters. They vote reflexively, based on team jersey, red or blue. Sure, they could consider an alternate candidate, but it would take some significant event for that to occur. As well, a second fairly large group of voters in the USA understands that a third party candidate can’t win. They understand the mathematics of our voting system — winner-take-all or, as it’s often called, first-past-the-post — that defines it as a two party system and ensures that third parties are either completely inert or act as spoilers. What’s a spoiler vote? Let’s say you vote for a third party candidate running very close to your ideology. Unless you are absolutely split between the two large party candidates, the most likely outcome of that vote is that you helped the candidate you least identify with, since it really will be a binary choice and you’re not voting for your best pick between the two choices. There are voting systems that eliminate the idea of a spoiler vote, such as Ranked Choice Voting, which is used for elections in Australia and even here in the USA: Alaska, Hawaii, Kansas, Wyoming, Nevada, and Maine have used it for some kinds of National elections, and it’s also used here and there at state and local levels. RCV lets a voter pick the order of their choices for a candidate. If their first pick is the lowest ranked vote, their second pick is used. This runs through until one candidate has a majority of the votership, even if not first choice votes. Going back through past elections, you’ll note that the occasional charismatic individual candidate does better in the popular vote than any third party. That’s not a surprise. Note that many Independents create a “party” label to run under, such as Roosevelt’s Bull Moose Party, but they’re still fundamentally charismatic Independents, and those “parties” generally collapse as quickly as they were formed. That’s pretty much it for the 20th and 21st Centuries. As far as established third parties go, they do far, far worse, historically. A big part of that is name recognition: no one knows about a tiny party, and their candidates are rarely well known. The best any established third party has done in recent years was the Socialist Party in 1912 (Eugene V. Debs at 6.0%, no electors), the Green Party in 2000 (Ralph Nader at 2.7%), and the Libertarian Party in 2016 (Garry Johnson, 3.3%).. those are the historical high water marks for major third parties in the USA. I’m not against the idea of more political parties. They just don’t work under our current political system. The Founders were against political parties, so they didn’t account for their existence within the system. If you go back to the original Constitution, the electoral college picked the President as the one with the majority of votes, but then the Vice President was the runner-up! Imagine Donald Trump serving with Hillary Clinton as the VP! George Washington was specifically very against the formation of parties, but unfortunately, they started being formed by his third year in office. In fact, it’s likely he ran a second term in a futile effort to stop the divisions that all of the Founders knew came from factionalizing the country into parties. He was not wrong. Under the Parliamentary systems used in many newer democracies, there’s some form of proportional representation: a party winning 10% of the vote will have about 10% of the power. So when you see countries “forming a government with a coalition” that’s what’s happening: no single party has won 50% of the power, and so at least two or three have to work together. That’s good for politics… you can’t so easily work together with someone you’ve spent decades casting as an enemy, not simply the loyal opposition. Different systems, different underlying mathematics, different results. So No Labels has all the problems normally associated with third parties. Including, it seems, little chance at attracting well known, well respected candidates. The premise of a No Labels Presidential run has been to form a “Unity” ticket, presumably centrists. They’ve suggested they’ll have a Republican for President and a Democrat as Vice President, both and necessarily well-known people, given the sad but critical role of notoriety (or even infamy) in Presidential races in the modern era. The group has had discussions with potential selections but received only “no” to date. So far, no career politician wants their legacy to include the title of “2024 Election Spoiler.“ So far, Jon Huntsman, Will Hurd, Larry Hogan, Admiral William H. McRaven, Condoleezza Rice, Geoff Duncan, and Joe Manchin III have rejected the offer. They were more recently talking to Nikki Haley, though she’s only “centrist” in the sense of being a mostly hard right Republican who’s spoke a tiny bit of truth about Trump and the MAGAs only when it was her last chance. She’s only been up to her waist in the sea of MAGA/Qanon conspiracy and disinformation… but sure, she’s also a political chameleon and could probably drop her more crazy, Trumpian-lite political nonsense overnight, if it suited her. Anyway, she said “no” because, at least in part, she wouldn’t run with a Democrat… there’s that hard right thing I mentioned again. Also in this last week, Governor Christie also said “no”… his goal this year was to see that Donald Trump doesn’t win the Presidency again, and an independent Christie run would only increase Trump’s chances. But even if they solve that, they’re still going to fail. At this point, I can guarantee that their candidate, if they field one, won’t win. No Labels has an even deeper problem: ballot access. A political party only gets automatically put on most states ballots if they have done very well in previous elections. New parties and small parties have lots of work to do every year to ensure they have ballot access: that they’re actually on the ballot in every state. As of January, No Labels has ballot access qualified in only Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Hawaii, Maine, Mississippi, Nevada, North Carolina, Oregon, South Dakota, and Utah. More recently, No Labels seems to have picked up Delaware, Kansas, Maryland, Montana, and Tennessee. So they have access to 186 electoral votes… not close to enough. They also have registered for write-ins in 6 additional states, but write-ins have never won a thing in a Presidential race, though they have occasionally be effectual at a local level, coupled with a very well run campaign. Still a far cry from the 270 needed to win. It should be a completely logical decision that if your candidate cannot possibly win the election, they’re not worth your vote. But voting is often from the emotions, not the brain… which is why we can’t have nice things! (full disclosure: I do have nice things, in spite of politics). No Labels originally claimed that they wouldn’t field a candidate if they didn’t see a viable path to the Presidency. And yet, they know they don’t have the ballot access to win no matter what, and yet, the group/party voted earlier this month (March 2024) to field a candidate. So in short, they’re making the same decisions that every third party makes: they get hungry for fame and power and run vanity candidates with absolutely no chance of winning a single electoral vote. In fairness, they haven’t done this yet, and maybe they get a few more states. But the clock’s ticking. That’s not to say that No Labels can’t influence the outcome of the Presidential election. Both Republican and Democratic state-level organizations have sued No Labels in states where their candidate could very easily swing the election to the other party — they would be a likely spoiler. Another reason No Labels can’t win is a very basic one: money. Like it or not, our ridiculously long Presidential election cycle is a huge marketing effort. Just like marketing a product. Money elects candidates. Some consumer product companies spend far more on the ad campaign around product introduction than they spend developing the product! It’s interesting to look up who donates to third party organizations, because it’s usually people trying to ensure they’ll be a spoiler. So while they didn’t bring in much money, every since Nader’s Green Party run in 2000 that tipped the election from Al Gore to George W. Bush, the Greens have received a good portion of their money from conservatives looking for that lightning to strike again… and while these things are never certain, the Greens absolutely did help Trump in 2016. There is no posted data yet on their 2024 campaign. But the most interesting thing about No Labels today is that, politically speaking, they’re broke. Poor. Skint. Indigent, impoverished, destitute, penniless! They have $424,871 cash on hand right now, and we’re already effectively into the general election for all intents and purposes, if not legally. No Labels hasn’t even officially announced a Presidential campaign. Note that parties also raise money, though my source, Open Secrets, doesn’t have statistics on political party fundraising yet for 2024. But in 2022 — not a Presidential year — both the Democrats and the Republicans raised over $1 billion each at the Party level. In 2020, it was closer to $2 billon. If you’re maybe a radical centrist (I have a good friend who makes this claim), you’re politically attuned and maybe watching to see if No Labels offers some kind of rational alternative, not just a spoiler. But you’re way, way in the minority of voters. So am I, since I’m paying attention to these things in late March, 2024, and most voters won’t be engaged in the election until September or October, at least in a typical year… sure, this isn’t exactly a typical year, given the crippling legal problems of one of the two candidates. So what if this year’s different, and No Labels did, somehow, manage to find an attractive candidate and win some states, rather than perhaps tilt a state vote away from Biden toward Trump, or vice-versa? One or two states, probably nothing happens: the Democrat or Republican still wins. But a handful of states and it’s quite possible that neither Trump nor Biden have enough electoral votes to win… but neither does the No Labels candidate, because they don’t have ballot access in enough states to win the necessary 270 electors. So that tosses the election into a contingency. The House of Representatives, one vote per state, gets to decide the President. In that event, given that currently there are more Republican-dominated than Democrat-dominated states in Congress, the likely choice is Donald Trump. That’s the perfect example of what you’ll no doubt hear, “a vote for No Labels is a vote for Donald Trump.” There’s a small but real possibility that is literally true. There is no possible outcome in which the No Labels candidate wins the Presidency. The No Labels response to this is a fairly typical third party fever dream: some Democratic and Republican electors will switch their votes to the No Labels candidate. That’s it. That’s their great solution to this problem, supposedly from an organization backed by the greated centrist minds in generations. That. Will. Never. Happen. Not. In. A. Million. Years. Particularly knowing, without question, that if the No Labels candidate won some electors, both Democrats and Republicans would have more. Statistically speaking, and again, it’s unlikely they win a single elector. Earlier on, they were suggesting that instead, they could “broker a deal” with one of the two parties for the faithless support of their electors. That is a far more likely possibility, that they managed to win one state or even just one elector (two states split their electors). A total of thirty-two states and D.C. have laws that Electors that bind electors to voting for their appointed candidate, but there’s no Federal law mandating that. Some states can simply fine faithless electors, but some: Colorado, Indiana, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Utah, Washington, can actually remove and replace a faithless elector…. some of these states have based laws based on the Uniform Faithful Presidential Electors Act. So it seems clear to me that No Labels is way out in the weeds of Presidential Election Fantasy, a very common disease caught by third parties of any kind. This is clearly not being steered by people who know what they’re doing. And while this right of states to outlaw faithless electors was supported by a SCOTUS in 2020, it’s entirely wrong, but now the law of the land. For one, the Constitution contains absolutely no concept of political parties until we get to Amendments passed after parties had been formed. So it’s impossible to claim that the Constitution requires or even supports party loyalty for electors. As well, the original vision of the Presidential election held and expected that any number of people (well, white male landowners, anyway) would run for President, all Independents, of course, since the Founders originally hated the idea of political parties. The electoral college would be and it would be a deliberative body, not a rubber stamp. If that had not been the intention, if the electoral college were meant to be a rubber stamp, then it would have served no real purpose under the original strictures, because it was largely expected that incoming electoral majorities would be rare. That would have made the contingency election commonplace, not, as it’s described in the Constitution, a contingency. Why don’t third parties do well. Again, it’s the overall effect of the political system defined by the mathematics of the voting system. In short, you win nothing coming in second, much less third, fourth, etc. The winner of any election is almost certainly the Democrat or the Republican. Because of this, most voters know that voting third party is a wasted vote and won’t vote for one. Because of that, third parties tend to move away from the mainstream and only attract zealots, only people who are either delusional about their chances of winning anything, or basically in it as a vanity project. So, for example, you rarely hear much about any third parties except in election years. Sure, there are exceptions, but for the most part, they’re once-every-four-years outlets for people who like to cosplay as political leaders. This year’s Green party candidate, for example, Dr. Jill Stein, is on her third run for President. Her sum total of actual political experience: she was elected to the town council of Lexington, Massachusetts, for two terms… though she left during that second term to run again, unsuccessfully, for Governor (she got 1.4% of the vote). She apparently just loves running for office more than trying to find an office she can win and hold. Read More

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: What are the benefits of buying a patent book or using online resources instead of taking classes on patents at university for engineering students?
Answer: Here’s the book I used, and found to be very useful. Versus a class, I have taken a bunch of online classes on things that I felt might be better in class, ranging from Cryptography to programming languages to music production, composition, and playing. But given my experience, the book was going to be a faster means to this end than taking a scheduled course, and with what I expected to be a similar outcome. Now, let’s take a look at what I was doing. First, some background. I’m an engineer, not a lawyer. Back when I worked at Commodore Computer, I was probably the best single person available to give advice on both Amiga Hardware and Software for various legal cases. So I spent a reasonable amount of time reading patents and advising our legal staff in several potential infringement cases. I also worked on my own patent, and unfortunately, I did NOT take the ship by the wheel on that one, and certainly spent more time telling the patent attorney what he got wrong, though repeated cycles, than if I had just written the thing myself. Years later, I was working at a different company, a small startup company, and asked to help with patents. Yeah, I was going to write the patent! But we’re not fools… I was going to do my best to write the patent, then we’d have our lawyer look it over, then get some advice from an actual patent attorney. So the book was very useful covering the technical aspects of patents. It helped me with the language, the organization, and the very specific kinds of drawings they’re going to want in the patent, which has been useful to me in writing both hardware, software, and systems patents over the years. After writing over a dozen patents, I would still consult a patent attorney before submitting anything. I’ve written several patents for my current employer, and it worked basically the same way: I wrote the patent after studying the invention, cycled that through the inventors (even for one of my own, because there were actually several pieces, some from other inventors) to be sure that I got it right, then ran through our in-house attorney, then finally had a review from a patent attorney. The patent attorney will have insights on language, on claims, and occasionally, on the things that get rejected. They may be able to hunt up some prior art that I’ve missed when I did a patent search (you are doing this, correct?). Now, I was covering some pretty complex inventions here. You may be just dandy without the patent attorney review, but ultimately, it could save you or your company time and money to just have your work double-checked. That’s a general rule — even when I design a computer or other electronics system, I like to run in by both software and other hardware engineers, just to get their opinions, to discuss trade-offs I might not have been thinking (this week it’s been a question of performance versus software development effort), etc.

Question: How has Rush Limbaugh achieved success in the talk radio industry despite the rise of the internet?
Answer: You can follow the rise of Limbaugh and see pretty much where he intersects the Internet. Some early experiments that would eventually lead to some of the Internet technologies — packet switching networks — were begun in 1969. Rush Limbaugh entered broadcasting as a DJ at WIXZ Radio, a Top 40 Station in Pennsylvania, back in 1971, using the on-air name “Bachelor Jeff,” and was basically trying to sound like Don Imus. He was fired after only eighteen months. About this time, a few colleges had been connected using the early Arpanet protocols that came out of those first experiments. He found another job, this time in Pittsburgh, but didn’t last a year there. In 1974, he temporarily left radio and want back to living with his parents. The first efforts to develop a more powerful “inter-network” to support large de-centralized networks that year, eventually leading to the TCP/IP protocol, one of the foundations of the internet. A year, in 1975, later he got an afternoon DJ gig at KUDL in Kansas City, Missouri, but was also able to host a weekend public affairs talk show. He lasted two years at this gig, was fired, and landed for a short gig at a competing radio station. Also in 1975, Email had become one of the killer applications on the early emerging Internet, still pretty much a research thing. Limbaugh left radio in 1979 and became a salesman for the Kansas City Royals. He didn’t go back to broadcasting until 1983, when he got a talk slot at KMBZ AM radio in Kansas City. His show didn’t last long, he was soon fired. But shortly thereafter, he found a position as the replacement for radio celebrity Morton Downy Jr. on KFBK radio in Sacramento, California. He decided to use his real name at this gig, and by 1985 he was “getting political” on the air. During these years, Usenet was invented (it’s a nerd thing), Arpanet had switched to TCP/IP protocols, and the Domain Name System (DNS) was invented. That latter is another one of the keys to enabling the modern internet. Also, Q-Link (aka Quantum Link) launched in 1985. Also in 1985, 1200 baud modems (V.22) overtook 300 baud as the most common used by consumers (I had a 1200 baud modem in 1982… thanks Bell Labs!). Oh, and that Fairness Doctrine thing? Conservative media company Capitol Cities had managed a leveraged buyout of the American Broadcasting System (ABC) in 1985. Not at all coincidentally, the FCC dropped enforcement of the Fairness Doctrine in 1985 — this is what allowed Limbaugh to get political without repercussions. See, as part of its purchase, Capitol Cities would own the ABC Radio Network, including a bunch of failing AM stations. So Capitol Cities had the idea to turn those toward selling conservative propaganda! If they couldn’t make money directly, they could sell Conservative notions — like tax cuts for the rich — to the hicks and poor people sill using AM radio, a thing that had largely fallen out use for music and anything else requiring a quality sound. Question: If you invent something and don't get a patent on it, can someone else get a patent on your idea later?
Answer: You can’t patent an idea. Period. End of discussion. You can patent an invention. If you invent something and don’t patent it, as long as it’s know to the public and/or supported with a great deal of documentation about its invention, a subsequent patent on the very same invention should be rejected. Public disclosure, shipping products, presentations at public conferences, articles about the invention, all serve to make it easier for the Patent Office to know about your prior art when that invention comes along. Of course, their first line of inquiry is among existing patents. They could miss the existence of your invention, and you might not know about the patent until someone comes after you. So save those engineering notebooks, just in case! That actually happened in a case I was helping on. In the 1980s, the PTO was issuing all kinds of software patents, but they didn’t actually have examiners who were “skilled in the art” of software engineering. I was helping the legal team at Commodore, against a stack of 30+ patents claimed against our Amiga computer series. Specifically, there was a patent dated 1984 that claimed, basically, “cut and paste between multiple text buffers.” Which, of course, was a thing that had existed for ages before that. They demonstrated this being done by using a sequence of characters in Amiga MicroEmacs, claiming that demonstrated violation of the patent. That exact same sequence of characters would have done the same thing in the CMU version of MIT’s TECO Emacs that I had used going back to 1979 when in college at Carnegie-Mellon. The original TECO Emacs — originally for Editing MACoS — was implemented at MIT in 1976 by Guy Steele, Jr. (my Comparative Languages professor) and finished up by Richard Stallman (RMS), and while I’m sure it had some evolution, it was pretty clear that prior art existed well before 1984. And in fact, in the early 80s, we also had James Gosling’s Emacs available at CMU on the various UNIX machines, though not on the TOP-20 systems used in most undergraduate classes. That was the first version of Emacs to offer a LISP-like macro language. I think it was written in 1980 or 1981, and also supported cut and paste between buffers. In fact, Gosling handed his version of Emacs over to a two-man company called Unipress — he was planning to graduate and didn’t want to be “Mr. Emacs” forever, as I hear it. So there was even this commercial version of Emacs available by 1982 or 1983. That’s just the one I know, being an Emacs guy. Text editor preferences for programmers are, of course, taken most seriously than your politics or your religion. So I know that the eventually popular UNIX text editor vi was written by Bill Joy in 1976, but since it was of course completely wrong about every possible aspect of text editing compared to Emacs, I don’t know if it was also supporting multiple buffers back then. I worked the summer of 1981 and 1982 at Bell Labs in Jersey, I learned a bit of the ed and ex text editors, but quickly found someone had a version of Emacs… and I was mostly doing hardware and embedded development on an Intel development system, so it wasn’t all that important. And looking back, while I didn’t use it, either, I’m pretty sure the Bravo text editor developed for the Xerox Alto systems at Xerox PARC was both visual and supported multiple buffers with cut and paste. That’s 1974, a decade before IBM grabbed the patent!

Question: How can multiple displays be connected via USB-C from one port on the new MacBook pros?
Answer: You want a docking station, which is basically a big Thunderbolt 4 breakout device. That’s how I hook my Dell laptop into my dual monitor rig. There are dozens of these on the market, at various prices. Pick the interface mix that you’re interest in. If you have monitors with USB ports, you may only care about the video outputs. If not, or if you’re dealing with a more complex setup with multiple computers, as I do, you might feed your breakout box into a KVM switch, which will switch display and some USB ports between two or more PCs. You’d have to check with the manufacturer to ensure Apple compatibility, though most of these use ports types defined by industry standards and ought to work okay with Apple. But do check… they can be weird sometimes. Another solution, if you have the right monitor, is to use Thunderbolt daisy-chaining. You’re hooked up from the computer to one monitor, and that monitor has another Thunderbolt port that chains to a similar monitors. This is possible but unusual. You can find devices that just deliver a video display pair, usually DisplayPort, without any other interfaces offered. This would be the budget choice.

Question: Can I patent someone else’s ideas?
Answer: You can't patent anyone's ideas. Patents cover inventions, which are very specific implementations of useful distillations of one or more component ideas. You can certainly pay for someone else's patent application and process. If you're knowledgeable enough, you can write a patent for someone else. I have done a bunch of those, and that is one of the basic jobs of a Patent Attorney. If the inventor is your employee and they created this invention as a product of their work for you, you can file as the asignee of the patent. But unless you are one of the inventors, you cannot be listed in the patent as an inventor. As well, you can't easily patent any invention that has already been publicly disclosed, whether in a product being sold, a paper given at a conference, even perhaps a detailed Quira article would qualify as prior art -- the invention existing before you filed the application. Technically in the USA you have a year after disclosure, but you don't in most other countries.
