Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Was the qualification of Donald Trump for the presidential primary in Colorado a win for democracy? Now, can the people now decide?
Answer: It’s really got nothing to do with democracy. It’s about the division between State and Federal power. The decision is based largely on Section 5 of the 14th Amendment, which details the powers of enforcement of the remainder of the 14th Amendment. In short, the unanimous Supreme Court ruling holds that a State can apply the Disqualification Clause for State-level candidates or elected officials, but not at the Federal level. Only at the Federal level, such as in a law passed by Congress or, presumably, as decision made in a Federal court, can a person be excluded from holding Federal Office. They did not make the assertion that the Disqualification Clause could not be used to bar candidates from elections, primary or general, as some pundits had suggested, and in fact, one state had already rules. However, they did allude to the idea that States may not have the right to apply any local rules to Federal elections. Given that the requirements to be placed on the ballot for President vary tremendously from State to State, I’d be surprised if this doesn’t get more third party candidates suing for ballot access, and maybe even weaken the sore loser laws that prevent a losing primary candidate from running as an Independent in the general election. A person realistically ineligible to hold office should not be permitted to run for office. Allowing them to isn’t democracy in action, it’s subverting democracy, since, if they’re elected and later found ineligible to hold office, their entire candidacy would have been a Trojan Horse that effectively put their running mate in office. This ruling, however, does make Trump’s eligibility now an issue for the Federal government, not the States. I guess the right wing’s penchant for States Rights only goes so far, but it’s hard to argue with their decision… at least, I haven’t found a flaw in it, personally, but I’m hardly a legal scholar. It’ll be interesting to see deeper analysis from our better legal minds. It is a unanimous decision, and that was rather expected for something as important as this. Read More

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: What do you think will happen if Trump wins the presidential nomination primary but is deemed ineligible to be on the general election ballot?
Answer: That’s a bit of a boondoggle, isn’t it. And for these days, not a bad question. Trump has been ruled ineligible to run for President in the Colorado primary. It’s been delayed so much, it’s a rather moot point now. And here’s the 14th Amendment’s disqualification clause in full… read and think: Fourteenth Amendment, Section 3: No person shall be a Senator or Representative in Congress, or elector of President and Vice-President, or hold any office, civil or military, under the United States, or under any State, who, having previously taken an oath, as a member of Congress, or as an officer of the United States, or as a member of any State legislature, or as an executive or judicial officer of any State, to support the Constitution of the United States, shall have engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the same, or given aid or comfort to the enemies thereof. But Congress may by a vote of two-thirds of each House, remove such disability. So if you read this specific part of the Constitution literally, it says nothing about an eligibility to run for office, only to hold that office. So it’s at least reasonable to assume that part of what the Supreme Court is looking at, if they’d like to issue a narrow interpretation — and they likely will, since they don’t want the heat of specifically disqualifying Trump — might just concentrate on the relationship between the wording of the disqualification clause with respect to the primaries. Also because it’s easier to rule on the literal wording than prove the intent of the framers of the Constitution or any Amendment. So they could rule in several ways: None of these are without their problems. In the first case, this would leave open the same suit for the general election, with a second pass of legislation, but in a much shorter timeframe. Not a good outcome. In the second case, that would effectively eliminate any other test of eligibility from primaries, or at the very least, move such restrictions as are generally accepted today into a whole slew of new court cases. If an insurrectionist can run for President, why can’t a naturalized citizen do the same, even if they can’t ultimately hold office. That last one could get the courts moving on finishing up some of the Trump cases, but SCOTUS has already chose to delay these based on their review of the entirely ludicrous claim by Trump of unlimited immunity as President. They could offer the answer expected by every Constitutional scholar on the planet — there is no such immunity — so late that no Trump trials can conclude before the election. If they decide the other way, the open the door to Biden ordering Seal Team Six (pretty much the only group ever mentioned in these things) to assassinate Trump, with full immunity. Of course, it would also open the door to Trump doing likewise for all of his political rivals and his 2500+ entry enemies list, should he be re-elected. It makes absolutely no sense they would not uphold the lower court’s decision. Their taking the case seems overtly political, but we’ll see when the decision is rendered. Of course, the question asks what happens if we get past that second option… Trump is elected but ruled ineligible. The likely case is that, just as in any other case of a President-elect being unable to fulfill his office, the Vice President elect would take his place. However, it depends on just when Trump is ruled ineligible. If it’s before the electoral college meets in December, it’s entirely possible that some electors pick Biden. Not entirely likely, because these things are so partisan, but if you were an honest Trump elector — if such exist — and saw though this ruling that Trump never should have run, the morally correct thing would be to pick Biden. But assuming that didn’t happen, Trump’s out and his Vice President is Inaugurated as President in January. That President appoints a replacement VP. Congress has to ratify that VP, then we’re done. But this also opens a huge can of worms. If Trump’s allowed to run as a person ineligible for the candidacy, what’s to stop Barack Obama, Arnold Schwarzenegger, or some other very popular person from running with no chance to win, just to ensure their party and their VP gets into office.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Will Trump running out of money due to legal issues actually affect him in the primaries? Or will Republican primary voters not care?
Answer: It’s unlikely Trump’s lack of money will have a huge effect on him in the primaries. Yes, Nikky Haley is bringing in more and staying within her means, while Trump’s donations are way down and he’s spending more than he takes in at the moment. Of course, he’s a billionaire, right, and can self-finance if he runs out…. tick tick tick… okay, if you’re not laughing by now, you’re lacking a fundamental understanding of objective reality. Trump is on the hook for about $450 billion in his New York business fraud case by March 25th, and doesn’t seem to have the money. He’s not going to self-finance his primary. But if you look at Trump’s numbers in the Red states, he’s been 20–40% ahead of Nikky Haley. She’s absolutely going to try to lower that gap, and she still has most of her supporters (the Koch Group recently backed out, moving support to down-ballot races, Congress and local, not shifting to support Trump. Trump was bad for most business once he took office… and the Koch Group has been a regular Republican megadonor for ages. They understand this with their bottom line. Trump’s lack of money will absolutely affect the general election, and in more ways than you might think. Ordinarily in an election year, the small donors have mostly had three years off — most donors to Presidential campaigns don’t donate to off-year Congressional campaigns, which is why it’s so east for those that do to buy themselves a nice Senator or Congressman in the off-year. But Trump has been draining the small MAGA donor since he lost the 2020 election and kept pushing donor to send him money… which in 2020 went 75% into Trump’s pocket and 25% to the RNC… to keep them quiet. T So they’re tapped out, and that’s not only reflected in Trump’s recent donation numbers, but the fact that at least 12 state-level Republican organizations are at or near bankruptcy. That’s the real problem, because there is a strong positive correlation between money spent and votes cast. That doesn’t mean a Trump who’s 20–40+ points ahead in a primary has much to worry about in the primary. The general’s another story. No one wins an election with just Republicans, just Democrats, much less the subset of the Republican electorate who identify as MAGAs. Trump will need to convince all those Nikki Haley voters to vote for him, not stay home or vote for Biden. As well as Independents, currently the largest voting bloc in the country. That takes money… that’s entirely why so many candidates are always worried about fundraising. It’s a shitty system, but that’s how it works. A bankrupt or money scarce RNC won’t just not elect Trump, they’ll skew their results for Congressional and State elections. This isn’t new: between money issues and the unprecedented dislike of Trump, Trump’s involvement, in various ways, has lost the overall elections for the Republicans in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023. This year is an election year, but the finances are worse and the anti-Trump sentiments are stronger than ever. Many Primary voters don’t understand these dynamics, and chances are, MAGAs are getting all their news from far right propaganda sources like Fox News. They’re not even being told about this stuff, and they’ll likely label this “fake news” if it does come their way. Trump can’t use that to increase donations, even if some are capable. However, Republican megadonors do know this, and don’t see a Trump run as a likely victory. So far, they’ve been supporting other candidates, not Trump. It’s down ot Haley now, and those megadonors dropping here — figuring Trump is inevitable — so far are not funding Trump, but rather working to fund those down-ballot Republican candidates hit with the double whammy of fewer small donations and Trump, unlike all normal Presidential candidates, not sharing his fundraising with his party organization and down-ballot candidates.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Trump beat Haley with 70% of the GOP presidential primary vote in Michigan. Is this enough to get her to drop out or does it show weakness that he can't bury her?
Answer: Candidates rarely drop out of a primary because they lose… just ask John Kasich. Rather, they drop out because they’re running low on money. Sometimes it’s earlier, knowing they can keep some of that sweet Presidential donation money to use in their next run for some other kind of office. Some because they’re flat broke. Haley right now is none of those things: she’s set her sites on the Presidency and has no political Plan B, and she’s got cash. She’s losing some supporters, but not all of them just yet. So she’ll stay in until she doesn’t. She has promised, repeatedly, to stick it out at least until Super Tuesday, March 5th… that’s less than a week away. I believe her. You should too. This definitely shows that Trump is favored by Republican voters, though that’s kind of been a given. Michigan has an open primary, so anyone can vote in one primary in any election without worrying about their party affiliation: Republicans, Independents, Democrats, Libertarians, Socialists, whatever. However, it’s also telling that, compared to the 2016 Republican primary, there were 222,992 fewer votes this time. That’s like thee complete Republican primaries here in Delaware! Maybe that signals voters think Trump is inevitable, or maybe there are fewer folks interested in supporting the Republicans. Hard to know for sure. Michigan lists 8,275,421 registered voters… only 13.3% voted in the Republican primary. Those are the devoted ones, as usual, including the Super MAGAs, and, probably, the Super-Never-Trumpers. It’s not a terribly sharp view of the general election dynamics.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: In the South Carolina primary, Trump got 59% of GOP and Biden got 98% of Democrat votes. Who will be stronger in the general election?
Answer: It’s not a terribly easy calculation, as South Carolina doesn’t register political parties. And a primary doesn’t bring out nearly as many voters as a general election. So we do know that Trump took South Carolina with 55.11% of the vote over Biden’s 43.3% in 2020. We also know there were a total of 3,300,161 registered voters in South Carolina in 2020. Thus, 75% of the voters in South Carolina made it to the general election polls in 2020. This also suggests that there are 27% more Republican voters than Democratic, but this is just a single snapshot. And since no one’s registered, when I say “Republican” or “Democrat”, read “likely voter” not party member. Since Biden’s an Incumbent in 2024 and Trump was in 2020, let’s look at the primary turnout for the Democrats in 2020 and the Republicans in 2024. There were 512,418 Democratic votes in 2020 and 754,256 Republican votes in 2024. This suggests that there are 47% more Republican voters than Democratic. This also might suggest that Republicans are more likely to come out for a primary. It’s also the case that in the 2016 Republican primary there were only about 5,000 fewer voters, so this is a pretty consistent turnout. But it’s also not entirely useful, because in both cases, South Carolina doesn’t track voters and any can vote in any primary, but only once. Let’s use the 27% number as a model and I’ll claim that there are 1,453,815 likely Democratic and 1,846,346 likely Republican voters in South Carolina. If the overall turnout rate is again 75%, and we have 98% of them voting for Biden, we get 1,068,554 votes for Biden. If the 59.8% number holds for Trump, he’s got 1,104,115 votes… Trump still wins South Carolina. But we still have the 39.5% of Republican who voted for Nikki Haley…. they liked her better than Trump, but does that mean they’re not going in on Trump over Biden in the general election? If the all did vote for Biden, he gets an additional 728,307 votes, for a total of 1,797,861 votes.. Biden wins big. But would they all really vote for Biden? Let’s take a look. In the South Carolina exit polls, 78% of voters identified themselves as Conservative… whatever that means today, I guess, but only 42% claimed to be “MAGA.” It’s interesting, too, that only 68% of the Republican voters claimed to be Republicans on exit polling, with 28% claiming to be Independents and 5% Democratic this year. While I couldn’t find a representative exit poll for South Carolina, Iowa shared numerous similarities, and on polling, 17% of Republican caucus goes claimed to be anti-MAGA. So let’s for now assume that no Haley voters go for Trump, but 17% are anti-MAGA and do vote for Biden as an anti-vote for Trump. That delivers an additional 313,879 votes for Biden, totaling 1,382,433 to Trump’s 1,104,115… Biden wins! But that other 22.5% who voted for Haley probably don’t all stay home. Let’s say that half stay home or vote for the Libertarian or maybe whoever No Labels picks if they manage to get ballot access in South Carolina. But the other half goes for Trump even though they don’t like the guy. That’s another 212,330 votes for Trump, bringing him to 1,316,445 votes and the win. And here you see in microcosm the weird world of the swingable voter: do they go Republican, Democratic, or “other.” They decide many elections at the state level, and every election for President. All those ads you see 24/7 during the final months of the extended election? They’re aimed at that guy! So even with Trump’s poor showing, it’s unlikely that Biden beats Trump with that kind of Republican advantage. That, of course, based on a late-February snapshot of Trump’s popularity among Republicans in South Carolina. What’s the trend line? Is he slowly losing support, and how strong is that loss? Can he gain some of it back? Will a felony conviction or twenty change voters minds at all?

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Some job requirements insist on stringent testing, like psychological, mental capacity, ability to multitask and make important decisions while under tremendous pressure, why not for the President of the USA?
Answer: Yes, we would like the President to be capable in these things. Unfortunately, too much of the insanely long election season has candidates concentrating not on their capacities and talents, but how they look on stage. Here’s the thing: the requirements for the President to serve are set in the Constitution. Period. There are some additional requirements, state-by-state, that permit a candidate to appear on the ballot as well as, at least in most cases, verification of their ability to legally serve. But that’s it… the only way to change requirements is by amending the Constitution. The campaign is, like it or not, their job interview. That’s it, and you’re one of the bosses. You get to judge the person’s temperament, intelligence, plans for the future, experience, anything you’d personally like as your personal criteria. And yes, it’s true that most US voters don’t have a bloody clue about what the job of the President entails. They could learn about governing, learn about the candidates in detail, read hundreds of pages — things I’ve actually done. But have you? Maybe. Has every voter? Not even close! But wait — we’re all the boss! Why would we hire an unqualified employee… and sure, most Americans don’t have a bloody clue about what the job of a boss/manager is, either. And if you think about it, locking the requirements away in the Constitution is A Good Thing™. Why? Because anything that can be flipped by Congress and the President can be flopped right back in the political wind. So rules change every 4–8 years… wonderful. Not. Or maybe they don’t, but that’s baaaad. In fact, allowing any random President and Congress to change the rules for electing the next President and/or Congress doesn’t seem like a particularly good idea to me. Politicians tend to pass laws that make it more likely they and their kind get elected, less likely that their opposition or any new people get elected, much as possible. Just ask any third party in USA how they’ve been supported by public election law and practice! Or take in the 2024 election… the battle of the codgers! Again! Let’s try a thought experiment… but first, an engineering story. Hey, you’re reading my stuff… what did you expect? Back when I was working at Commodore Computer, we had this wonderful system called Amiga, the first personal computer system on the market with multitasking, stereo audio, a graphical user interface, built-in animation primitives, automatic add-in configurations, hardware graphics acceleration. But it had a weakness: our software was built to run on an affordable 1980s microcomputer, the Motorola 68000. A great chip, but no memory protection. So a program running with errors could technically cause errors anywhere in RAM, including other program’s code or data memory, or even those of the operating system. To help developers create programs without these bugs, one of our software engineers, Michael Sinz, wrote a tool called Enforcer. This turned on the MMU in a system with an MMU (I helped design the first ones we had in-house at Commodore) and caught pretty much anything it might do wrong, a harder wall than you might find in some protected operating systems. There were a few other tools as well to ensure good code, but this was the best known. When you ran your program with Enforcer, it generated “Enforcer hits” that indicated any errant code. The program was released to the community, and a funny thing happened: regular users started using it to find out which program might be the one causing problems. Magazines doing software reviews started running Enforcer, and if your program showed Enforcer hits to the reviewer, you were not getting a great review. There was no one enforcing the use of Enforcer, but it came to be expected. If your program didn’t pass, you lost potential customers. So, could be make such a test voluntary but effectively required? How do we do this? Well, to start with, someone’s got to make a test. Let’s assume some neutral party assembles experts: scientists, psychologists, including military psychologists, physiologists, sports medicine doctors, etc. We create a test that’s very good at verifying the level of a candidate’s physical and mental physical base condition, their mental ability to work under pressure, their ability make decisions under pressure, their ability to meet a crisis with little sleep for days, little or no food, etc. There’s no pass/fail, you get a number, as on an IQ test, or perhaps two different numbers, but something fairly simple for the masses to use to compare candidates. So we have a test. And there is something attractive about putting politicians though a harder version of the Boot Camp and Jeopardy game shows, done simultaneously. What do we do now? It’s useless if no one’s willing to take it, so now we have to discuss this test with actual politicians, maybe some celebrities, etc. Get people taking the test… all results automatically published. Like the old SATs, you can take it over, the system will use your best result, but you can’t un-take it. This all costs money, but baby, you ain’t seen nothin’ yet. You would need a sales and education job, to tell the public the test is useful. What’s your ad budget… if the answer’s not in the tens of millions, you’re not serious about this. You need to get politicians to agree to take it (well, they do have egos… maybe some would jump on it, but I bet many would take a pass), and now, years later, it’s starting to show up in campaign ads… both for and against candidates. Pretty soon, lots of candidates are taking it, it’s seeming to become a standard campaign thing to do, voters are giving their candidates flack if they don’t take the test! So we’ve won… right? Not yet, and not really anyway. Because now you’re starting to hear from other people, scientists, historians, psychologists, etc. who are calling to question the validity of your test. Is this really at all useful at testing candidates? Maybe some fairly famous and successful ex-President or Senator takes the test and does poorly, reinforcing the idea it’s not a valid test. Where’s your experimental data that it’s at all predictive of future success in office? You don’t have any, because that would take some decades of development, testing, analysis, refinement, etc. Critics will see that: the test isn’t even old enough to know if a test result has any correlation to actual performance in office, and yet, we’re going to be using this as a basis for candidates’ qualifications? So once you hear that, all those running for office who didn’t want the test in the first place are now “bravely taking a stand for science and fairness!” by opposing the test. Maybe that starts to be the big trend, and before you know it, it’s over. No one wants the test. Not only that, but there’s a good chance that cultural/political memory ensures there’s no new attempt at such a test for over a century. This kind of test would be really complex and inherently controversial. But we have, over time, had various “rules of campaigning” that most candidates follow, because they’re tradition, but also because they’re kind of necessary. In usual politics, you release your tax returns, you participate in debates, you speak about your extensive experience in state or local politics, you generally speak truth (sure, you spin things, but you expect to be called out on lies, and you expect that to hurt your campaign), and do a bunch of other things that have become usual for this weird job interview we call an election. And yet, in 2016, a nepo baby who never held a job of any kind (much less an elected one) and never served in the military, who never spoke the truth about much of anything, ran for President, skipped one debate, never released a single tax return, and yet, won (just barely, but he did). It’s also interesting that, after Trump ran, a bunch of states started seriously looking into making the release of tax returns a requirement to appear on the state ballot. But none of them carried through with it, as that would be effectively adding a new requirement to run as President, which of course the Constitution sets in stone… sort of. It is also true that each state can set requirements for a candidate to appear on the ballot, such as a number of signatures on a petition, and those numbers can range from zero to hundreds of thousands, depending on state. State law can also band candidates who ran but lost in a primary election from being on the ballot in the ensuing general election. So there is certainly some plasticity here. The Supreme Court has thrown out some state requirements for Federal Office in the past, but I didn’t look up those decisions. And what we saw with Trump: these de-facto requirements, unlike those in the Constitution, can never be considered “cast in stone” because they’re in force until someone ignores them, but more importantly, gets away with ignoring them. If all the traditions that seem to be rules are cast aside and the voters don’t penalize that, then the rules don’t work. Back in the day, Enforcer only became pretty close to mandatory because buyers complained about software that either didn’t pass Enforcer or wasn’t tested. So not using it was punished by the market. The first big problem with this kind of test is that the voluntary use of it only goes as far as the public demand for it. If candidates don’t have to take it, and they don’t pay an electoral penalty, then many won’t bother to take it… just like Trump not releasing his tax returns. That was a de-facto requirement until it wasn’t. So now, of course, you’re going to tell me, as you asked, that you want it put into an Amendment, of course. An actual hard requirement. But do we really want that? My scenario above made a test. Let’s define that test as done as well as current science can do it … not really possible, but again, this is just a model, and models can be perfect. It’s the perfect test, and it’s proven to be predictive of future success. The politicians eventually embraced it, rather than revolt as I suggested they probably would, in time. Problem Scenario 1 After some years of everyone using it, we get some dire statistics: Democrats are testing overall 10% better than Republicans on the test. No reason given or known. The test would be challenged for bias, because, of course, given the public results, that’s giving the Democrats an edge. So Congress gets a new committee together, more psychologists and physiologists, and they study the testing process, study the results, try to find bias. They don’t… it just seems that people who have conservative values don’t do as good as those with more liberal values. So they change the test to put in some artificial bias that levels the playing field, essentially handicapping the Democrats natural abilities: rating the parts of the tests done best by Democrats as less heavily weighted. This takes two years, and finally the new test is approved and recommended. Now, sure enough, over time, the Democrats and the Republicans do about the same. But over another long period of time, there the same problem: Democrats start doing better, despite the handicaps. No one understands this. So now, Congress appoints a Testing Czar, empowered to study everyone in Congress. Those in office have mandatory testing, and the tests are revised regularly. Eventually, the Testing Czar decides it’s too inefficient to keep changing the test, so the test is changed back to base, and each Congressman or Senator is fitted with enough accessories: earpieces that blare a tone every so often to disrupt their thinking, automatic supplemental adrenaline or morphine microdosing to keep everyone at the same excitement level, weights if they’re at too much of a physical advantage. Eventually, it becomes mandatory to wear all this gear while serving in office… everyone’s now at exactly the same performance level. Yeah, sometimes politics can forget or even reverse the purpose of a law… you don’t want this. I’m sure you’ve heard this story before. Question: If Nikki Haley does not win the South Carolina Republican primary, will it be harder for her to run as an independent or third-party candidate in November?
Answer: That reality — she had 40% to Trump’s 60% — will have absolutely nothing to do with her ability to run as an Independent, or to join another party and run as their candidate. What will stop her almost certainly are the sore loser laws on the books in most states and obtaining ballot access. Sore Loser Laws Some states ban former candidates in primaries from running in the general election, period. South Carolina’s law reads: A person who was defeated as a candidate for nomination to an office in a party primary or party convention” cannot appear on the general election ballot unless the nominee dies or, for other reasons, is no longer the party’s nominee. Some states put in mechanisms that achieve the same effect. Kansas, for example, has really early filing deadlines — by the time the primaries are underway, it’s too late to register. Montana requires a candidate to have not been associated with another party for a year before running as an Independent, running as a party’s candidate, or even holding political office as a member of a party. Ballot Access She’d also have trouble at this date filing in time to obtain ballot access in every state. States have deadlines and requirements for candidates to show up on the state ballot. You can’t have a chance at winning an election if you’re not on nearly every ballot. So it’s difficult to decide late that you want to run as an Independent. If she became another party’s candidate, she’d have the advantage that real political parties started filing for ballot access last year. It’s even hard if you’re a minor political party in the USA. For example, Alabama, a candidate needs a petition with 3% of the vote from the last gubernatorial election. That’s 42,071 signatures this year. New Hampshire has a similar number, but also makes it illegal to circulate such a petition in an odd year. And the party has to meet that requirement every new election unless they win 20% of the vote in an statewide election in the current year. Florida doesn’t require any petition to gain ballot access except a person running as an Independent for President, who must get 110,000 signatures. Texas requires a Presidential candidate to get 1% of the last Presidential election vote total, which is over 111,500 this year. The Green Party, which has been active for decades, only has ballot access in 20 states plus D.C. at the time I’m writing this. The No Labels group (they don’t like to be called a party, but they’re behaving like one) has managed to secure ballot access in 13 states (Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Hawaii, Maine, Mississippi, Nevada, North Carolina, Oregon, South Dakota and Utah) and they’re working on 14 more… still way short of the number you’d need to win an election. They seem to have access to 109 electors… less than 40% of what they’d need to win if they carried every one of these states. They stated this process a year or more ago! There has been talk about Nikki Haley joining No Labels, though not necessarily from her, though they seem interested. It’s a bit of a legal question as to whether sore loser laws apply to a Presidential candidate. A study by lawyers Jason Torchinsky, Steve Roberts, Dennis Polio, and Andrew Pardue claim that sore losers in at least 28 states will apply to the Presidential election. That includes 20 states that voted for Trump in the last election, which would be critical to Nikki Haley as a third party candidate. If Nikki Haley did join another party, or run as an Independent, it’s pretty inevitable that the Trump campaign and/or the RNC would sue in any state she registered if they have some kind of sore loser law … that’s 47 out of 50 states plus D.C… assuming Trump’s campaign has any money left over for that sort of thing… they’ve been paying his legal bills, and donors are dropping their support as a result. Question: If Haley loses the Republican primary, can she be written in at the general election for president? Has any president been voted in by write-ins?
Answer: She can be written in for President, sure… if you’re in a state that allows this. The light green states… those allow write-ins the way most folks think write-ins work. You show up to the polling place and write the candidate’s name in. Those votes are tallied, and if that person has the most votes, they win the election. Those in green require a candidate to register as a write-in. If Nikki Haley wanted to be considered as a write-in candidate, she would have to register in each of these states. Otherwise, while you could certainly write-in her name, those votes wouldn’t be tallied. They go in the pile with voted for Mickey Mouse and Vermin Supreme. Finally, for the Presidential election, there probably is no write-in possible in the states shown as Orange, Red, or Brown. The Orange states allow registered write-ins for non-Presidential elections, but none for the Presidency. The Red states allow for write-ins only in the case of a substitute candidate who’s come along after the ballots were printed. In the brown states, “no” means “no” — no possible way to write in a candidate. So a Nikki Haley write-in campaign starts without access to 54 electoral votes. That’s of course on top of being in competition with Trump in every state. The most likely effect of a really well organized write in campaign, just like an Independent or third party campaign, is that she splits a bit of the vote with Trump, doesn’t win a single state, but maybe hands a few to Biden. That’s the spoiler effect in our winner-take-all system. It’s unlikely that she’d win any Democratic votes, and most anti-Trump Conservatives are going to vote against Trump rather than pick an alternate candidate, that vote increasing the likelihood that Trump wins. No President has won via write-ins. No President has even come close. In fact, no President has won on with a Party other then the Republicans or Democrats since Zachery Taylor in 1848. His Vice President, Millard Filmore, was the last person to hold the Presidency not affiliated with the Republicans or the Democrats, after Taylor died of cholera in 1850. At the time, the Democrats and the Whigs were the two strong parties in the USA mandated by the mathematics of our voting system — the only point of stability is two strong parties. So even this was business as usual, though the Whig Party fell apart shortly after this last stand. It will not be any different in 2024.

Answer: Nope. Smartphones, being tiny battery powered devices, have a limit to the power available for use. You’d kind of like your battery to last all day, and your phone’s power management system, a mix of hardware and software, works to optimize power. A typical battery in 2024 can provide maybe 8–16 Watt-hours of power depending on the battery. So that’s 8 hours of operation at 1 Watt continuous power, 4 hours of operation at 2 Watts continuous power, 2 hours at 4 Watts, etc. But there’s also a limit on power dissipation. The more power a phone uses, the more heat it generates. Too much heat and it’ll slow down or even go dormant, via your phone’s thermal management system. The alternative is damage to the phone. The fully lit screen, a busy CPU/GPU, or a weak cellular connection are some of the primary power sinks in your phone. A typical phone can probably dissipate 2W, and some newer designs might manage 4W of heat. If your phone’s design can’t dissipate heat faster than it’s generated, the phone will slow down, as thermal and power management kick in, and ultimately shut down if it’s too much heat. My work laptop includes the nVidia RTX A3000 GPU, a pretty good, professional grade GPU for mobile computers. It’s got a peak rated power draw of 115W! That’s 30–50x as much heat as your phone could dissipate. And you’d get about 8 minutes of operation from your phone’s large battery at peak. The Dell Precision 5770 has a 97Whr battery — laptops keep that below 100Whr or they become a problem for air travel. That’s substantially better than your phone, but it’s still quite possible to run a laptop down pretty fast if you’re pushing your GPU to the limit. More important, between heat pipes and fans, the laptop can dissipate all that heat, at least at normal office temperatures. Like all modern mobile devices, it’s doing power and thermal management and will reduce performance and ultimately power down if heat becomes dangerous. Many modern GPUs and CPUs could actually get hot enough to self-destruct if they didn’t manage power. My largest desktop PC has two GPUs in it. Just the RTX 2070 can draw 175W by spec, and the CPU, a 16-core Threadripper, can draw another 180W. The second GPU is only about 100W, and all that heat does mean additional performance. Technically, I could dump both of those and put in dual RTX 4080s at 320W each… but not without a serious power supply upgrade and probably another case fan or two. That’s the key factor in desktop/tower PCs: they’re fully modular, so you can do your own heat management planning. You can also screw that up complete if you don’t know what your’re doing. The closest you might get these days is Apple. Since they design their own system-on-chip, they use versions of the same CPU, GPU, NPU, etc. for phone, laptop, and desktop systems. The iPhone 15 Pro Max has 6 GPU cores, based on Apple’s proprietary GPU… and Apple’s phones typically downclock the SOC these days, because they’re actually a bit too powerful for the heat management system. The M3 processor, used for Apple’s lower-end laptops, contains 8 GPU cores. The M3 Max, used in higher end laptops and desktops, contains 30 of the same GPU cores. There’s an expected M3 Ultra some time this year that will have 60 GPU cores. So yeah, the desktop is way, way more powerful than the phone, even when you’re comparing, um, apples to apples (sic)! The salient point here is that there’s no technology you can put into a smartphone — which really is a tiny low-end pocket sized personal computer, not a “telephone” — that you can’t deliver, much larger and more powerful, on the desktop. One place the smartphones do pretty well is on AI benchmarks. That’s because PC-class CPUs don’t have AI engines. You can run AI algorithms on x86 processors, but they’re only so good at this. I ran the Geekbench ML benchmark on my laptop and saw a CPU result of 3400 , a DirectML (uses GPU/NPU) of 8250. Using it NPU, the iPhone 15 Pro Max saw a result of 5943 on the NPU, versus 3420 on the GPU and 2288 on the CPU. The NPU result is faster than many laptop/integrated GPUs on PCs. The x86 PC industry has fallen a bit behind on AI processing, having left that job to the GPU for years. However, with the right GPU, the PC blows away smartphones here, too: a higher end AMD PC with nVidia GeForce RTX 4090 managed to hit 28,061… that’s the kind of a GPU you’d pick as a consumer, at least, for serious AI work on your PC.

Question: Can a person who never code or knew anything about coding before, learn how to code and design a very developed indie video game like shovel knight, if yes, how smart does he or she often need to be to achieve this, and how long will it usually take?
Answer: It depends on your specific goals, of course. For one, a single person isn’t going to make a modern console/PC type game, because this class of game is basically run like a film production, with storyboarding, graphics artists, actors, and yeah, even some programmers. On the other hand, if you’re thinking something smaller, it’s absolutely possible. You can skip this tale, but I wanted folks to know that, since I actually did this as a kid, back when it was difficult due to the state of computer resources. Without having the goal of necessarily writing games in mind, I started teaching myself to program when I was 12 years old. This was not easy back in the 1970s. My Dad brought home a TI Silent 700 terminal on the weekends, which connected to his department’s computer at Bell Labs. When I was 17, I bought an Exidy Sorcerer personal computer… it had 16K of DRAM (I upgraded it to 32K). It could read/write programs to a cassette deck, but it didn’t come with one (I modified a Radio Shack cassette player for use). It had a composite video output, in B&W. TVs in the day didn’t have composite video input (the yellow jack). I started with an RF modulator, but ultimately designed my own composite input port, which I added to my bedroom TV. Then I proceeded to write a bunch of games… very primitive stuff, even by today’s mobile gaming standards. Still, I sold two tapes worth to Creative Computing Software in 1979, making more money on that than I had washing dishes the previous summer! I was writing in BASIC and Z-80 Assembly language. That was about the only option on that machine in those days, but these days, there are a bunch of options for mobile games. It’s not only the language, as you’re probably not going to write a game purely from scratch as I used to. It’s possible, but there are game engines that both simplify development and as well support cross-platform targets (Android, iOS, Windows, MacOS, Linux, consoles, etc). Don’t be afraid! Today, you have a ton of available online resources. Full documentation for pretty much any language you’d like to use, and probably the language too, are available online, as freebies. There are online classes in coding.. I took a courses in Android Programming and in the ChucK Programming Language (it’s a very weird language for music creation) on Coursera. There are subject-related courses, including courses on game development, mobile app development, graphics and animation, pretty much anything you like. It’s so very easy to learn things today versus back when I first did it. And taking a class, you’ll learn better disciplines that I stated out with (I fixed much of that in college). Some classes let you choose your own pace. And really, when you’re coding, it’s just you and the computer… the computer shows your mistakes but it’s not critical, not judgmental, just there to help you figure things out. So it can be a very different kind of learning, and for some kinds of brains, exactly right! So you can — and should — go find a course on programming, sign up, and get started this very week if you can, assuming this is your actual interest and not just a casual “is this possible” question. The best way to learn anything is to go out an Just Do It, as the sneaker people say! If you have a personal computer or even an Android tablet — it’s technically possible even on a phone, but you’ll drive yourself mad on that tiny screen — you have all the hardware you need to learn programming. If you know where the first version of your game is going to run: phone, PC, etc. you’ll need one of those, too, once you’ve picked up enough coding to start thinking about the game. There’s also a discipline to it, planning things out, structuring the game design, etc., so I’d strongly recommend reading about or taking a class on game development, just to grease the wheels for your own work. I also know this is possible today because I have a cousin who actually did this. He and his wife, actually. He did the game design and all coding, she did the graphic design, artwork, etc. Now, my cousin was a professional programmer with decades of experience, including working on games for Disney, and he discovered that mobile game development is a tricky business, but he did release games. Then he found a better paying, less stressful coding job :-) I would recommend anyone thinking about this start it out as a hobby, of course, not at attempted profession. It will take you some time to learn, though depending on how high you shoot, you could be playing your own game this year if you’re dedicated. It really has to become your passion, as with any creative thing, for you to get good at it. And… how do you feel about sleep? When I was learning, I was often up all most nights until 2–3am coding… and in fact, I’m usually up at 2–3am still. It can make you weird, but good-weird! It’s ultimately going to depend on you. Do you take to coding, or do you find it difficult… you won’t know until you try. If you have a talent for it, give it a try. You’ll probably write a bunch of less than great games before you come up with something pretty good, because this is like any other creative endeavor… your first wood carving, your first painting, your first house (well, treehouse, dog house, at least in my case), your first photograph, your first cabinet, your first song, etc. are not going to be your best (I have made all of these things at some point in life). Question: Which is better, a TV with a higher pixel count or one with a higher pixel density like a mobile device?
Answer: Unless you’re holding your television on your hand, you’re not buying on the basis of pixel density. First of all, while phones come in a wide variety of screen sizes and resolutions, TVs come in all sizes, but nearly all these days are either Full HD (1920x1080 pixels) or UltraHD-4K (3840x2160 pixels). Yes, there are very old displays at HD (1280x720) and some very high end models at UltraHD-8K (7680x4320 pixels), but I’m thinking that no one asking this question is looking at 8K screens. So pick high or low resolution, and within that resolution, screen size and pixel density are inversely proportional, but the ratio is unchanged. Thus, no one thinks about pixel density. If you’re buying a real 2024 vintage television (and I’m in the market, so I have been thinking about these things), your first consideration is your screen size. Here’s another useful area of consideration: you never worry about pixel density because you’ll never sit close enough to resolve individual pixels if you buy the right television. Your first move is to decide where the television goes and how far away you’ll be viewing from. This will suggest the smallest television that will give you the full resolution experience. Here’s a calculator to help with this. So I have a Livingroom awaiting delivery of a console my wife custom ordered… we’re expecting it early next month. This is going to put the television about 12ft from the couch. The other one goes in the Florida room. We don’t have a couch there yet, but I just completed some construction there (the room contained a hot water heater, washer, and dryer which are all now in my new laundry room) and left a nice hookup place for a new TV on the wall, about 9ft from where the couch goes. By this chart, the Livingroom TV should be 95″ and the Florida room TV should be And sure, opinions vary on resolution distance. Some charts and calculators claim if I’m 12ft away I’ll need about a 120″ television, but this one claims 85″ should be good. That’s might take some negotiations with the wife, but I’m confident I’ll get at least 75″ there. For the Florida room, the calculator recommends 65″ or better. That’ll be easy. There’s also another guideline which has nothing to do with resolution: optimal screen viewing angle. In short, how large should the TV be in your visual field for a good theatrical experience. Both THX and SMPTE have guidelines for this. For my Livingroom, a 75″ screen will give me a 25.6° viewing angle. The recommended SMPTE viewing distance would be 10.2ft for the preferred 30° viewing angle. The maximum THX viewing distance is 11.8ft, for a 26° viewing angle… pretty close. The optimal THX viewing angle is 36°. If I swapped that for an 85″ television, I’m still a bit short at 28.9° for optimal SMPTE viewing recommendations, but past the 26° minimum THX angle of view. In the Florida room, a 65″ television gets me a 29.4° field of view, close to nailing the SMPTE ideal spec, but still short of the THX ideal of 36°. If I bump that up to 75″ — maybe buy two of the same television for both rooms — I’m now at 33.7°, which is in excess of the SMPTE recommendation and not that far from the THX optimal. Again, this is out of concern for the screen size, not the screen resolution. I just happened to have notice awhile back that the recommended viewing distances for Ultra-4K displays are generally very close to the SMPTE/THX viewing distances visual field. This is important because it tells me that an Ultra-8K screen is essentially pointless. If I’m sitting close enough to resolve 8K with my eyes, I’m too close for comfortable viewing. If I sit as a proper THX or SMPTE recommended visual distance, I’m only resolving 4K resolution with my eyes regardless of the resolution of the display.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Is the pixel, for example of the sensor designed for a mid-range smartphone, larger or smaller than the Airy disc that emerges from the lens optics? How big would the 13MP sensor pixel be (sensor format maybe 1/2.3")?
Answer: One of the main reasons that smartphones going back to 2015 or so standardized on the 1/2.6″ or so 12 megapixel sensor was the fact that, with a fast enough lens, they could avoid diffraction limitations. That’s about the time smartphones, with their single main camera and f/1.8 lens or so, started delivering better images, at least at wide angle, than your average point-and-shoot camera, most of which had a 12–20 megapixel sensor but f/3.0-f/3.5 maximum aperture, so maybe 10 megapixels of optical resolution, best-case. So some technical numbers. For a 1/2.3″ sensor at 12 megapixels with an f/1.8 lens, your pixel size is 1.5µm, your maximum circle of confusion is 3.83µm, and your Airy Disc is 2.4µm. So yes, the pixel size is below the size of the Airy Disc.. but you’re not yet diffraction limited. Remember that the Airy Disc isn’t a hard border, but a point spread function. You can see this with two point sources modeled. There can be a partial overlap that still allows the resolution of the individual points of light. The Rayleigh criterion for the diffraction limit to resolution states that two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one is directly over the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other. There was a time when every smartphone camera was diffraction limited. If you check out today’s sensors, they’re delivering 12 megapixel sensors (well, sort of) that offer something like the 2.4µm pixel pitch of a 1″ sensor at 20 megapixels, as in my Sony RX10. The RX10 sensor is large enough that you don’t get diffraction limiting over the f/2.4–f/4.0 range of the lens, and in fact, you can stop down… of course, unless you’re toting an 8x10 view camera, you can get diffraction limiting with any camera if you stop down enough. My “well sort of” from above is because, while we have these large 12 megapixel (and greater) sensor in phones, they’re actually much higher resolution these days. Sony first did this in a sensor they dubbed Quad Bayer, while Samsung’s answer was dubbed tetracell. Either way, it’s simply a sensor that’s got a color matrix that’s at 1/4 the resolution of the sensor itself. There are some good uses for this, and some that are kind of evil. If, for example, you take a normal shot and average together each 800nm quad in this example, you have basically the performance of a 1.6µm sensor, in terms of light sensitivity, noise, etc. and you’re not worried about diffraction. Another option, supported these days, is variable exposure within each group. In fact, I first ran into this not on a phone, but on my old Fujifilm X-F1 pocket camera. Fujifilm championed weird sensor configurations for years, and the 12 megapixel EXR sensor was pretty cool. You could shoot a normal 12 megapixel shot. Or you could shoot a lower noise 6 megapixel shot, with groups of two R, G, and B pixels averaged together. Or you could take a single frame HDR shot at 6 megapixels, in which the two paired pixels used different exposures. This was way back in 2012! So yeah, Quad Bayer sensors can do that too, and without the need to tilt the sensor by 45 degrees. But take the pixels separately, read out the 800nm pixels individually, and you’re getting diffraction even though you boosted the sensor size to 1/2″. You’d need about an f/1.2 lens to resolve that resolution, but no one’s made a phone with an f/1.2 lens… and it wouldn’t help, because the processing of the image is even more evil! So we have this sensor — this is the Samsung version, but the same basic thing — and the (b) image is the 12 megapixel version for a 48 megapixel sensor. So how do you interpolate the 48 megapixel color readout? Well, what I’d do is separate the readout into red, green, and blue planes and run some kind of gradient interpolation. That’s not what happens. Rather, the R, G, and B pixels are shuffled around, spatially, to create a convention Bayer pattern, which is run though the conventional dematrixing engine in your phone’s image processor. So essentially, you’re scrambling pixels around, losing nearly any hint of an actual 48 megapixel image, other than the file size. Yuck. Disclaimer: I actually own a professional camera, the OMDS Olympus OM-1, with a “Quad Bayer” sensor… same arrangement: 80 million photodiodes, 20 million color filters. However, in the Quad Bayer case, you’ll have one microlens for each photodiode, while in this case, you have one microlens for each quad. Thus, the quads can function for cross-type phase detect autofocus, rather than some convoluted variable resolution scheme. But wait… it gets worse. A few years ago, Samsung introduced their 108 megapixel sensor with a nonacell color matrix. Yup, friends and neighbors, that’s nine pixels per color filter. So you can still get a good 12 megapixel output from this, but if you want 108 megapixels, it’s going to resort to that same pixel scrambling thing as before. Yikes! This delivered a 2.4µm area for a 12 megapixel image — that’s the 1″ sensor pixel pitch, albeit at a lower overall resolution — and that’s an improvement. But the same 800nm size as in the tetracell or Quad Bayer sensor. But wait… there’s more! Samsung kept shrinking the pixels. The have versions of this tetracell/nonacell technology down to 650nm pixels. And, clearly mad from all of this shrinking, they kept going. The Samsung HP3 sensor boosts pixel count to 200 megapixels in a 1/1.4″ chip and shrinks pixel size to 560nm! This is so far off the map I can’t even calculate what kind of lens you’d need for that, but clearly, no aperture that fast would be sharp enough anyway. They use a thing Samsung calls a tetra²pixel color array… 16x16 pixels per color filter. Yikes again! And yet, some phones using this will happily scramble up all 200 megapixels and call the result a 200 megapixel image. Back in the 1990s I was, for a brief moment, at the forefront of computer-based digital audio, even travelling to Frieberg, Germany to see a man about one of the first 16-bit audio CODECs for connection to a DSP in a personal computer (sadly a project that was cancelled by new management). I kept following the market, and a funny thing happened: the ADC depth kept increasing: 18-bit, 20-bit, 24-bit. But the analog characteristics didn’t change… still usually around 90dB SNR. And such was born the industry term “marketing bits” versus real bit. That first 24-bit DAC had 16 or maybe 17 audio bit, 7–8 marketing bits. The one-shot HDR idea, yeah, that’s useful, particularly if you want HDR in your video. Computational HDR has been the primary reason smartphones outpaced point-and-shoot cameras on image quality. It also was the first time that phone makers happened to notice that, unlike real cameras, while they had limited sensor capabilities (and still do), but they also had a full blown personal computer to use, and to improve. You can’t fight physics, but you can throw a 10 teraflop AI engine at the problem! But for spatial resolution, we’re looking at 12–16 image megapixels and 96–184 marketing megapixels! The lenses are all good for 12 megapixels, they have been for nearly a decade. On the main camera, anyway. On the others, you’re still getting smaller sensors, either based on costs or the need for a longer telephoto camera. The typical smartphone form factor has allowed up to about a 6mm focal length, and yeah, they’re creeping up, but only so much. Adding too much of a camera doesn’t sell… it still has to be a pocket computer we still comically call “phone.” All those square lens openings house periscope cameras, which are based on the same kind of camera technology Minolta used in their 2002 Dimage X pocket camera. Light is redirected by 90°, allowing the length or width of the phone for the lens, rather than the thickness. But this also means the sensor size itself is determined by camera thickness, and the path through the phone limits maximum aperture, too. G. Love captured at the 35mm equivalent of 373mm with a Panasonic SZ70. In an odd case of everything old being new again, we’ve had Superzoom/Travel Zoom pocket cameras since the 1990s at least. These started with 10x zoom lenses and today get downright crazy. Yeah, you have diffraction out the wazoo… but you can still get a crazy telephoto shot that’s better than, say, trying to extract anything from a 30x crop of your 20 megapixel sensor. Phones beat the point-and-shoot by delivering a better image, but now they’re trying to offer the same kind of flexibility as these old pocket cameras even if that means delivering lower image quality than you might have seen with your pocket camera. Question: How much money has Donald Trump made off of his Gold Trump sneakers?
Answer: It’s impossible to say for sure. But it’s interesting to follow the money. Let’s look at the Trump Sneakers website. There are lots of interesting little disclaimers there. Good to know. So I guess they’re not like the NFTs, eh? So you can’t be exactly sure what you’re buying. Hmm… why didn’t he list this on Kickstarter or Indiegogo‽‽ And I didn’t notice at first, but I’m not sure Trump even knows what he’s selling. Here’s the image of the ugly gold shoe — the “Never Surrender High Top” from the web site, ironically form the guy who’s constantly surrendering and then never, every shutting the hell up about how unfair his pathetic life is… but I digress. It’s a little dress-shoe-like for a sneaker, once you get past the gold paint. Most sneakers have vented areas to keep your feet cool while working out, playing ball, etc. These look like some hot, sweaty pleather, if you ever did wear them. Design-wise, these are pretty odd, given that there are ten rivet-reinforced eyelet rows. I think there are a few shoes out there higher, but they deal with the hiking boot problem: you want the shoe snug, but you also want to get it on and off easily. I’ve never seen a sneaker with 10 rows of eyelets, and those that go way up usually have some means of releasing the ankle. These don’t, other than loosening everything. Hiking boots — about the only real shoes I wear — have hooks on top rows, not eyelets. These look like some hot, sweaty pleather, if you ever did wear them. Now here’s the actual shoes Trump was hawking at Sneaker Con… no eyelet rivets and only nine rows of eyelets. So maybe this one’s closer to reality? But of course, he could deliver something completely different, based on the many web site disclaimers (I kind of fell asleep on page 4…). And yet, here’s Roman Sharf, a Russian immigrant, businessman, and apparent MAGA cultist, who paid $9,000 for the one signed pair Trump auctioned off at Sneaker Con, presumably with he paid of kicks he just bought. Now we’re back to ten eyelets… confusing. Maybe Trump’s showing off the prototype, before some changes were made… hey, how about one more eyelet than anyone else! Regardless, Sharf plans to display them, not wear them. That seems like a good move… they do not seem to be well designed as sneakers. Sorry, I just had to get the engineer crap out first, before I put on my detective hat! I didn’t find that the Trump folks had directly clones any sneaker I could located, but there hundreds out there. But you can see kind of what they were going for, compared to the FUBU (left) and Air Jordan (right). I imagine that Trump’s people could have taken either of these shoes, a list of customizations/changes, and found a Chinese sneaker-cloning operation to make what he wanted. But did they? First, let’s find out more about the companies, which was my real plan here. To find the companies, we want to start with the disclaimer on the bottom of the home page: Unlike most of the small print on Trump web sites, that doesn’t tell you that you’re secretly paying $400 every month for your shoe purchase. But what does it say? This: Trump™ and the associated design are registered trademarks and/or trademarks of CIC Ventures LLC. Trump Sneakers are not designed, manufactured, distributed or sold by Donald J. Trump, The Trump Organization or any of their respective affiliates or principals. 45Footwear, LLC uses the Trump name, image, and likeness under a license agreement which may be terminated or revoked according to its terms. The Trump Sneakers web site claims to be owned by CIC Ventures, which is a company established in 2022. And do they currently hold all the Trump trademarks under license? I suppose they could — they never said it was an exclusive license. But Trump “puts that shit on everything” — his name — and certainly wouldn’t offer exclusive licenses to just anyone, eh? This is likely a very tiny company… can we follow it back to Trump, or is it just some rando that made a deal with Trump? What can we find out about this company? Nicholas Luna was a White House aid to Trump. John B. Marion IV has been one of Trump’s lawyers in the Palm Beach area for some years now. He’s the lawyer who represented Trump when the city of Palm Beach tried to hold Trump to his agreement that Mar-a-Lago was forever a club, not a personal residence. Oh, and by the way, CIC Ventures LLC was also the company behind the Trump “Trading Cards” NFTs. So yeah, CIC Ventures LLC is a Trump company, whether or not his name is on the official corporate documents. Technically, CIC Ventures is licensing the Trump name and paying Trump some unknown royalty per shoe. And of course, the address, not surprisingly, is a Trump property: Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach. It sure looks like they’re trying to make this thing look as if there’s a company just licensing Trump’s name for the collection of very fine Joker products, er, very fine Trump products. But if that is their intention, they’re really, really bad at this. Sure, they want to make it legally true that this Trump products company, CIC Ventures, is not any part of the criminal organization known as The Trump Corporation. After all, they don’t want any of this money to be subject to any specific legal action taken against Trump Corp. So that’s easy. But the claim is that the shoes are manufactured by a company called 45Footwear LLC. So just what is the poorly named “45Footwear LLC” if not some company organized by Trump or Trump’s people at CIC Ventures. So of course, even if you believe the disclaimer, it’s certainly possible that Nick Luna owns, manages, or controls 45Footwear LLC, just as he’s the official point of contact for CIC Ventures, which is obviously a thing Trump put together, even if he’s not the legal owner. And how would we even know? As well, the suggestion, anyway, is that 45Footwear is a manufacturing company. If so, we should be able to find it, and if it’s the USA, there will be some kind of paper trail. My expectation is that, just like every other Trump product so far, these are made of pure Chinesium in some sweat shop in Shenzhen, Gaungzhou, or similar. Or heck, if you have a favorite shoe you’d like to conterfeit or copy with changes, you can contact any number of factories in Putian, send them a shoe, the modifications, and money, and you’ll have 1,000 counterfeits in a month or so. Could I be wrong? Is there actually a US factory? So 45Footwear, LLC, which by its name sure sounds like a shell corporation made up for this project alone, is given as: 45Footwear LLC, 1309 Coffeen Avenue, Suite 1200, Sheridan, WY 82801. Name: Dave Haynie
Question: I was awake until midnight thinking about how they make programming language with programming language, can someone explain this to me?
Answer: Very early on, you didn’t necessarily have a computer language for a computer. But every computer has a native set of instructions. These are implemented in binary strings, called machine language when given to the computer. The pattern of each instruction either directly sets up the various mathematical, memory, and other units in a computer to do a certain function, or it addresses a series of microcode instructions that each do a very simple thing. Humans can’t easily read machine language, though I’ve met a few 6502 programmers who pretty much did have the binary pattens memorized. Your Machine’s First Program So we’ve made a whole new computer… let’s pretend it’s the very first computer, so no others are available to help out here. We’re going to want some way to efficiently program it! And we’re going to write a program to help — the most fundamental programming language — and write it not only in a computer language, but in itself! When a computer is designed, the engineering team creates an instruction set which is at least going to deliver a Turing Complete machine language. What that means is a set of computer instructions that can achieve the same result as any other set of computer instructions. Not necessarily as quickly or efficiently, but able to do any computing task put to it.[1] [2] That set of machine instructions is defined along with a symbolic assembly language that maps 1:1 into the machine instructions. Being symbolic, this is far easier for humans to understand. A program called an assembler does the translation of assembly code into machine code. Your first programming task for that new machine will be to write an assembler to turn your assembly language into machine language that will run on your new hardware. [3] But how to write the assembler in the first place? You’ll do what I used to do back in High School: you’ll write the assembler in assembly language, then hand assemble the code into machine language. I didn’t write a whole assembler… I was writing video games, mostly Exidy Sorcerer BASIC. But when I needed more speed for some operation, I’d code it up as a Z-80 assembly language subroutine. I didn’t actually have an assembler! So for our new machine, I’d start by writing a very, very simple assembler in assembly language. Check it over and then hand assemble it: look up the bit patterns for each instruction you’re using. If you had a machine like the IMSAI shown above, you could toggle the binary patterns for the program in using switches. Lacking any other computer, that’s what we’re going to have to do here… eventually we’ll want to write input and output routines, keyboard routines, display routines, etc. Though of course, very early computers were programmed a line at a time using punched paper cards. In fact, some older languages were specifically designed as line-oriented, and limited to 80 characters per line, to ensure they worked with punched cards. Some older machines had only a tape for long-term storage, like my old Exidy, which I had hook up to a highly modified cassette player from Radio Shack. But for now, let’s ignore those little details. So you work on the assembler by feeding it it’s own assembly code. When the output of your assembler is the same as your hand-assembled code (or better… did you accidently fix a bug?), you’re done! Well, not exactly done, but congratulations, you just bootstrapped an assembler onto our new machine. Once we have the basic assemble able to assemble itself, it’ll be improved, and much faster than if we stuck to hand assembly. If we left out any instruction, we’ll add them. We probably didn’t include symbolic labels or symbolic memory locations… we’ll add those, too. And macros, which are named collections of reusable chunks of code. We’ll need them for more complex programs. Remember what I mentioned about our machine being Turing complete. That’s important because with that, not a terribly complex set of requirements, we know that any program we can run on another computer, we can run on our new machine once translated into this new machine’s language. So we know that assemblers, compilers, and operating systems are possible. The assembler code demonstrates some of the things that you can do on any such machine: With a relatively small set of instructions — some actual designs have used as few as 20 — we can do all of these things and more. A High-Level Language Most programming these days in done in high level languages. These are more abstract languages, easier for human coding, less prone to errors, faster, etc. Not all high level languages are the same in these aspects, and different languages are useful for different things. One kind of high level language implementation is called an interpreter. Think of a set of high level constructs you’d like to do: floating point mathematics, string processing, arrays of numbers or strings, subroutines or functions, conditional loops, etc… obviously you need to know a little about computer programming to know what you’d like to put into your language. An interpreter processes your input source code statement by statement, and calls up machine language subroutines to implement each operation. An interpreted program needs the interpreter in order to run, there’s never any machine-language version of the whole program created. If you’ve ever used a 1970s or 1980s era 8-bit personal computer, such as my old buddy the Commodore 128, the BASIC in that machine runs in an interpreter. The oldest interpreted language is LISP, and modern examples are Python, Ruby, Perl, JavaScript, and PHP. These don’t have to be interpreted, and some languages are sometimes a mix of both interpreted and compiled code. So what’s compiled code. A compiler takes in a high-level language, but rather than run it line by line via subroutines, it translates line by line into assembly language (or something similar). That assembly language is then fed to an assembler, and out pops machine language, ready to run. It will run independently of the compiler, since it’s a machine program, same as any other. Just as we bootstrapped that assembler, we can bootstrap a high-level language for our new machine. We would have to write a compiler, of course. I’ve done this, but then again, I took at semester long course on compiler design. It’s beyond the scope of this article to teach you how a compiler is written. So let’s assume someone knows how to write a compiler. We decide on the high level language we want, probably something like the C Programming Language[4] , something that’s good for writing very low level code, as a replacement for our assembler. Plus, these days, once you have C language, you can open source find C code for hundreds of other languages! We start with a minimal version of our language written in assembly language. We get that producing good code output, then we translate out assembly code into the new high level code, and ensure we get the same results. The output of our compiler won’t directly match the code of our assembly version, but the same code run though both assembly and new high-level compiler should be identical. We have now bootstrapped a high level language onto our new CPU. As with the assembler we wrote, we can work on improving that compiler, and much faster than if we stuck to the assembly version. How We’d Really Do It Today In truth, other than for fun, no one’s going to need to bootstrap their assembler on a new computer. What you’d do, at the very least, is write an assembler for your new machine on another computer, using all the modern tools available. This allows you to get an assembler up and running quickly, using high level coding from the start. In fact, there are plenty of open source assemblers around, which could likely be modified for our new instruction set. So there’s no reason we’d have to write a new one from scratch. This is called a cross assembler. Of course, we can do the same thing with a compiler. There are very good compilers available in open source, and we could add support for our new machine by working on that code rather than starting from scratch. When you compile code on one computer for another, that’s called a cross compiler. This is actually how a great deal of coding is done these days. Anytime you’re working on a small microcomputer system, it’s very common to work in a coding environment on a big computer, with the ability to download and test code on the small computer system. In reality, a compiler that produces assembly code output is basically just a very specialized text processor. It reads in a long string of characters and generates a long string of characters in response. The process may be complex in some cases, but the idea is pretty simple. And it’s easy to understand that’s exactly the basic idea of Alan Turing’s conceptual machine: reading in characters, writing out characters, on an endless strip of tape.

Question: Is it democratic for a candidate who has been found guilty of zero crimes be removed from ballots? Is that democratic? Should more candidates without criminal records be disqualified?
Answer: The qualifications to run for office are entirely different than the issue of crimes. Yes, it’s true that in many states, a felon may not run for local or state office, at least not until their rights are restored. When you commit a crime, are caught, and found guilty by a jury of your peers, you have given up your Constitutional rights. Serve your time, pay your fine, and do anything else you need to do, and your rights are restored. That’s just one of many possible requirements for candidates for office. And in fact, for Federal office, there are not restrictions based on felonies. Presidential candidates have, in the past, been convicted of felonies and, in fact, were able to run for President from prison. Sure, it’s probably not going to make the most effective argument, but it’s legal. As far as other qualifications to run for an office, those are civil judgements and don’t have anything directly to do with crimes. If you’re too young to run for office, you’re disqualified. Is that democratic? If you don’t fulfill local residency requirements, you’re disqualified from office. Is that democratic? Yes. The fact is, those laws were enacted under democratic rule, or established in the Constitution, the basis for our laws, our democracy, our very civilization. So if our democratic civilization said that 12 year olds are too young to run for President, we really ought to respect that. Another restriction against running for office, also based on civil law, is the Disqualification Clause in the 14th Amendment. That says, pretty clearly, that any official, anyone in the military, anyone who’s taken an oath of any kind to the serve, follow, or defend the Constitution as part of their official service to the government, then proceeds to engage in Insurrection or Rebellion, is automatically ineligible to serve in office. Since we’re not in a video game in which this kind of gease or gift is automatically bestowed on the doing, we have courts to make these decisions. Did a person fulfill meaning and intent of the Disqualification Clause? If so, their Disqualification can be officially recognized by a court, by Congress, and probably by other means. They are also free to contest those things, or to go get a different job that doesn’t require them to keep their oath to our country and Constitution.

Question: If a presidential candidate is pardoned by another US president, do they lose their right to run for office in future elections?
Answer: How did that Presidential candidate lose their right to run for office? The only thing that can cause that is being disqualified for 14th Amendment’s Disqualification Clause. And this only applies to people who have previously sworn an oath to the Constitution as an elected or appointed official or in military service and proceeded to become involved in Insurrection or Rebellion, or gave aid and comfort to the country’s enemies, foreign or domestic. So, for example, this would not prevent January 6th Insurrectionists from running for office if they had never service in office or the military. Though it did result in one Insurrectionist currently serving in office being removed in New Mexico! No person shall be a Senator or Representative in Congress, or elector of President and Vice-President, or hold any office, civil or military, under the United States, or under any state, who, having previously taken an oath, as a member of Congress, or as an officer of the United States, or as a member of any State legislature, or as an executive or judicial officer of any State, to support the Constitution of the United States, shall have engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the same, or given aid or comfort to the enemies thereof But Congress may by a vote of two-thirds of each House, remove such disability. The actual criminal code crimes of Treason or Insurrection automatically apply disqualification — which is a civil, not a criminal judgement — along with punishment for the criminal act itself. It’s also possible for the Disqualification Clause to be applied directly by court, and in fact, the Supreme Court is currently exploring whether a State has the right to invoke the 14th Amendment to disqualify a candidate in a Presidential Primary election. Regardless of how it happens, once a person is disqualified, a President can’t remove that disqualification. A pardon doesn’t eliminate a person’s guilt, it simply eliminates the criminal penalty for that crime, and in fact, in accepting the pardon, a person is accepting their guilt and giving up any chance to appeal that guilt. Presidents can’t pardon civil judgements. Under the 14th Amendment, disqualification can only be removed by a 2/3 vote in the House and in the Senate. Note well that a simple felony conviction does not, on its own, prevent a candidate from running for President. Donald Trump could technically be convicted of 91 felonies and he’d still be eligible to run for President or other Federal office, even from prison, as long as the Disqualification Clause had not been invoked against him. Most states have stronger requirements. For example, under the Florida Constitution, a convicted felon may not vote, serve on a jury, or run for any local or State office until their civil rights have been restored. Civil rights may be restored once a convicted individual has completed their sentences, including parole and probation, and paid any fines. That supposed to be automatic except in some severe cases, such as murder or sexual crimes, in which the rights are not restored until reviewed by the Governor’s Clemency Review Board. I would presume that a Presidential pardon would allow a person’s rights to be restored, but especially since the “automatic” part in Florida is imperfect at best, such a person would file their case with the Clemency Review Board.
